Thus, there is no logical consequence of the evolving consciousness being a [primary] causal condition.
Because it is without cause or condition.
"Experience" refers to feeling;
it is called experience because all three types are experienced.
The meaning is that it is experienced.
Feeling has the essential nature of the sap of the flavor of existence.
Therefore, the fool clings to sense objects for the sake of experiencing that [feeling].
Others maintain that not only feeling (*vedanā*) but also the apprehension of objects (*arthopalabdhi*) constitutes experience (*upabhoga*).
But that is not correct, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, which states: "Experience is feeling."
Furthermore, since the apprehension of an object is not distinct from consciousness, it is not appropriate for it to be classified as a mental factor (*caitasika*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the discernment of what has been felt, because its nature consists in the grasping of specific qualities such as pleasure and so forth.
Regarding experience and perception, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are those which set consciousness in motion.
Volition, attention,
and so forth; or alternatively,
experience is feeling (*vedanā*).
Because it experiences its respective objects and because it experiences karma to be felt as pleasure and so forth,
sensation (*vedanā*) is the experience of both objects and karma; thus, it is "enjoyment" (*upabhoga*).

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is "delimitation" because it delimits the signs of objects, which are the causes for conventional usage. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the mental orientations (*ābhoga*) of consciousness toward various internal and external objects.
Thereafter, through the predominance of volition and so forth, consciousness takes up another object;
by the word "and so forth," desire and the rest are included.
Thus it has been explained from what cause, in what manner, and for what purpose the process of activity occurs.

And it reveals the characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśalakṣaṇa*). The characteristic of affliction refers to how the afflictions of defilement (*kleśa*), karma, and birth function to bring about the total suffering of the world. This is explained for the purpose of demonstrating that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) arises from the mere unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpamātra*) of a self (*ātman*) that does not even exist. "Because of concealing, because of planting, because of leading, and because of grasping..."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
This twelvefold dependent origination has been shown with reference to the side of active involvement (*pravṛtti*).
In that regard, the final statement, "the world is afflicted because of concealment," is to be connected with every [member].
By what means is there concealment, or in what way does one suffer through concealment?
To this he says: "Because of the obstruction of seeing things as they truly are by means of ignorance."
For since ignorance consists in non-seeing, when the object of the vision of reality is concealed by it, the vision of reality does not arise.
Thus, because it obstructs the arising of the vision of reality, ignorance is an obstruction to the vision of reality.
Furthermore, the vision of reality is primarily supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*).

Because it arises from that, because it is obtained through that, because it is understood through that, and because of its application to that, it is called "the vision of reality" (*bhūtadarśana*) regarding me. Because it obstructs the vision of reality, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); thus, by way of such concealment, the world is afflicted by ignorance.
The phrase "the world is afflicted by planting" is connected [to the previous statement].
To the question "By what planting? Where? Of what? he says:
"By the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), in consciousness (*vijñāna*), of the latent tendencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*). [36]

In this context, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are bodily, vocal, and mental actions consisting of merit, demerit, and immovability. They are called "formations" because they form a new existence;
the meaning is that they cause [rebirth] to sprout without being willed.
And that alone is expressed by the term "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*), but not everything.
Furthermore, it is through the predominance of ignorance (*avidyā*) that these become capable of projecting renewed existence (*punarbhava*), and not by their mere existence.
Thus, it is said: "Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition."
For it is thus: those [formative forces] produce renewed existence for one in whom knowledge has not arisen, but not for one in whom knowledge has arisen.
Furthermore, a condition is not called "indeterminate" merely by virtue of its predominance over the formative forces.
Even regarding origination by way of a universal condition (*sāmānyapratyaya*):

since ignorance (*avidyā*) is associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*), it is a universal condition for the afflictions that originate from it, and likewise for the volitions (*cetanā*) originating from them;
this also applies to meritorious formations (*puṇyāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) that follow from the aspiration for various forms of existence and enjoyment.
Regarding origination, the ignorance co-arising with them is the general condition (*sāmānyapratyaya*).

For the immovable (*āniñjya*) formations as well—which originate from the view of escape regarding that level—the ignorance co-arising with them is the general condition; thus, the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) has been explained.
Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is intended here.

But it is not the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*). This is because it is impossible for the active consciousness—which has already ceased—to be led to the place of rebirth; because there is no coexistence of the wholesome and the afflicted; and because the latencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*) cannot be established therein by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). What, then, is this so-called "latency of karma"?
The seed of a future birth is its causal state.

For example, a grain of rice, depending upon specific conditions such as soil, ash, and manure, becomes the cause for the production of a sprout through transformation; this is what is called a "seed.
By the phrase "due to establishing," he expresses planting by means of another synonym.

Furthermore, "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) here refers to the initial nourishment of that seed within the continuum of consciousness (*vijñāna-saṃtāna*). For no new seed is ever deposited for any impure (*sāśrava*) phenomenon in the way that it is for a pure (*anāśrava*) one.
Thus, through the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the world is afflicted by the implanting of the seed of renewed existence within consciousness.
Regarding the statement "the world is afflicted by leading," since it is not understood by whom, where, or of what there is leading, he says:
"by consciousness, because of its dispatching [the being] to the place of rebirth.

Leading (*nayanam*) is the bringing of the latent impression (*vāsanā*), which serves as the seed for renewed existence, from the place of death to the place of rebirth by means of consciousness—conditioned by karma—which proceeds as a continuum.
And this being the case, it follows that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are not the condition for the consciousness at rebirth;
rather, it is demonstrated that only the consciousness of the preceding existence is the condition for the formative forces.
For it is not logical that an effect should arise from a cause that has already perished.

For those who have attained the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they are reborn in the very place where they pass away; how then can there be "reaching a place of rebirth" in the formless realms? This should be understood according to the circumstances, as in the case of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Regarding the statement that "the world is afflicted through grasping," by what grasping and of what is it so? To this he says:
Regarding the phrase "the personal existence by means of name-and-form":

from the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) onward, the stages known as the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*—prior to the emergence of the six sense-bases—are "name-and-form" conditioned by consciousness.
Indeed, it is through the specific development of that [consciousness] that it becomes distinguished within the various homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).

And when that [consciousness] has arisen, the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is differentiated according to the distinctions of the homogeneous classes (*nikāyasabhāga*) such as humans, animals, and so forth;
thus it is said that the personal existence is "appropriated" by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Alternatively, one appropriates the entire personal existence until death, because from the very beginning it is established as the causal basis for everything.
Alternatively, although the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is not distinct from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is grasped as such; therefore, he shows it as separate,
just as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subsumed under the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
However, for those who possess feet, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are conditioned by consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Therefore, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) should be understood as being conditioned by consciousness according to what is possible.
[The phrase] "it is afflicted because of filling" means: by what is it filled, or of what?
By means of the six sense bases, the body is comprised within name-and-form;
for in the state of name-and-form, the body is said to be incomplete because of the absence of the sense bases such as the eye.
And in that state, although there is the sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*) and the sense-base of the mind (*mana-āyatana*), even these are not yet complete,
because the support and the supported have not yet reached completion.
However, in the stage of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the support becomes complete through the manifestation of the eye and the other [senses].
The sense-base of the body is also complete,
because of the completeness of those [faculties] based on the eye and so forth.
How is it that they are based on the eye and so forth?

Because its activity is bound to that [the body], the sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*), which is comprised within the six consciousnesses, also becomes complete at that time due to the fulfillment of its basis (*āśraya*) without remainder.

Furthermore, because of the fulfillment of the major and minor limbs, it is said that "the world is afflicted by the six sense-bases" precisely during the stage of the six sense-bases, owing to the fulfillment of the basis.

The phrase "the world is afflicted by the discernment of the three" is thus connected. For when there is a conjunction of the three—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness—there occurs a threefold modification of the sense faculty that is conducive to the arising of feelings such as pleasure; the discernment of that [modification] is contact (*sparśa*).
For this very reason, that which touches upon the similarity to the modification of the sense faculty by way of its own form is called "contact" (*sparśa*).
Alternatively, contact, conditioned by the six sense bases, produces a threefold modification of the sense faculty that is conducive to feelings such as pleasure;
it is [called] "feeling" (*vedanā*) because of its experience.
For feeling (vedanā) is experienced through craving;
the meaning is that it is relished.
Alternatively, it is called "feeling" because of the experience of the fruits of meritorious and other types of karma.
[It is] enjoyment (*pabhoga*). Alternatively, "enjoyment" here refers to the experience of sensation (*vedanā*).
And while pleasure and so forth are being experienced, because of the indulgence in that pleasure and so forth, the world is afflicted by passion, which is established upon it.
Regarding the phrase "from plowing" (*karṣaṇāt*), since it is not understood by whom or of what there is plowing, he says:

"of renewed existence (*punarbhava*) projected by karma through craving. Since renewed existence has been projected by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) through the nourishment of the seed of renewed existence within consciousness, craving acts as water for that [existence]. By means of craving—which, without distinction across all destinies, is a longing for personal existence (*ātmabhāva*)—one moistens renewed existence and employs it for its arising, and thereby establishes its birth; that is "plowing."
Regarding the question of by what means of binding, where, and for whom there might be binding, he himself provides the answer:
"By means of the appropriations (*upādāna*), [consciousness] is bound to the desire-realm and so forth that are conducive to rebirth.

By means of the four appropriations—characterized by attachment and the thirst for sensual pleasure—consciousness, impelled by karma, binds and establishes itself within the desire-realm, views, ascetic rules and observances, and doctrines of self, which are conducive to rebirth.
For consciousness operates there by way of desire and attachment.
Regarding the phrase "because of being directed toward," he himself provides the explanation here in response to the question of others:
"Because it brings about the manifestation [of the fruit] for the sake of granting the maturation of renewed existence to the karma performed by *bhava*."

Just as the basis of consciousness— namely, previously performed karma leading to rebirth— is a representation existing in the state of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that corresponds to its ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*),

so too, having obtained this representation, existence (*bhava*) becomes real and, being projected, turns toward actualization. Thus, because existence is brought to face [actualization], the world is afflicted.
"How are beings afflicted by suffering through birth and through old age and death?
Thus, when there is the production of renewed existence from becoming, one is afflicted right from the beginning at conception, due to the coagulation of consciousness within the semen and blood.
Likewise, it suffers from being turned over between the mother’s stomach and the intestines;
and it also suffers because the mother does not avoid heavy or light food and conduct.
Thus,
the world emerges through a narrow and impure path and is afflicted;
once born, it [suffers].

Furthermore, the world is afflicted as it is being deprived of its two beloveds— youth and life— by old age, characterized by baldness, graying hair, and so forth, and by death, characterized by the dissolution of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It is called "the world" (*jagat*) because it goes (*gacchati*).
The meaning is that one goes from a common interval to a momentary interval.
"Is afflicted" means that one is tormented by birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth, within the three realms through a succession of moments and by way of constant flux.
Others say that "it is afflicted" means "it is not purified.

Thus, this twelve-linked dependent origination, characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa*), arises as the opposite of purification through eleven modes of meaning beginning with "because of concealing. The sequence beginning with ignorance [proceeds] because each preceding factor brings about each succeeding one.
Furthermore, in how many ways is defilement (*saṃkleśa*) shown in brief by means of this twelvefold dependent origination? For this very reason, it is said:
"This is that twelvefold dependent origination."
"Defilement is threefold, twofold, and sevenfold.
The word "and" (ca) signifies both conjunction and alternation.
Affliction itself is defilement; thus, there is the defilement of afflictions.
Likewise, there are the defilements of karma and birth.
For affliction (*kleśa*), when it arises, is a defilement (*saṃkleśa*) because it causes harm to oneself and others.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "One who is lustful and overwhelmed by lust intends even for his own harm."
One intends for the affliction of others;
one also intends for the affliction of both.
Thus [41].

Hatred and delusion are also to be understood [as afflictions] because they are the cause of the arising of both the defilement of karma and the defilement of birth. For it is through the predominance of the afflictions that karma projects birth; since for one who has seen the truths, there is no projection of a future existence even though karma exists, and because the seed of future existence is made actual by the manifestation of the afflictions, and because the connection to rebirth occurs for one with an afflicted mind, these are indeed the causes of the defilement of birth.

Consequently, for an Arhat, there is no connection to rebirth because of the absence of afflicted mind (*kliṣṭacitta*). Furthermore, wholesome and unwholesome karma is a defilement (*saṃkleśa*) because it causes exhaustion of body and mind in the present and because it yields maturation (*vipāka*) in the future. Birth (*janman*) is also a defilement because it is the locus of all calamities; thus, defilement is threefold. It is divided into two types according to the cause: the defilement of afflictions (*kleśasaṃkleśa*) consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*), as all three have the nature of affliction; the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*) consists of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), as both have the nature of karma.

However, this is the distinction: action (*karman*) in its state as intrinsic nature (*svarūpāvastha*) is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), while in its state as a seed (*bījāvastha*) it is existence (*bhava*). This constitutes the affliction of birth (*janmasaṃkleśa*). The remaining members—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are included within birth, because they are comprised within that [affliction].

Defilement is divided into two types by way of cause and fruit: defilement as cause consists of the members whose nature is affliction and karma, while defilement as fruit consists of the remaining members. In this regard, karma and the afflictions constitute "defilement as cause" because they are engaged in producing birth—which has the nature of old age, death, and disadvantage—beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling; and the remaining members, beginning with consciousness, constitute "defilement as fruit" because they are the fruit of karma and the afflictions.

Furthermore, that same dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is a sevenfold defilement. It is a sevenfold cause because it is the cause of perversion (*viparyāsa*), projection (*ākṣepa*), leading (*upanayana*), grasping (*parigraha*), enjoyment (*upabhoga*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and agitation (*udvega*). Among these, the cause of perversion is ignorance (*avidyā*).
For one who has fallen into ignorance is said to be "perverted" because, due to delusion regarding reality, they perceive the impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth.
The cause of projection is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). This is because they establish the seed of birth—consisting of four factors—within consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness is the cause of leading [to rebirth],
because it leads one who has passed away here toward a new birth.
Name-and-form and the six sense bases are the causes of appropriation.
Because of the appropriation of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) by means of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) for one who has been brought [into existence],
the appropriation was previously stated to be by name-and-form alone with reference to the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) and other modes of birth;
now, with reference to the spontaneously born (*upapāduka*), appropriation is stated to be by the six sense bases as well.
Alternatively, it may be intended that by "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), the mere individual existence (*ātmabhāva*) at its initial stage is meant to be included;
however, there is no contradiction here, as [the term] refers both to the incomplete and the complete state.
Contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the causes of experience (*upabhoga*).

Because one experiences the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma through experience accompanied by its causes, craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of attraction. Thus, that fool who has experienced the maturation of karma craves each respective feeling;
and with craving having increased, he grasps at sensual pleasures and so forth through the craving for union with and non-separation from them.

And because of that appropriation (*upādāna*), his previously existing karma pertaining to rebirth—which exists in the state of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—attains a transformation and proceeds toward the giving of its ripened fruit as it was projected; thus, it becomes "existence" (*bhava*). And that [existence] is drawn forth by craving, appropriation, and becoming for the sake of the production of a new birth projected by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); it is brought face-to-face. Thus, craving, appropriation, and becoming are the cause of drawing forth (*ākarṣaṇa-hetu*).

Alternatively, by the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because one is oriented toward the latencies of various karmas corresponding to desire and attachment, craving, grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) constitute the cause of attraction. Birth, aging, and death are the cause of agitation. Thus, through the attraction of birth into this or that class of sentient beings, one experiences the suffering of birth, aging, and death, as well as other sufferings—sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—which have infinite subdivisions. In this context, by the designation of the threefold defilement (*saṃkleśa*), [the relationship between] affliction (*kleśa*), karma, and birth is [established].
The fact that meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the uncommon cause has been shown.

For affliction (*kleśa*) is the common cause of the sprout of birth, like the earth and so forth; whereas karma is the uncommon cause, like the seed of a sprout, because different births arise from different types of karma.

Alternatively, he demonstrates that what are presented here are not the three sections consisting of the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit, but rather karma, affliction, and their fruit.
By means of this twofold designation, he demonstrates that this is merely cause and effect, and that herein no other agent or experiencer is defiled.
Alternatively, here karma and afflictions alone are the cause, because it is observed that the existence or non-existence of birth follows from the existence or non-existence of those two;
therefore, birth is indeed their fruit.
Therefore, it is shown that here there is neither cause nor fruit, but rather in all cases a state consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhika-avasthā*).
Furthermore, by the exposition of the sevenfold causes, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is shown to be twofold:
characterized by projection (*ākṣepa-lakṣaṇa*) and characterized by actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).

Therein, the characteristic of projection (*ākṣepa-lakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination is indicated by seven members, because of the demonstration of that which projects, how it projects, and what is projected. The characteristic of actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) is indicated by five members:
that by which there is the actualization of what has been projected, and how there is the actualization.
And as for that which is "arising" and the "danger" therein—
by what is this projected?
Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Just as one who is deluded regarding reality perceives things erroneously, one performs wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable formative forces.
How is one projected by those formative forces?
Because it nourishes the seeds within consciousness, it establishes the potential for rebirth.
What is projected? The name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling pertaining to future existence, as appropriate. Once thus projected, by what is it brought to completion?
In the manner previously described, depending on the feeling arisen here from what was projected before, there arises craving; and with that craving as a condition, there is grasping.
How is [existence] brought about by that?
Because through that grasping, the karma—which exists in the state of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within consciousness—is made to become existence (*bhava*).
For indeed, various kinds of karmic latencies reside within consciousness.

Because it is permeated by diverse formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and is grasped by a specific appropriation (*upādāna*), that by which there occurs the state of renewed existence (*punarbhava*) therein is called "becoming" (*bhava*) in this context.
What, then, is that "actualization"?
It is the birth in the future of that projected name-and-form and so forth.
When that exists, what is the disadvantage?
If it is argued that "old age and death [result] from the loss of dear youth and life," and therefore the cause of leading [the subject] here is purposeless, we reply:
it is not purposeless.
The intermediate state of death (*maraṇābhava*) is interrupted for the purpose of refuting [the notion of] attainment during the process of entering the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
All these afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) proceed from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*);
the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are the basis because they are the foundation of affliction.
For it has been said: "The unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms."
[The Summary Meaning of Unreal Imagination:

Furthermore, regarding the summary meaning of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), the detailed explanation of its meaning is for the sake of easy comprehension, and the presentation of the summary meaning is for the sake of not forgetting it.
Therefore, two points have been stated here concerning its meaning.
The characteristic of existence is that unreal imagination exists;
the characteristic of non-existence is that duality is not found therein.
Thus,
consciousness arises manifesting as the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of objects, sentient beings, self, and representations. [45]
Thus:
"The characteristic of the summary consists of the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected."
Thus:
having relied upon perception, which is the characteristic of the means for entering into the characteristic of non-existence, non-perception arises.
And so forth.
Regarding the characteristic of differentiation:
"The imagination of the unreal, however, consists of mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms."
Thus [it is said].
Regarding the definition of the synonyms:
therein, the perception of the object is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while the mental factors (*caitasāḥ*) pertain to its specific qualities.
Thus:
one is the consciousness characterized by active engagement (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), and the second is that which pertains to experience (*aupabhogika*).
Thus:
the characteristic of affliction is due to concealing, planting, leading, and grasping.
And so forth [Tib. 41, b].
[2] Having thus explained the ninefold characteristic of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), he now clarifies how emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is to be understood.
What is the connection here?

By this, two things have been asserted: the imagination of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as well as purification preceded by affliction and the determination of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) based upon the realization of phenomena. Therefore, immediately after the explanation of the imagination of the unreal, he explains how emptiness is to be understood. [46] First, its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and then its synonyms (*paryāya*).
Thus is the detailed explanation.
In that regard, the characteristic consists in the nature of the negation of both existence and non-existence,
because it pervades all the various divisions of emptiness.
A synonym (*paryāya*) is another name.
The meaning of a synonym is the ground for the application of that synonym, which conforms to it;
this is so even though [the ultimate reality] is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), because its characteristic is non-differentiated like space.
The distinction [of emptiness] arises from the difference in states regarding the conjunction and disjunction with adventitious secondary afflictions;
furthermore, there is another sixteenfold distinction based on the non-superimposition of persons and phenomena.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the various classifications of emptiness through the means of proof.
The reasoning: What, then, is the reason that emptiness must be understood through these modes?
Because it is the objective support for purification, it should be understood according to its characteristics by those who seek purification.
The meaning of the synonyms is taught through synonyms for the sake of avoiding confusion regarding the various explanations in other sūtras;
it is the meaning of the synonyms because emptiness is determined as the object of purification.
It is taught by way of its divisions for the sake of generating an effort to abandon those defilements, since it is purified once defilement has been removed.
Since one easily understands difference through the realization of the means for establishing difference— even when there is an absence of modification—
it should be understood as being established by the means of establishing difference.
[a) The Characteristic of Emptiness] How is the characteristic to be understood? Since the characteristic was indeed indicated previously, it is therefore asked about first.
"The non-existence of duality and the existence of that non-existence is the characteristic of emptiness"—
this is what should be understood.
"Duality" refers to the grasped object and the grasping subject.
Because it has a nature imagined by unreal imagination or through unreal imagination, it is non-existent in the form of a real entity.
And that which is the existence of this very absence of duality is the definition of emptiness.
Furthermore, in accordance with the *kārikā*, it should be understood here that the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) has been omitted in the expression.
What is this "existence of non-existence" (*abhāvasya bhāva*)?
The nature of non-existence is its existence;
otherwise, there would be the mere existence of duality itself,
because that [dual] state would not be empty.
Therefore, he says:
"Thus, the characteristic of emptiness is elucidated as being the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva*), and not a characteristic consisting of the nature of existence (*bhāva-rūpa*).
Because the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) expresses the negation of existence, this meaning is understood even in the absence of the word "existence"; thus, the word "existence" is implied here.

If it were stated merely that "the absence of duality is the nature of the goddess, characterized by emptiness," then the absence of duality would be understood as a mere independence, like the absence of a rabbit's horn;
it would not be understood as having the nature of *dharmatā*, as is the case with suffering (*duḥkhatā*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is said: "Emptiness is the absence of duality."
And the existence of that non-existence within the imagination of the unreal is called "emptiness.
Because this non-existence is grasped as having the characteristic of existence, it is shown to have the nature of the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Alternatively, since the word "non-existence" (abhāva) is a general term, it is not understood which kind of non-existence is intended here when it is said that "the state of the goddess is emptiness.
To demonstrate absolute non-existence, it is stated:
"The existence of the non-existence of duality within the construction of the unreal."
For it is not logical to describe antecedent absence and destructive absence as being other than their own substrata;
nor is mutual absence logically possible when it has only a single locus, because it necessarily depends upon both [relata].
Therefore, because the characteristic of non-existence is taken up by existence, it is made known that emptiness is indeed the absolute non-existence of the grasped and the grasper.
If emptiness has the nature of non-existence, how can it be called the ultimate truth?
Because it is the object of supreme knowledge, just like impermanence.
But it is not so because of its being a real entity.
Furthermore, this is not of the nature of non-existence;
for that which has the nature of the non-existence of something is neither an entity nor a nature.
How is it not an entity?
Because there is the non-existence of duality;
for if there were existence, [it would not be so].
The absolute non-existence of the absence of duality would not be the nature of unreal conceptualization;
how could it not be non-existent? Because the existence of the absence of duality is the very reality (dharmatā) that is emptiness, which is neither real nor unreal conceptualization.
Should this be said to be other than that, or not other? To this he says:
"This is the characteristic of emptiness," meaning it is the very intrinsic nature of non-existence.

Alternatively, existence itself consists precisely in the negation of non-existence; therefore, it does not have a characteristic that is either distinct from or identical to the construction of the unreal.
If there were separateness, it would not be tenable for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to be other than the phenomena (*dharma*). What, then, is the untenability?
Because its characteristic would be distinct from the phenomenon, the nature of phenomena would become merely another phenomenon, just like any other phenomenon different from it.
Furthermore, one dharma cannot constitute the *dharmatā* (true nature) of another dharma; if another dharma were required for that, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress,
just as in the cases of impermanence and suffering.
Just as impermanence is not other than impermanent things and suffering is not other than what is suffering, so too emptiness is not other than the empty.
If there were identity [between them], there would be no object of purification, nor would there be a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"Purification" (*viśuddhi*) refers to the path, in the sense that "by this one is purified."
Because it is not other than the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, the path would not have [the universal] as its object, just like the specific characteristic of phenomena;
and for that reason, a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is not tenable, because it is not other than the specific characteristic.
Furthermore, since that [universal] would also possess mutual differentiation just like the nature of the individual entities (*dharmasvarūpa*), its status as a universal (*sāmānyatā*) is lost.

Alternatively, because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is non-different from that [universal], there would be an absence of differentiation just as in the case of the nature of an entity; consequently, the universal itself would also be non-existent, because the definition of a universal depends upon differentiation.
Alternatively, the object of focus for the sake of purification is the "object of purification.
An entity's own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when taken as an object of focus, does not bring about purification,
because it would follow that all sentient beings are already purified.
If [emptiness] is inexpressible as being either other or non-other, how is it that the doctrine of the Nirgranthas is not thereby adopted?
For he who explains an existing entity in terms of its identity or difference [from something else] adopts the doctrine of the Nirgranthas.
But since emptiness is not an entity, this fault does not apply.
Thus, this emptiness is characterized by sixteen aspects, characterized by the nature of non-existence, and characterized by non-duality.
It has also been explained as being characterized by freedom from identity and difference.
The definition of emptiness has been stated.
[b) Synonyms for Emptiness] Now the synonyms are stated: suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, and the ultimate truth.
And the *dharmadhātu* is, in brief, a synonym (*paryāya*) for emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
A synonym is that which conveys the state of having different words for a single referent. For a synonym is said to be the expression of the meaning of a single thing through various terms.
In other sūtras, emptiness itself is taught by various designations.

And just as these five synonyms have been stated in the verse according to their primary importance, other synonyms not mentioned here should also be understood from the scriptures (*pravacana*), such as: non-duality, the realm of non-conceptuality, the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), ineffability, non-cessation, the unconditioned, nirvāṇa, and so forth.
He demonstrates how the meaning of these synonyms is to be understood:

"These words are not figurative; rather, they are literal (anvartha). The meaning of the synonyms is according to their sequence, because they correspond respectively to non-alteration, non-perversion, the cessation thereof, the domain of the noble ones, and the cause of the noble dharmas.

Thus, "suchness" (*tathatā*) means "not otherwise"; the meaning is that it is "unchanging. To demonstrate this very point, he says: "because it is eternally such. "Eternally" means at all times; because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it does not undergo transformation—this is the meaning. The "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) means in the sense of being non-erroneous. "Reality" (*bhūta*) means truth, that which is non-perverted. "Limit" (*koṭi*) means the boundary; since there is no other object of knowledge beyond it, it is called the limit of reality, the ultimate limit of what is real.
How is suchness said to be an object of knowledge? Because it is the domain of the wisdom that purifies the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

"In the sense of non-perversion" means in the sense of neither superimposition nor denial. He states the reason for this very point: "because it is the object of perversion. For perversion is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); since it is not an objective support (*ālambana*) for conceptual construction, it is not an object of perversion. Because signs (*nimitta*) have ceased, it is "signless" (*animitta*). Here, "signlessness" is said to be the cessation of signs. To demonstrate this very point, he says: "due to the absence of all signs. Emptiness is called "signless" because it is empty of all signs, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because it is devoid of all signs (*nimitta*), it is signless (*animitta*); it is "signless" precisely because it is signless, since it is the domain of noble gnosis (*āryajñāna*). It is called the "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) because it is the object of the supreme; for the supreme is supramundane gnosis, and its object is the ultimate reality. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "because it is the domain of supreme gnosis. It is the "dharma-sphere" (*dharmadhātu*) because it is the cause of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*);

here, by the word "dharma," the noble dharmas beginning with right view and ending with the knowledge of right liberation are meant, and because it is their cause, it is a "sphere" (*dhātu*). This is its analysis.

As for what was said—that [the term *dhātu*] refers to the noble qualities (*āryadharma*) because they arise from that as their objective support (*ālambana*)—it is stated that this word *dhātu* also applies to the maintenance of form (*rūpa*) by means of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For here, the meaning of *dhātu* is the sense of "cause" (*hetu*); thus, for example, there are the gold-element (*suvarṇadhātu*), the copper-element (*tāmradhātu*), and the silver-element (*rūpyadhātu*). Even though other synonyms are mentioned in other sūtras, they too should be explained according to their own specific meanings by this very same principle.

Since emptiness consists in the absence of the apprehended and the apprehender, one asks [this question] while not conceiving of any differentiation; or else, since it was stated that "differentiation is to be understood immediately after the meaning of the synonyms," one asks immediately after that exposition: "How is the differentiation of emptiness to be understood? For unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is defilement (*saṃkleśa*), and when that is exhausted, purification (*viśuddhi*) is said to occur. Furthermore, at the time of defilement and purification, there is nothing other than emptiness itself that is either defiled or purified. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that it is emptiness alone that is defiled and purified during the periods of defilement and purification, he says: [the following verse].

Regarding its divisions—being both defiled and purified—one asks, "When is it defiled? When is it stainless? because of a lack of understanding; thus [the text] asks, "When is it defiled? When is it purified?
It is both with stains and stainless.

Thus it is said in detail: with respect to the non-transformation and transformation of the basis (*āśraya*), emptiness is established as being "with stains" and "with stains removed. For those ignorant ones whose mental continuums are defiled by the afflictions such as passion and by their adherence to the grasped and the grasper, and for whom emptiness does not manifest due to the faults of non-comprehension and miscomprehension—it is established as "with stains" in relation to them. For those Noble Ones (*ārya*) whose minds are non-erroneous due to the knowledge of reality, and for whom emptiness manifests continuously, stainless like space—it is called "with stains removed" in relation to them. In this way, the defilement and purification of emptiness are to be understood as relative.
That which does not exist by way of an essential nature of its own, because it is luminous by virtue of being the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).
"If there were equality," and so forth;
for indeed, a difference in state does not constitute a transformation.
It has been observed that transformation is permeated by arising and perishing;
therefore, he says:
How is it that they are not impermanent due to having the nature of transformation?
For there is no other transformation from the state of affliction to the state of the purity of emptiness.
But the state of abiding in reality does not undergo any change in its intrinsic nature,
because adventitious impurities have been removed.
For:
Purity is held to be like the purity of the water element, gold, and space.
Therefore, they are not impermanent.

For just as with the elements of water, gold, and space— which do not have that [impurity] as their intrinsic nature— because the nature of impurity is absent, they are pure both when possessed of adventitious impurities and when those adventitious impurities have been removed.
Even without the apprehension of another intrinsic nature,
emptiness likewise becomes defiled by adventitious stains;
though its own nature is unchanging, it becomes purified through their removal.
For one who establishes that very same entity as first having the characteristic of affliction and later having the nature of purity, there is no occurrence of a change in its dharma-nature,
because it is a change in its own-being (svabhāva). But this is not the case where [the affliction] is merely adventitious.
Both of these [are thus];
therefore, it does not touch upon the nature of being subject to transformation.
Regarding the section on the detailed exposition of classifications, since all the classifications of emptiness must be stated, he says: [The sixteenfold emptiness].
"This is another classification," thus it is said that "emptiness is sixteenfold.
It becomes sixteenfold by way of the distinction of entities (*vastu*),
but in the essential nature of the non-existence of duality, there is no distinction.
This sixteenfold emptiness is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
this is to be understood in brief.

The emptiness of the eater, the eating, the body thereof, and the objects upon which it rests—such is the general characteristic of emptiness, because all phenomena have an indivisible nature. Therefore, one demonstrates its multiplicity through the multiplicity of entities; otherwise, that multiplicity could not be demonstrated.

First of all, the eater is to be contemplated for the sake of abandoning attachment and clinging to him; for such attachment and clinging constitute an obstacle to the attainment of Buddhahood and liberation. Immediately after that, his food is to be contemplated; immediately after that, their substratum, the body; and immediately after that, the receptacle-world, which is the support for that body as its substratum, is to be contemplated. This is done because [the world] is beneficial to the eater, for the purpose of turning away from the grasping of "mine-ness. These four types of entities are called the emptiness of entities (*vastu-śūnyatā*).

In this context, the emptiness of the experiencer (*bhoktṛśūnyatā*) is indeed initiated by the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*). These range from the eye up to the mind; because there is no experiencer other than these, and because the engagement in the enjoyment of objects is observed in the eye and the other [senses], people conceive the pride of being an experiencer (*bhoktrabhimāna*) with respect to the eye and the rest. Therefore, the emptiness of the sense bases, such as the eye, is called the emptiness of the experiencer.

The emptiness of food refers to external things; from form (*rūpa*) up to and including mental objects (*dharma*), these are called "food" because they are enjoyed as sense-objects. Therefore, the emptiness of the external sense-bases is called the "emptiness of food.

Because that body—the locus of both the eater and the food—exists in a state of mutual inseparability within the physical frame, its emptiness is called "internal-external emptiness. The basis of support refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), since it is known to be the basis of support for sentient beings everywhere.
Therefore it is said: "Because of its vastness, the emptiness of that is called 'great emptiness' (*mahāśūnyatā*).
The word *vastu* (thing/entity) is connected to each [term].

When this fourfold emptiness of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*) is being attended to by that yogic Bodhisattva through reasoned and thorough mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*), another grasping of signs (*nimittagrāha*) arises.

By means of this knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*), the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth are seen as empty. In that regard, the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) which consists of the adherence to the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)—namely, the thought "this very thing is the aspect of ultimate reality (*paramārthākāra*) just as it was seen by that knowledge of emptiness"—is the [object of negation]. For the sake of eliminating these two types of conceptualization, which are the causes of error regarding the stages of yoga (*yogibhūmi*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*) and emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) are taught respectively, having set aside the aspects of the knowledge itself.
Alternatively, that knowledge is called "emptiness" because its object is emptiness.
Its emptiness of the nature of grasped and grasper is the "emptiness of emptiness.

Furthermore, the internal sense bases and so forth, as they are perceived by that knowledge of emptiness—that which is the ultimate reality here—is the emptiness of this aspect, namely, the "emptiness of the ultimate."
What is the reason? For the ultimate reality is empty of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This other grasping at signs (*nimitta-grāha*) is likewise a source of affliction for the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*).
The intrinsic nature of that object for the sake of which a bodhisattva practices emptiness is superimposed [upon it].
To dismantle that [superimposition], the various forms of emptiness—beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned and culminating in the emptiness of all phenomena—are taught.
And for what purpose does he practice?
It is for the sake of attaining the two kinds of merit;
that is to say, he practices emptiness and cultivates emptiness for the sake of purifying all the Buddha-qualities.
For the two kinds of merit are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The unconditioned consists of the path and nirvāṇa; these two are connected respectively with conditioned emptiness and unconditioned emptiness,
and always for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus, "I must act for the benefit of sentient beings in every way and at all times"—
the emptiness of that [resolve] is absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*),
and it is for the sake of not abandoning *saṃsāra*.

Thus, for the sake of sentient beings, I must not abandon cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). For if cyclic existence were abandoned, one who does not [realize] that would fall from the awakening of a bodhisattva and become established in the awakening of a śrāvaka. Why, then, should emptiness be taught to him? To this he says: "For cyclic existence is without beginning or end."
Seeing emptiness, one does not become weary and abandon cyclic existence for the sake of imperishable virtue;
thus, by me, the roots of merit have been established so that they do not perish even in the nirvana without remainder.

"He does not scatter" is explained as "he does not emit. If this is so, how then is the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu* (the realm of nirvana without remainder) established? It is established because of the absence of a body that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena; for the *dharmakāya*, which consists of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, there is no cessation even in the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu* of the Blessed Buddhas—this is the established tenet (*siddhānta*). Therefore, its emptiness is called the "emptiness of non-scattering" (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).

And for the sake of purifying the lineage (*gotra*), its emptiness is "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "For the lineage is the intrinsic nature.
From where is this [known]? To this he says: "Because it is innate" (*svābhāvikāt*). It is innate.
The meaning is that it is beginningless and not adventitious.

Just as in beginningless saṃsāra some things are sentient and some are insentient, so too here, some of the six sense-bases constitute the Buddha-lineage (*buddhagotra*), while others constitute the lineage of the śrāvakas and so forth.
Furthermore, the lineage is not accidental, because it has been transmitted through a beginningless succession, just like the distinction between the sentient and the insentient.
Others maintain that because all sentient beings possess the lineage (*gotra*) of the Tathāgata, "lineage" here should be understood as suchness (*tathātva*). Furthermore,
for the sake of attaining the primary marks and secondary signs,
the emptiness of the major marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), together with their secondary signs, is called the "emptiness of marks" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore,
the bodhisattva applies himself to the purification of the Buddha-qualities;
this is because the word "applies" is stated at the end [of the verse].
A bodhisattva undertakes [the path] everywhere for the sake of attaining the two-fold auspiciousness;
and it should be understood that a bodhisattva always undertakes it for the welfare of sentient beings.
To the question, "Of which Buddha-qualities? he says:
Regarding the phrase "the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the unique qualities, and so forth":
one practices with the thought, "I must strive for the attainment of all the Buddha-qualities in brief. Therefore, their cultivation is described.
Its emptiness is called the emptiness of all phenomena. How is it manifested?
It is the unimpeded engagement of cognition with respect to the object of knowledge.

In this way, first of all, the systematic presentation of the fourteen [emptinesses], beginning with internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and ending with the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), should be understood. What, then, is the emptiness regarding the consumer (*bhoktṛ*) and so forth? How is it? It is as follows: [57] What is the emptiness of the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the consumer and so forth is established. Furthermore, what is the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the six internal sense-bases. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the internal is established. What is the emptiness of the external (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the six external sense-bases. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the external is established. What is the emptiness of the internal and external (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the six internal sense-bases and the six external sense-bases. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the internal and external is established. What is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the emptiness of all phenomena. Why? Because it is empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of emptiness is established. What is the emptiness of the great (*mahā-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the ten directions. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the great is established. What is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the three realms of existence (*traidhātuka*). Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the conditioned is established. What is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the unconditioned. Why? Because it is empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the unconditioned is established. What is the emptiness of the ultimate (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the limit of past time, the limit of future time, and the interval between them. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the ultimate is established. What is the emptiness of the beginningless and endless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the beginningless and endless cycle of saṃsāra. Why? Because it is empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless is established. What is the emptiness of non-repudiation (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the non-repudiation of all phenomena. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of non-repudiation is established. What is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the nature of all phenomena. Why? Because it is empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of nature is established. What is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within all phenomena whatsoever. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of all phenomena is established. What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within the characteristics of all phenomena. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of emptiness. Why? Because emptiness does not make things empty; rather, things are empty by their own nature. Therefore, emptiness is not an agent, nor is it an object of action. Thus, the emptiness of characteristics is established. What is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)? It is the absence of a self and what belongs to a self within non-existent things. Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, how is that emptiness itself empty? It is because that emptiness is also empty of the intrinsic nature of empt
Therefore,
here,
the emptiness of persons and phenomena is their lack of intrinsic nature.
In that which is the existence of the non-existent entity,
there is another emptiness.
Thus it was said.
Regarding the profound meaning of the *Dela jiskaddu beadpa* and so forth, the absence of intrinsic nature in persons and phenomena is emptiness itself.
The existence of the nature of that which lacks nature is also emptiness itself.
The non-substantiality of both persons and phenomena is the emptiness of non-substantiality.
The existence of the nature of that which is without nature is precisely the emptiness of the very essence of being without nature.
Furthermore, for what purpose are these two kinds of emptiness established? To this he says: "In order to demonstrate the characteristic of emptiness."
For what purpose, then, is emptiness demonstrated? To this he says:
for the sake of avoiding, respectively, the superimposition of a person and phenomena, as well as the denial of that very emptiness.
He establishes the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of avoiding the superimposition (*samāropa*) of persons and phenomena;
and he establishes the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*) for the purpose of avoiding the denial (*apavāda*) of that emptiness.
For if the emptiness of non-existence were not taught, it would follow as a logical consequence that persons and phenomena—which are of an imagined nature—would indeed exist.
If the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence were not taught, then by means of that emptiness, non-existence itself would follow as a consequence.
And because of that non-existence, there would be the existence of the person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*), as before.

In that regard, within the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*) which have the nature of resultant consciousness and are considered by the ignorant to be an enjoyer, there is the non-existence of a person who is an enjoyer, as well as the non-existence of the eyes and so forth whose characteristics are imagined; and the true existence of that non-existence is [the meaning of] "internal" (*adhyātma*).

Internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*): [is the absence] of a self and what belongs to a self within the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*), which consist of the appearances of representations such as form and are considered by the foolish to be objects of enjoyment; it is the non-existence of those imagined characteristics such as form and the actual existence of that non-existence. External emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*): [is the absence] of an enjoyer, a person (*pudgala*), and of the body, as well as of form and so forth imagined by foolish people, within that very body; it is the non-existence of those and the existence of that non-existence. Internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*): [is the absence] of the enjoyer-person and of the body, along with the forms and so forth imagined by foolish people, within the body itself; it is the non-existence of those and the existence of that non-existence.

The non-existence of the world of sentient beings within the container-world (*bhājanaloka*), the non-existence of its imagined intrinsic nature, and the existence of that non-existence constitute the "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of emptiness and the aspect of the ultimate truth, there is respectively the non-existence of the knower—the person who grasps the aspects—and the knowledge of emptiness characterized by the imagined, as well as the non-existence of the aspect of the ultimate truth; and the existence of that non-existence constitutes, in due order, the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*) and the "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārthaśūnyatā*).

Regarding those things for the sake of which a bodhisattva practices—ranging from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) up to all the qualities of a Buddha (*sarvabuddhadharma*) that are to be practiced by a bodhisattva—the non-existence of a person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*) characterized by conceptual construction, as well as the actual existence of that non-existence, are respectively the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
For indeed, there is no person who is the owner or the agent of the conditioned, nor does the conditioned exist by way of the selfhood imagined by foolish people.

In brief, these sixteen emptinesses, which are not shared by the Śrāvakas, have been taught for the sake of counteracting the grasping of all conceptual constructions and for the sake of explaining the intentional meaning of all the Sūtras.
In this regard, the Blessed One has demonstrated the domain of emptiness, the intrinsic nature of emptiness, and the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness.
Therein, the domain of emptiness ranges from the referent of the "enjoyer" and so forth, up to the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, that demonstration is for the purpose of making known that emptiness pervades all phenomena.
Its nature is emptiness, its nature is non-existence, and its nature is the existence of non-existence. [59]

Furthermore, the demonstration of the intrinsic nature of emptiness is for the purpose of making known that which consists in the departure from all views by means of the antidote to superimposition and denial; the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness begins with "for the sake of attaining the auspicious substance" and extends up to "for the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha. This demonstration is again for the purpose of showing that the excellence of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) for oneself and others is what is to be attained through the cultivation of emptiness.
Thus, the classification of emptiness is to be understood as follows: it is afflicted in its state with stains and purified in its stainless state;
and the sixteen types of classifications just mentioned, such as internal emptiness and so forth, are to be known as the means for establishing emptiness.

Since the means of proof for that [distinction] was indicated immediately after the enumeration of the distinctions, he asks immediately after that explanation: "How is the means of proof to be known?
In this regard, what is being proven? It is the state of being defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions and the state of natural purity.
Among these, the proof for the state of being defiled is now undertaken.
If that affliction did not exist, all embodied beings would be liberated;
thus, liberation is the abandonment of affliction, and that abandonment of affliction results from the cultivation of the path.

In this regard, if the emptiness of phenomena were not defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions even when the antidote has not arisen—the word "even" implying as if it had arisen—then, because there would be an absence of defilement, all sentient beings would be liberated without effort; that is, without effort, meaning without the antidote. However, since there is no liberation for living beings without the antidote, one must necessarily admit that in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), suchness (*tathatā*) is defiled by adventitious stains.
Thus, the classification of emptiness as being defiled has been established.
Now, establishing the classification of its purification, he says:
"If that purification did not exist, effort would be fruitless."
Thus [it is said].
This is connected with the word "of embodied beings" (*dehinām*).

Now, even if the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) has arisen, because of the word "also" (*api*), it would not be pure as if it had not arisen; this being the case, the undertaking for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*) would be fruitless.
Because even through the cultivation of counteragents (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), one attains the purification of those stains, and because liberation is impossible for that which is defiled;
yet, it is not maintained that the undertaking for the sake of liberation is fruitless.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the purification of emptiness results from the removal of adventitious secondary afflictions (*āgantukopakleśa*) through the practice of counteragents.
Thus, the differentiation of the purity of emptiness is established.
Here, "affliction" is designated by the inclusion of afflicted phenomena, and "purity" is designated by the inclusion of purified phenomena;
however, affliction or purity is not directly predicated of emptiness itself.
Because the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is dependent upon phenomena themselves;
for this very reason, he said:
"All embodied beings would be liberated."
Thus it is said.
For here, by the term "embodied beings" (*dehinaḥ*), their very appropriation (*upādāna*) is expressed.

Otherwise, if defilement or purification were to belong directly to emptiness itself, what connection would there be with embodied beings, such that it is said that the purification of embodied beings results from the purification of emptiness, and their defilement results from the defilement of emptiness?
And since emptiness is afflicted during the stage of an ordinary person and pure during the stage of an noble one, for this very reason the following is also established:
it is neither afflicted nor non-afflicted, and it is neither pure nor impure. [61]
Thus:
how is it that [the purity] is neither afflicted nor impure, but is indeed pure? Because the purity of both is understood from the context.
Regarding this very point, he cites scripture:
"Because the mind is luminous by its very nature.
And here, it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind that is expressed by the word "mind."
Because the characteristic of defilement belongs to the mind alone,
he demonstrates through a double negation— asking "how could it be neither afflicted nor pure?"— that it is indeed afflicted.

This shows that it is afflicted by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) and not by its own nature (*prakṛti*). There is also scriptural authority for this, stating that "it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Since the twofold distinction has already been stated by way of being defiled and purified, for what purpose is it stated again?
The fourfold division is stated for the purpose of demonstrating its distinction from both the mundane and supramundane paths.
For the mundane path is [contaminated] by the impurities belonging to its own level.

The afflicted [mind] is not [purified] by the lower stages because they are its antidotes; the supramundane path, though impure due to its divisions of weak, medium, and so forth, is pure because it is untainted (anāsrava). Emptiness, however, is not like that.
Having stated that it is not "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*), it is further said to be not "impure" (*aśuddha*) for the sake of distinguishing it from the eye and other [faculties];
for others hold that the eye and so forth are not [so characterized] because they are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
It is afflicted;
and because they possess outflows (*sāsrava*), there is no natural purity for them,
and thus it is impure.
Thus, it is not the case that it is "defiled" either.
It is said: it is not "pure," which is stated for the purpose of distinguishing it from the wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*).
For wholesome contaminated [phenomena], because they are included within cyclic existence, are not afflicted;
and because their maturation is desirable, they are pure.
They are not, however, the true nature (dharmatā).
For that [emptiness] is indeed afflicted and impure in its afflicted state;
thus, this exposition of the differentiation of emptiness in terms of affliction and purification is established.
[The Summary Meaning of Emptiness] The summary meaning of emptiness should be understood in terms of its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and its formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*).

Among these, in terms of its characteristic, it is both the characteristic of non-existence and the characteristic of existence. It is the characteristic of non-existence because of the statement: "For there is the non-existence of duality."
Because of the statement, "And the existence of non-existence," it is characterized as existence;
and because of the statement, "By way of being characterized as existence, it is neither existence nor non-existence."
[It is] from the perspective of being free from existence and non-existence,
and from the perspective of being free from identity and difference;
and this is the characteristic of emptiness.

Therefore, because of the statement that "the unreal imagination does not have the characteristic of being either different or identical," such is the summary of the meaning from the perspective of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). How is the summary of the meaning to be understood from the perspective of its formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*)? It should be understood from the perspective of its formal establishment by way of the establishment of synonyms (*paryāya*) and so forth.
The meaning is: its synonyms, their referents, their divisions, and their means of proof.

Having thus pointed out these four aspects beginning with the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of affliction and purification (*saṃkleśavyavadānalakṣaṇa*) are presented as the antidotes to the four types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Furthermore, this is the characteristic of knowledge (*vidyālakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of those who harbor uncertainty regarding [these matters].
The first chapter on characteristics from the treatise *Madhyāntavibhāga* has been concluded; this is the commentary on the first [chapter].

Following the explanation of the characteristics, there is now the occasion for explaining the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*). Therefore, as will be stated subsequently, it says: "Consequently, they are established as the obscurations."
Pervasive, dual, and exceeding;
Equanimity, taking up, and abandoning.
This is taught as the obscuration of both.
The two types of obscurations are the obscurations of those belonging to the lineage of bodhisattvas and the obscurations of those belonging to the lineages of śrāvakas and so forth.
This chapter is composed in order to demonstrate that obscurations are diverse, because the objects to be obscured are diverse.
Regarding "pervasive" (*vyāpin*): for those belonging to the lineage of bodhisattvas, it refers to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is called "pervasive" because it pervades;
that is, because it obscures all objects of knowledge.
The ultimate goal for oneself and the goals of others.
Because it pervades the obscurations of the bodhisattvas—which are designated as the two types of obscuration, namely the afflictive and the cognitive—it is called "pervasive."
Affliction itself is an obscuration because it is an obscuration.
While it is only the phenomena of affliction (*kleśa*) that are similar [to the aforementioned],
here even the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are to be understood by the term "affliction."

The nine types of characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*) should be known as follows: envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are not included [among the primary afflictions], because those two are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Because it obscures the knowable, it is the obscuration of the knowable;
since it thoroughly obscures the knowable by that [obscuration], it does not become an object of knowledge.
Furthermore, that which is to be known is not itself the obscuration to primordial wisdom;
rather, it is the obstacle that hinders the arising of the primordial wisdom that knows it.
The words regarding the objects of knowledge and the obscurations are like a jar [filled with] molasses.
Furthermore, that is non-afflicted ignorance.
Since those belonging to the lineage of bodhisattvas must fully accomplish all the various accumulations of merit and wisdom in order to attain the supreme benefit for themselves and others—
that is, to attain Buddhahood—
and since both of these [accumulations] are obstructed [by the aforementioned faults], therefore:
Thus, the obscurations of those belonging to the lineage of bodhisattvas are established.
Although pervasiveness has all things as its object, "knowing everything" refers to all aspects.
How is it that one comes to know them as being pervaded by all [aspects]? It is called an obscuration to pervasive knowledge because it obstructs knowing everything.
It is established by the teaching of the cause.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that the term "pervasive" does not have the sense of being coarse, it says:
"Because it is at the limits."
Regarding the statement "the afflictive obscurations of those belonging to the class of the three vehicles,
such as the śrāvakas," they are called "two" because they are designated as obscurations by virtue of obscuring only one's own welfare, and not because they are pervasive.
Do Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack non-afflicted ignorance?
Although they do indeed possess the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
that is not their [specific] obscuration.
This is for the sake of attaining the enlightenment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in that very place.
Furthermore, would not the knowledge of Śrāvakas and others regarding the objects of the truths, such as the suffering of sentient beings,
also be an obstacle?
Therefore, it follows that they too possess both types of obscurations.
