Therefore, one should not say that only the śrāvakas and others possess the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This is because ignorance is both an affliction and the discordant factor (*vipakṣa*) to knowledge.
Because it serves as the root of cyclic existence, the afflictive obscuration alone is classified [as such];
the cognitive obscuration is not,
just as in the case of doubt.
For example, the doubt and afflictions regarding the objects such as the truth of suffering are not [doubt and afflictions] regarding other objects.
In other lands, however, it is indeed considered a dream.
It is neither affliction nor doubt.
Ignorance and the afflictions are defined as the lack of knowledge regarding objects such as the truth of suffering; they do not pertain to other objects.
In other realms, it is not even recognized as such;
it is neither ignorance nor an affliction.
Because it obstructs the entry of wisdom that knows the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, it is called the "obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is not as if afflictions, karma, and birth arise from ignorance in the same manner [as the obscuration of the knowable].
If one asks whether the obscurations of bodhisattvas are not purified in such a way,
it is not so;
for bodhisattvas are distinguished by their accumulation of merit.
The obscurations of the aggregates are the cognitive obscurations; therefore,
without having applied oneself to the five bases of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*),
even the Noble Ones cannot attain omniscience.
Because it does not change,
it is said that one exerts effort therein either to refute the arguments of others and to uphold them,
or for the sake of knowing it by oneself.

Even though the actual substance of [afflictions] such as excessive desire is slight, they arise extensively and continuously in those belonging to the lineage of bodhisattvas, as well as in those belonging to the lineages of śrāvakas and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the obscurations of the activities such as desire and so forth":
even if one encounters objects that are disagreeable, whatever intense and continuous arising of desire and so forth occurs is the activity of desire and so forth.
It is equal because it is an obscuration for those of the bodhisattva lineage as well as for those of the śrāvaka lineage and so forth;
it is equal because there is no distinction between these two types.
Regarding what is called "the obscuration of those who practice the sensory objects":
when afflictions arise in a manner similar to pure objects, yet the continuum is not [truly] so,
these are those who practice the sensory objects.
Regarding the obscuration of taking up and abandoning cyclic existence:
through the power of compassion, bodhisattvas take up cyclic existence; and through the power of wisdom, they see the faults of cyclic existence exactly as they are.
Because it is empty, they are free from afflictions; thus, viewing sentient beings with such regard, they fully undertake birth.
It abides in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa,
because it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Its obscurations are twofold: being oppressed by afflictions and thus taking up cyclic existence, and, due to not seeing faults as they truly are, abandoning cyclic existence out of a lack of compassion.
Because ignorance acts as an obstacle to both compassion and wisdom within sentient beings, it is here called an "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa*:
"His intention [is such that] even nirvāṇa remains... [53a] [68]
Furthermore,
it is taught that even remaining engaged in cyclic existence is like this;
this is the non-abiding nirvāṇa of the bodhisattvas.
Because they turn their backs on nirvāṇa through the application of thought,
they wander in saṃsāra like beings who lack the spiritual lineage (agotraka).
Because they have turned their backs on the power of saṃsāra,
through both the intention and the application of having gone toward nirvāṇa,
they completely relinquish saṃsāra.
It is just as it is for those of the class of beings such as the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, taking up cyclic existence and abandoning it are obscurations to the non-abiding nirvāṇa of bodhisattvas,
because they cause one to fall into one-sided extremes regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

When Bodhisattvas become Tathāgatas, because they do not abide in cyclic existence due to having abandoned the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, and yet the *dharmakāya* continues without interruption even in the *nirvāṇa* without remainder of the aggregates,
they do not enter a *nirvāṇa* like that of the Śrāvakas and others.
The bodhisattvas have no attachment to either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Here,

these five types of obscurations are enumerated respectively because they act as obstacles to the paths of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and so forth, as well as to the application and fruition of those two, and to the nirvāṇa that is non-abiding.
Regarding the statement "the fire of the hearth is known as the 'one who is satisfied,'" it is exactly as it appears.
In the beginning and at the end, these are the obscurations of the bodhisattva lineage.
Furthermore, there are the obscurations of those belonging to the class of śrāvakas and so forth.
The other two are obscurations of both.

The cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is explained as the obscuration of the bodhisattvas; furthermore, it should be understood as non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). The Second Chapter: The Investigation of Obscurations.

[2] Regarding the obscuration that hinders application and the non-attainment of union, one should not distinguish between the various types of afflictive obscurations among the two [obscurations], nor their intrinsic nature, nor what constitutes their obstacle.
Therefore, the characteristics of the afflictions are ninefold.
It is said that "knowledge" (jñāna) should be connected with "obscuration" (āvaraṇa).
The characteristic of affliction is the intrinsic nature of affliction.
What are those nine aspects?
Therefore,
[it says] "the confusions."
Thus it was said: "It is known."
Because they are bound to all varieties of suffering, they are called "those who are bound" (saṃyojana).
Furthermore, the various types of suffering are comprised within the realms of desire,
form, and formlessness;
they consist of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and [the all-pervasive suffering of conditioned existence].
The suffering of change should be applied accordingly to the three realms.
Furthermore, that [craving] is the subsequent bond of attachment; it is the further development of the bond of passion.
This is the sixth section on the internal cavities.
One cannot endure the excellence of others' wealth and status.
All forms of attachment are included therein;
these three are comprised within the realm of desire.
The "confusion that follows after" refers to existence within the three realms.
Desire, hatred, ignorance, views, clinging to the supreme, and doubt— these fetters constitute the three realms.
The views of the transitory collection, the views of extremes,
and wrong views constitute the universal fetter of views.
Adherence to views, ethical discipline, and ascetic observances as supreme is the fetter of adherence to supreme views.
Doubt is a state of mental vacillation regarding the truths and the various objects of refuge.
[71] And that [is] the accomplishment of men, through the divisions of pride and so forth.

The vision of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which consists in the discernment of the absence of self and what belongs to a self, as well as the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in phenomena as imagined by foolish people— that is the full comprehension of the view of a self-identity;
its mental association constitutes an obscuration.
Because its arising depends upon that [ignorance], one might ask: "When, then, and how? To this he says:

"At the time of clear realization (abhisamaya), because of the non-abandonment of that [ignorance] due to the manifestation of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna), both with intervals and without intervals."
At the time of the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), during the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīyāvasthā*),
there is the "interrupted" (*vyantara*) [attainment], which is separated from the antidote (*pratipakṣa*),
and the "uninterrupted" (*avyantara*), which is not separated from the antidote.
And that [path] should be understood as being both intense and mild with respect to the counteragent;
as long as the conceit "I am" continues to manifest, even if it is at intervals or sporadic, there is no abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the view of a self-identity:
Because it functions through the conceit "I am" by means of power,
the fetter of ignorance is connected as an obscuration to the full comprehension of the basis for the view of a self-identity.
The basis for the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) consists of the five aggregates of clinging,
because it arises with them as its object,
as stated in the Sūtra.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, while perceiving, perceive a self as "self," and while adhering, adhere to it, they do so only by taking up these very five aggregates of clinging.
What, then, is that thorough knowledge?

It is the vision of the self and what belongs to the self within the aggregates, and the vision of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of phenomena as imagined by foolish people—whether it be the vision of them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, or as arising and so forth; that vision is their thorough knowledge.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason:
"Because of the lack of full comprehension of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).

For, since there is an absence of full comprehension regarding the aggregates that are obscured by modes such as permanence through ignorance (*avidyā*), ignorance is an obscuration to the full comprehension of the aggregates; likewise, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) is an obscuration to the full comprehension of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*). This is how it continues.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) consists of three views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Among these, the view of a self-identity is the vision that perceives the five aggregates of clinging as "self" or "belonging to a self.
The view of extremes is the vision of either eternalism or nihilism regarding that very same entity imagined to be a self.
That view by which one denies the cause, the fruit, the activity, or an existing entity, or falsely conceptualizes them, is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Furthermore,
how is it that the thorough knowledge of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*)— by way of its aspects such as peace (*śānta*) and so forth— is an obscuration to that [wrong view]?

For this very reason, he said: "Because of fear of that [cessation] due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and because of its denial through false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
In this context, by means of the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, one fears cessation, thinking, "I shall not exist there."
Furthermore, by means of wrong view, one denies [the truth], saying, "There is no cessation at all.
In that regard, by means of the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes, one ultimately fails to fully comprehend [reality] in terms of its excellence and its transcendence.
Through wrong view, one does not fully understand cessation.
Thus, the fetter of views is an obscuration to the full understanding of cessation.
The fetter of grasping is an obscuration to the full understanding of the Truth of the Path.
Among these, the fetter of adherence consists of the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Therein, the adherence to views is the viewing of a view, or of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) which are the basis for views, as being superior and so forth. The adherence to rules and observances is the viewing of morality, or of ascetic observance, or of both, or of the five aggregates of clinging which are their basis, as being purification, liberation, or the means of deliverance; that viewing is the adherence to rules and observances.
Furthermore, the full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the path is by way of aspects such as its leading to liberation (*nairyāṇika*).
But how is it that the fetter of clinging (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) is an obscuration to the full comprehension of the path? To this he says:
"Because of the adherence to purity through another aspect" means:

because of the adherence to purity through mere rules and observances (*śīla-vrata*), or through dwelling in sensual pleasure (*kāma-sukhālaya*), or through difficult austerities (*duṣkara-caryā*), or through the knowledge of the Sāṃkhya and other systems.
However, by the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), one adheres as supreme precisely that [view] through which one believes purity is attained.

Thus, by means of the fetter of adherence (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), one avoids the Path, while adhering to purity through another mode. It follows that the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is an obscuration regarding the thorough knowledge of the Three Jewels. To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of faith in those qualities":

the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is indecision regarding the [Four] Truths and the [Three] Jewels. Full comprehension of the Jewel of the Buddha consists in his being the ultimate refuge for all qualities and defects that have been either perfected or eliminated.

Regarding the Jewel of the Dharma, thorough knowledge consists in its being that which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra, its being the nature of the absolute separation from all suffering together with its causes, and its being the means for realizing that [separation]. [75]

Those seeking liberation must first cause their minds to feel revulsion toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); thereafter, they must maintain equanimity toward all things. Next, because it is the root of all misfortune, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) must be fully understood; immediately following that, its objective basis must be fully understood as being of the nature of suffering and its origin. Thereafter, its cessation must be known, and immediately after that, the path leading to it must be known. Then, through the vision of the truths and the realization of the qualities of the Three Jewels, one attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*). By the power of seeing the truths alone, one comes to perceive the faults in gain and honor and the virtues in renunciation. Thus, by means of this sequence of factors that constitute the objects of obscuration, the sequence of those obscurations itself should be understood.

[Objection: Since everything can potentially be an obscuration in every respect, is it not improper to specify obscurations according to their respective objects? [Response: No object-restriction is being made here; rather, this specification is made on the basis of proximity and predominance. Is this alone the obscuration? This is the general [obscuration] for those such as the *bodhisattvavṛttaka* and others. But what is the specific obscuration for Bodhisattvas? It is that which is other than the ten non-virtues and so forth. Since it is not known what the "virtues" (*śubha*) and so forth are, he says: "Non-application, [application] to an improper object, and that which is practiced incorrectly."

Such are the obscurations and so forth. Furthermore, the "pure" [factors] and so on refer to ten topics beginning with purity, enlightenment, and formal undertaking. Among these, purity consists of all roots of virtue that serve as the causes of enlightenment, while enlightenment is their fruit.

In that regard, since the wholesome has been indicated in general but is not yet understood in terms of its specific divisions and intrinsic nature, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of explaining it:
undertaking, intelligence, non-delusion, non-obstruction,
lack of fear, and lack of stinginess.

"This is auspicious" means that awakening (*bodhi*) is not understood by its very nature through mere words; therefore, he shows that this is "mastery" (*vibhutva*). Some maintain that because the obscurations regarding the auspicious and awakening are explained here with independence—just as they are for the undertaking [of the precepts] and so forth—it is independence itself that is understood here, rather than the relationship between a brief statement (*uddeśa*) and its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).
For the obscuration to arising is established in relation to the wholesome;

and that is common to the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, because that wholesome is something to be produced. However, the obscuration to [the wholesome such as] faith and so forth is the obscuration to undertaking and so forth, because there is a distinction in meaning between "arising" and "undertaking" with respect to those acts of undertaking and the like.
Since awakening (*bodhi*) is likewise unshakable and must be attained, the obscuration to its persistence and the obscuration to its attainment are established for it.
Therefore, there is no consequence here of [awakening] being independent.
Furthermore, their sequence is as follows: in brief, having brought the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) to completion without remainder, awakening is to be attained.
Furthermore, in detail, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) must first of all be generated,
because it is the foundation for the accomplishment of the welfare of both oneself and others.
Following that generation of the thought, there is the practice of generosity and the other perfections in accordance with that resolve, by means of which one obtains the designation "Bodhisattva."

Then, having practiced for incalculable eons and accumulated the equipment of merit and wisdom, one must generate the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is non-delusive in nature as the antidote to the delusions regarding persons and phenomena, for the sake of purifying the underlying intention (*āśaya*).
Following that, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)— which arises from the removal of obscurations— must be brought to its culmination for the sake of attaining a superior degree of purity.
Then, through the application of transcending the stage of the śrāvakas and others, all these mundane and supramundane roots of virtue accumulated in that manner should be dedicated toward awakening.
And having reached that state, because of his aspiration for great awakening, he does not tremble at the profound and vast teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Then, endowed with extensive learning and spiritual practice, he teaches the sublime Dharma for the sake of maturing sentient beings. Thereafter, when those to be trained have been matured, he attains mastery and Buddhahood for the sake of their liberation.
For here, thirty obscurations have been mentioned, as well as the ten objects such as the wholesome that are to be obscured; therefore, he asks:
To the question of which [of the] auspicious factors (*śubha*) and so forth have how many obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) that are to be known, he says:
"Indeed, three obscurations for each of these are to be known."

In that regard, there are three obstructions: lack of application and lack of undertaking. What is the obstruction here? It is that affliction by which one does not apply oneself, whether it be negligence or laziness.
In whichever particular state—whether it be neutral (*avyākṛta*) or afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), yet accompanied by the seeds of the afflictions—one does not apply [the mind];
or one does not apply it continuously due to a sense of reverence;
such non-application is called "non-engagement" because of its brevity, but not because of a total absence of engagement.
Because an obscuration is impossible in that case.
Regarding the application to a non-abode (*anāyatana*): the Abode (*āyatana*) is that teaching which is the gateway for the arising of awakening and of the roots of virtue that bring about awakening;
other than that is the non-abode.
In that regard, "application" refers to application in an improper sphere (*anāyatana*), which is external to these [objects].
What is the obscuration therein? It is that ignorance or affliction of views by which one applies oneself to an improper sphere.
And that very application is the obscuration.
"Improper application" (*ayoniśah prayoga*) means that for which there is a source (*yoni*), namely a method (*upāya*); an application other than that method is improper application.
And it is recited right here on this very seat:
namely, "Indeed,
the non-cultivation of passion and hatred is not the means for the cessation of passion."
Regarding the statement "the cultivation of the foul is for one whose conduct is characterized by aversion," here too,
improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) or the preparatory application (*prayoga*) caused by it constitutes an obscuration.
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is the realization of the three as they truly are;
that "the non-arising of the wholesome" is precisely what was stated previously.
How is non-arising an obscuration?
If the wholesome does not exist, awakening would not occur;
therefore, the non-arising of the wholesome is an obscuration to awakening.
Whatever affliction or specific state is an obstruction to the arising of the wholesome is also an obstruction to awakening;
for whatever is necessarily an obstruction to the equipment for a certain [result] is also an obstruction to that result itself.
This also applies to its fruit.
Non-cultivation (*abhāvanā*) is the failure to attend to (*amanasīkaraṇa*) even that which has arisen;
it means non-neglect (*anupekṣā*).
The affliction, such as stinginess and so forth, by which one does not repeatedly bring to mind even that which is wholesome when it has arisen in a particular state— this is the obscuration here.
And "incompleteness of the accumulations" means that the accumulation of merit and wisdom by which awakening is attained is not yet full;
as before, this refers either to the afflictions of the [present] state or to the deficiency in the accumulations.

Another, however, says: although the statement is made without distinction, it is specifically the non-arising of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that is intended here as the obscuration, and not that of others.
Even for those [hindrances] that have already arisen, the failure to attend to them while one is attending [to other things], as well as the lack of accumulated equipment, is called an obscuration.

"Taking up" refers to the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); thus, the accumulations of merit and wisdom in their entirety, their fruit which is Buddhahood, and all sentient beings are unsurpassed.

The generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is the formal undertaking (*samādāna*), which consists of that which is to be accepted and grasped with the intention of establishing [all beings] in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*). Furthermore, it is the volition (*cetanā*) accompanied by aspiration (*chanda*), characterized by the intent to accomplish the welfare of oneself and others, regarding those obstacles [to such accomplishment].
The lack of the lineage (*gotra*) in three ways: being without a lineage (*agotraka*), or belonging to the lineage of the *śrāvakas* and so forth;

the lack of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), which means that even when the lineage exists, there is no association with those who would encourage one to generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), or by relying on whom awakening is turned away from, or by whom one does not increase in wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
Even when in the company of spiritual friends, there is weariness of mind due to fear of the suffering of saṃsāra; and for beings who have fallen into wrong paths,
there is the intention to attain parinirvāṇa quickly because of a mind of agitation.
What is the obscuration here?
It is the deficiency of causes, the deficiency of conditions, lack of compassion toward sentient beings, or laziness.
For one who lacks compassion becomes weary of working for the sake of sentient beings, as does one who is lazy.
Wisdom is the state of being a bodhisattva; thus, by its very nature, it consists in having sharp faculties compared to the lineages of the śrāvakas and others.
Because he alone possesses the authority to investigate all objects of knowledge in every respect,
and because of his resolute faith in the profound and vast Dharma, it is only the wise Bodhisattva who is so called, and no other.
The state of being a Bodhisattva consists in non-perversion and the practice of reaching the further shore for the sake of others.
Because of the deficiency in practice regarding the perfections and so forth, one does not engage in them;
for a bodhisattva devoid of practice should be understood as such.
"In a crowd of fools" means, in other words, among people who lack discernment.
For a base person does not understand even that which is expressed as practice, though it is comparable to a bodhisattva;
being of corrupt intellect and hostile, they are those who hate the bodhisattva.
For, because they are intent upon finding faults, they do not see the actual virtues of the bodhisattva;
either by perceiving non-existent defects or through a mind fierce with resentment, they conceal his actual virtues and, having superimposed them, they proclaim non-existent defects.
What is the obscuration here?
It is ignorance and aversion, which are the opposites of the perfection of generosity and the other perfections. Non-delusion is the third [perfection].
Error arises from superimposition and negation;
its antidote, however, is the path of vision, which is the absence of error.
Some say that it is the nourishment of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the adherence to the grasped and the grasper, [arising] from perversion and functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Others say it is the nourishment of the seeds residing in the *ālayavijñāna* of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by vision, as well as of the non-afflicted ignorance obstructing the realization of the all-pervading *dharmadhātu*.
Others maintain that the conceptualization of a self and so forth, which is the absence of light and so on, is indeed a misconception (*viparyāsa*);
furthermore, it is the state where any one of the three obscurations, such as the afflictions (*kleśa*), remains.

Among these, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to those afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*) that manifest intensely and for a long duration; it is an obscuration because it provides no opportunity for the application of their antidotes and thus prevents non-delusion (*abhrānti*).
The obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) refers to actions such as the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) which lead to rebirth in the miserable states;
the obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) refers to those miserable states themselves. For one born therein, there is no portion for the arising of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Among these—afflictions, karma, and birth—if even one remains, it constitutes an obstruction, though not necessarily all of them together.

And there is the state of being unripened regarding the thorough knowledge that ripens liberation. Some say this refers to the unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) of the wisdom that brings about liberation, because the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) have not yet been attained.

Others, however, say: here, non-conceptual wisdom is that which ripens liberation, and the preparatory stage for it is the second [type]. The "unripened state" of these two is, respectively, the unserviceability for the realization of reality and the unserviceability for becoming its proximate cause, due to the incompleteness of the accumulations.

What is the obscuration here? It is the nourished latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing; the remaining presence of any one of the obscurations of the afflictions and so forth; the ignorance that acts as an impediment to the maturation of wisdom; and the incompleteness of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*).

"The abandonment of obscuration" (*āvaraṇaprahāṇa*) means that by this [path], obscuration is abandoned. "Non-obscuration" (*anāvaraṇa*) refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is the antidote to obscuration.
Its three [aspects] are: innate dysfunctions (*sahajadauṣṭhulya*), existence... [81]... [and so forth].
It is not the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of afflictions that are not to be abandoned;

nor is it the nourished seed residing in the *ālayavijñāna* of the non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) which obstructs the penetration of the ultimate meaning of the *dharmadhātu* and so forth, such as the innate views of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the like.
Laziness (*kausīdya*) is the mind’s lack of exertion due to a distinct indolence born of delusion (*moha*).
For negligence (*pramāda*) consists in attachment to sense objects and a lack of heedfulness toward the wholesome.
Some say that here negligence is the relishing of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In that state, due to inner corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) and laziness (*kausīdya*), one does not cultivate the path.
One does not protect the mind from negligence and unwholesome states.
What is the obstruction here?
It is precisely these three.

There are three obstructions to dedication (*pariṇati*), by which one directs the mind toward something else. In this context, dedication is the determination of arisen roots of virtue toward Buddhahood alone by means of the resolve for enlightenment.
It has three obstructions.

Which are the three by which others, like the Buddhas, direct their minds toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) or toward the enlightenment of the *śrāvakas* and so forth, rather than toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
They are: attachment to existence (*bhava*), attachment to enjoyments (*bhoga*), and a dejected mind (*līnacittatā*). Existence refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
"Enjoyments" (*bhoga*) refers to objects such as forms and so forth, because they are enjoyed.
"Attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*) to these two is clinging.
"Constricted state of mind" (*līnacittatā*) is a lack of magnanimity of mind.
"Where is Buddhahood, and where are those like me?"—this is self-disparagement (*ātmany asaṃbhāvanā*).
Furthermore, due to attachment to existence (*bhava*) and attachment to enjoyments (*bhoga*), one directs the mind toward a happy rebirth (*sugati*);
due to a depressed mind (*līnacittatā*), one directs it toward the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and so forth.
What is the obscuration here?
It is craving for existence and enjoyments, laziness, and lack of compassion. There are three [obscurations] regarding fearlessness.
What is this fearlessness?
It is confidence and lack of timidity regarding emptiness and the profound and sublime qualities of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
[82] Asaṃbhā...

"Delusion regarding persons" refers to the misconception and false speech concerning a person who proclaims the Mahāyāna system, as well as a lack of conviction in their qualities such as ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

"Lack of faith in the Dharma" refers to a lack of conviction that the teachings which set forth the profound and vast method are the word of the Buddha and possess an unerring meaning. Furthermore, it is the investigation according to the literal expression; one explains the meaning of terms such as "unproduced," "unceasing," and "quiescent" merely according to the literal words, without understanding the reality of the intended meaning. Therefore, there is a lack of conviction regarding the meaning of being unproduced and so forth.
What is the obscuration here?

It is doubt, which is the adversary of wisdom and meditative concentration; and ignorance, which is the adversary of investigating the intended meaning. Regarding non-avarice, there are three [obscuring factors].
He teaches the Dharma without stinginess, either for the sake of establishing the true Dharma or for the sake of favoring another;
yet he lacks reverence for the true Dharma and has not practiced its observance.
Because he does not cause [the teaching] to reach other mental continua, he does not make the True Dharma long-lasting.
Regarding gain, honor, and worship, there is respect and admiration;
however, regarding a lack of respect for the True Dharma, there is the apprehension: "Lest another person equal or superior to me should arise."
Therefore, fearing that there will be an interruption by gain and so forth, he does not teach the Dharma.
Furthermore, even when there is no attachment to gain and honor, if there is a lack of compassion toward sentient beings, he does not teach the Dharma because of this absence of compassion for them;
for one who lacks compassion is not moved by the suffering of sentient beings.
What are the obscurations here? They are lack of respect, the power of gain and honor, and lack of compassion.
Regarding mastery, there are three obscurations; for mastery is the attainment of all forms of mental mastery, which is the mastery of the Buddhas.
Since these three obscurations to it are not yet known, he says:

Regarding the phrase "by which one does not attain mastery": since mastery is dependent upon eloquence (*vāgitva*), those factors by which one does not attain eloquence are themselves the obscurations to eloquence. Thus he says: "Mastery, moreover, is the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and power (*prabhāva*). Alternatively, in the context of the synonyms for eloquence, the phrase "by which one does not attain eloquence" means that one does not attain Buddhahood.

The calamity of hearing is the absolute separation from the hearing of the true Dharma; the calamity of kinsmen is the absolute separation from one's relatives. Furthermore, that calamity of hearing arises from the production of karma conducive to the ruin of the true Dharma.

Because they remain fixed in attachment to their own views or because they have been influenced by non-virtuous friends, those who do not repent reject the Mahāyāna sūtras, saying, "This was spoken by Māra; this is not the word of the Buddha, and it is a cause for rebirth in the miserable states. They discourage others from [the Mahāyāna] as well, and they erase what has been written, burn it, or drown it. Through such means, karma conducive to the ruin of the True Dharma (*saddharmavyasana*) arises. This occurs through the nourishment of the seed of a personal existence that is deprived of hearing the True Dharma. Even when there is no ruin of what has been heard, having little learning (*alpaśrutatva*) constitutes an obscuration to the fulfillment of the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*); this is the subject at hand.

The connection is as follows: one who has heard little is unable to discern the dharmas; furthermore, even for one who has heard much, the lack of cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) constitutes an obscuration. This lack of cultivation of concentration occurs either because the [five] faculties such as desire (*chanda*) are incomplete due to the absence of any one of them, or because there is an absence of any one of the seven formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) during the practice of cultivation. Thus, it is the lack of cultivation of concentration.

Regarding the incompleteness and lack of cultivation of the Buddha-concentrations, such as the *vrajopama* and others, what is the obstacle here? It is karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma, limited learning, poor wisdom, and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) antagonistic to concentration, such as lethargy and restlessness. Furthermore, this obstacle—consisting of non-application and so forth—pertains to the tenfold object beginning with the "wholesome" (*śubha*) and ending with "mastery" (*vaśitva*).
Regarding the statement that there are ten causes for a given object:

from origination up to attainment, for whatever object these exist, there are ten causes—beginning with application and ending with the cultivation of concentration—which function as the opposites of the obscurations to that object.

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in their being causes for origination and so forth, they are designated without differentiation even though they are distinct and each occurs individually.
"By way of being the predominant factor for those objects" means by way of predominance over the arising and so forth of those objects.
For it is said that the obstruction of the causes of the arising and so forth of those [factors] such as the wholesome is the "obscuration to arising" and so forth.
For example, a wall or the like, by obstructing light, is called an obstruction to its effect, namely visual consciousness.
Having established this, the thirty causes of these ten factors are taught as the opposites of the thirty obstructions.
In that regard, there are three causes for the arising of the wholesome: application (*prayoga*), extensive application (*āyatana-prayoga*), and appropriate application (*yoniśaḥ-prayoga*).
The example for this is "the eye and so forth";
the eye and so forth are indeed the cause for the arising of consciousness, but not the cause for its duration and so on.

In this context, since non-application and the like act as direct obstacles to application and the rest, they are also indirectly obstructive to the arising of the wholesome; thus he says that the "obstruction to arising" is the obstruction to the wholesome. By stating "because its arising is certain," he shows that since stability and so forth are impossible in the absence of the wholesome, this is indeed an obstruction to arising.
The cause of stability is enlightenment;
enlightenment is the revolution of the basis;
the basis is stainless suchness.
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Because of its immovability.
It is called "immovable" because it remains as long as the world exists.
It does not become otherwise, nor does it cease.
However, the awakening (*bodhi*) of the *śrāvakas* and others ceases because their purpose is fulfilled within their own mental continua alone.

For Bodhisattvas, however, who engage in the accumulations with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, it is said that their awakening—characterized by the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)—endures as long as sentient beings exist; it is not, like that of the *śrāvakas* and others, characterized by non-arising or ineffability.
Since stability cannot exist without origination, origination also occurs here;
therefore, only the cause of the stability of awakening is mentioned, not the cause of its origination.
Furthermore, there is no other cause for stability apart from that [origination]; hence, only that has been stated.
Alternatively, awakening (*bodhi*) is the thoroughly purified suchness (*tathatā*); because its intrinsic nature is pure, there is no arising.
What then? Due to the removal of adventitious defilements, it is by these causes that its ultimate abiding alone is spoken of, not its arising.
Furthermore, the causes for the abiding of awakening are the production of roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the fulfillment of the accumulations (*sambhāra*).

In this context, the non-arising of the wholesome and so forth, which exist as obstacles to the arising of the wholesome and so forth, are said to constitute "obstructions to stability" because they cause the departure from the stability of enlightenment.
An illustration of this is found in the very passage concerning the four nutriments of sentient beings:
for by means of the physical food and the others, new sentient beings are not produced, but those already born are merely maintained.

The cause of steadfastness (*dhruvīkāraṇa*) is resolve (*dhṛti*), which is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), because it serves as the foundation for all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*). An illustration of this very point is that whatever serves as the support for something is the steadfastness of that thing, in the sense that "it is supported by this. For example, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is the support for the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). Its causes are the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the excellence of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and the absence of weariness in the mind.

In that regard, because it is incompatible with the cause of steadfastness (*dhruvīkāraṇa*), the lack of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and so forth are said to be obscurations even to steadfastness (*dhṛti*).
For this very reason, he says: "The obscuration to steadfastness is the obscuration to undertaking [the vow], because it serves as the support for the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)."
The cause of manifestation regarding the possession of intelligence (*dhimattva*) in a bodhisattva is that which makes it manifest;
and that consists of the perfection of practice, dwelling among people who are habituated [to virtue], and not dwelling among people whose minds are characterized by passion and hatred.
In this context, the deficiency in practice and so forth are said to be obscurations to the manifestation of that possession of intelligence.
Therefore he says: "The obscuration of manifestation exists in the case of the intellect, because that [intellect] is necessarily luminous.
An illustration of this is found in the phrase, "the appearance of form."
For illumination is indeed the cause of the manifestation of mere form, not the cause of its production and so forth.
It is the cause of transformation in the non-erroneous state;
because it consists in the reversal of the errors of superimposition and denial, the non-erroneous is the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
A transformation of non-delusion is described;
for example, the transformation of wood and so forth into ashes and so forth.
There are three causes for this: the destruction of erroneous views and coarse rigidity.
It is the absence of the three obstructions, beginning with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is the state of being fully ripened by the wisdom that brings about liberation.
This is just as fire and so forth [act upon] things to be cooked; for that which is to be cooked, such as boiled rice, is distinct from the raw rice grains and yet is included within their continuum.
For its cause is fire and so forth.
Regarding "non-obstruction" as the cause of disjunction:
since the remaining obstruction—other than that which is to be abandoned by the path of seeing—is abandoned by this [path], the path of cultivation is "non-obstruction."
It has three causes: the destruction of innate dysfunction (*sahajadauṣṭhulya*), vigor, and heedfulness.
Because these serve as the counteragents to the causes of separation, he said accordingly: "The obscuration of separation [is the obstacle] to non-obscuration."
This too is a non-obscuration by virtue of being the antidote to the cause of separation.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason:
"Because it is the dissociation from that obscuration."
"Viśleṣa" (separation) means that by means of this, one is disjoined [from defilements].
"Pariṇāme" refers to the cause of transformation;
by means of that, [one directs] the roots of merit toward great enlightenment.
Because it has the characteristic of being the instigator [of that state].
Furthermore, that consists of both a turning away from existence and enjoyment, and the absence of a sunken mind.
Consequently, the obscuration of transformation should be understood as an obstruction to the causes of transformation.
What is the reason?
Because inclination is characterized by the transformation of the mind toward great enlightenment.
The cause for conviction lies in the absence of fear.
There is also the esteem for the person, faith in the Dharma, and the attainment of the intended meaning.
Through these factors, conviction arises; therefore, because it obstructs the cause of conviction, there is an obscuration of conviction regarding fearlessness.
He states the reason for this very point:
"Because of trembling due to lack of conviction.
For one trembles at the Dharma because of a lack of conviction;
the cause for producing conviction is non-avarice.
Furthermore, that consists of regarding the True Dharma as one's teacher and being indifferent toward gain, honor, worship, and the like, as well as compassion for sentient beings.
Because it is contrary to the cause of inspiring confidence, the obscuration to inspiring confidence is established within the context of non-avarice.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason:

"Because, through lack of stinginess regarding the Dharma, one inspires confidence in others. This means that due to a lack of respect for the true Dharma and so forth, one practices stinginess regarding the Dharma;
and because of this stinginess regarding the Dharma, one does not teach the Dharma to others.
Therefore, non-avarice is the absence of obstruction regarding the communication [of the Dharma].
There are three causes for mastery:
the absence of karma that leads to the ruin of the Dharma; [the absence of karma that leads to the ruin of the Sangha]; and [the absence of karma that leads to the ruin of oneself].
Extensive learning,
and proficiency in meditative concentration;
because they are opposed to these, the loss of what has been heard and so forth are established as obscurations to mastery.
The reason for this is precisely that mastery has the characteristic of being produced by the attainment of sovereignty.
However, some state the reason for the sequence of the virtuous factors and so forth as follows:
A continuum supported by wholesome factors is destined to attain enlightenment;
therefore,
virtue is said to be the true nature of reality.
Immediately following that, awakening (bodhi) is mentioned;
for it is by resorting to the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) that one becomes capable of accomplishing both of these.
This is because, until awakening is attained, the thought of awakening serves as the support for the dharmas of all the families (kula).
Therefore, immediately following that, the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*) is taught.
For one who has generated the awakening mind, there is the application to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the avoidance of both base and wicked persons.
In this way, his status as a bodhisattva becomes manifest.
Therefore, immediately after the formal undertaking [of the vow], wisdom is taught.
And practicing in this manner, one abandons cognitive error and generates non-erroneous knowledge.
Therefore, immediately after wisdom (*dhīmattva*), application (*abhyāsa*) is mentioned;
that, moreover, is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Because one abandons the obscurations through the cultivation of that [path], immediately following it, the absence of obscuration (*anāvaraṇa*), which is the relinquishment of obscurations (*āvaraṇaparihāṇa*), is mentioned.
Because one who is free from obscurations lacks the capacity for the enjoyment of existence, he transforms his mind toward Buddhahood alone and not otherwise;
therefore, homage is mentioned immediately after that.
And for one who has become thus, there arises a sense of joy even regarding the most profound qualities of a Buddha.
Because there is no fear (*atrāsa*) [regarding this], "fearlessness" (*atrāsa*) is mentioned immediately after that.

Thus, when one perceives through direct realization of the Dharma whatever means by which the discipline of sentient beings is to be achieved, one employs that very means; how then could there be any stinginess (*mātsarya*) on his part? Therefore, "non-stinginess" (*amātsarya*) is mentioned immediately after fearlessness. Likewise, because the Bodhisattva has abandoned all obscurations and possesses the complete white dharmas, mastery (*vaśitva*) over the mind proceeds; therefore, "mastery" is mentioned immediately after that.
This is the sequence.
Since this chapter concerns the topic of obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), the causes for the arising of the wholesome and so forth are set forth as aphorisms alongside those obscurations.
A summary of these topics introduced by the context is now provided in an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*).
The cause is tenfold: in production, persistence, support, manifestation, transformation, separation, contraction, faith, arrival, and acquisition.
This is the second intermediate verse for the purpose of summarizing the examples: "The eye, food, and so forth; fire and the like; their illustration;
the sickle, skill in craftsmanship, smoke, the cause, the path, and so on—these are considered [the examples]."
Thus.
[4) Obstructions regarding the stages of the factors conducive to enlightenment and the perfections] [a) Obstructions regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment:
Furthermore, there is another obstruction regarding the stages of the factors conducive to enlightenment and the perfections.
Previously, indeed, the wholesome and its obscuration were taught without distinction;
now, however, he teaches the wholesome by means of distinctions such as "the side" (*pakṣa*) and so forth, and by the distinction between the common and the uncommon.
[The obstacles are] lack of skill regarding the subject matter and laziness.

And by such distinctions as these, there is the obscuration of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and so forth. Among these, the factors conducive to enlightenment are common to both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas without distinction, because they do not differ therein.
However, the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the stages (*bhūmi*) are the uncommon causes for Bodhisattvas alone, because they are under the sovereign influence of Bodhisattvas themselves.
Previously, the obscuration to the fruit was explained by way of the obscuration to the cause of virtue;
here, however, it is stated that this is a direct obscuration to the fruit itself, and thus it is described as distinct from the former.
Alternatively, since lack of skill regarding the objective (*vastvakauśala*) and so forth are distinct from non-application (*aprayoga*) and the rest, they are stated as something else.

Or rather, in the passage "the auspicious and awakening," non-application and so forth were described as the obscurations to the practice and its fruit of a bodhisattva alone when accompanied by skillful means.

Here, however, it should be understood that lack of skill regarding the objective and so forth—which are distinct from non-application and the rest—are the obscurations to the auspicious itself, both common and uncommon, categorized according to the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika*) and so on.
In that regard, there are three types of enlightenment according to the distinctions of the Śrāvakas and others.
Corresponding to those, the factors from the applications of mindfulness up to the path are called the "aids to enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa).
The ten perfections and the ten stages are as described in the sūtras.

Lack of skill regarding the objects of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is an obscuration. Furthermore, these consist of the four applications of mindfulness—of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Moreover, their objects are the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, because they have those as their respective domains.
In this context, the body is the basis for attachment to a locus;
feeling is the basis for attachment to the self’s enjoyment;
and the mind is the basis for attachment to a self.
"Phenomena (dharma) are the basis for the attachment to the defilement and purification of the self.
Regarding the body and so forth, that which is the lack of comprehension of their specific and general characteristics is "lack of skill" (akauśalya) therein.
Among these, the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the body is its nature as a composite comprised of many impure substances.
The existence of pleasure and so forth is the [nature] of feeling;
the specific cognition of objects is that of consciousness;
and [the nature] of phenomena is according to their respective possibilities.
The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), moreover, consists of the aspects (*ākāra*) of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth.

Alternatively, the failure to comprehend the body and so on through the aspects of impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self, or the conceptualization [of them] through the aspects of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self, constitutes unskillfulness regarding the real entity (*vastvakauśala*).
This is because ignorance or [wrong] vision is an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) with respect to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Since the nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*), why is it said that lack of skill regarding the object (*vastvakauśalya*) alone is the obscuration, and not the non-recollection of the object as well? It is because their activity is dependent upon wisdom. For, since wisdom has the nature of vision (*darśana*), mindfulness and the other factors proceed toward the objective support (*ālambana*) following after wisdom; they do not possess independence like wisdom itself.
Therefore, it is not non-remembrance that is stated here to be the obscuration.
The context concerns what the obscuration is for the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).

For it is energy (*vīrya*)—operating here toward the abandonment of arisen and unarisen discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) so they do not arise, and toward the cultivation of arisen and unarisen antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) so they may arise—that receives the name "right abandonment."
Furthermore, although there is no difference in their essential nature, they are established as fourfold due to the difference in their results; such is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).

Therefore, because the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) consist of vigor (*vīrya*), laziness is said to be their obscuration. Regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the obscuration is the twofold deficiency of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); by this [concentration], one succeeds, thus it is called "psychic power" (*ṛddhi*).
And that is the concentration of desire, energy, mind, and investigation.
It is thus called a "basis of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), because it serves as the foundation for psychic powers such as traveling through the sky and the manifestation of emanations.
"Going" refers to supernatural power (*ṛddhi*);
the meaning is that it is the accomplishment of traveling through space and so forth. The "feet" of that power are the bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because it is the support for that.
"Śaiva" refers to the fourfold concentration beginning with *chanda-samādhi*.
Among these, in *chanda-samādhi*, there is a predominance of desire (*chanda*).
This is because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained by means of that [desire];

however, it is not that energy (*vīrya*) and the other factors are absent there. Rather, because they are accompanied by desire, they are subordinate in that context and thus were not explicitly mentioned.
The same should be stated regarding the concentrations of vigor, mind, and investigation.
It has been said that the obscuration of concentration consists in its being deficient in two respects,
yet that is not understood.
Therefore, he says:

"Because of the incompleteness of desire, vigor, mind, and investigation due to the deficiency of any one of them, and because of the deficiency of the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) due to incomplete cultivation. [92]

In that regard, there is deficiency in fulfillment due to the absence of concentration (*samādhi*) resulting from the lack of any one of these—desire (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), or investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).
There is deficiency in cultivation because of the lack of any one of the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
These consist of faith (*śraddhā*), desire, vigor, serenity (*praśrabdhi*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), volition (*cetanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

For it is through the cultivation of these formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) that mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained, and not otherwise; therefore, due to their deficiency and the lack of cultivation, mastery over concentration is not attained.
What is the obscuration here?
It is the side of the opposites (*vipakṣapakṣa*) of the formative forces of abandonment, such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth.
Namely:
laziness, loss of the object of focus,
lethargy and excitement, non-application, and application.
Regarding "the non-planting of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in the faculties":
when one who is terrified of *saṃsāra* cultivates a root of virtue with liberation as the objective, that which is certain for the attainment of liberation is called "conducive to liberation.

And when that has been planted, faith and the other [faculties] acquire the designation of "faculties" (*indriya*), but not otherwise; therefore, the non-planting of the factors conducive to liberation is said to be an obscuration regarding the faculties.
What is the obscuration here? It is that secondary affliction by which the fortune for liberation is not cultivated;
it consists, moreover, of attachment to renewed existence and fear of nirvāṇa.
Among those many [factors], the weakness of the faculties (*indriya*) is what is under discussion as an "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*).
But how is there weakness of the faculties? To this, he says:
"Because of being interspersed with opposing factors" means because they are overcome by opposing factors consisting of lack of faith, laziness, loss of mindfulness, distraction, and faulty wisdom.
For the faculties are manifested through heat, moisture, and firmness.
And both of these types of factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are weak, because they are overcome by their opposites, such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*).
For this very reason, falling away from them is possible.

However, because their opposites have been conquered, faith and the other [faculties] receive the name "powers" (*bala*) during the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). [93]

Therefore, that weakness of those very same factors—faith and so forth—which occurs during the stages of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and "Summits" (mūrdhan) due to being overcome by opposing factors, is the obscuration of the powers (balas). For as long as that [weakness] exists, the state of the powers cannot arise. What, then, is the obscuration in this case?
That very same [set of] adverse factors, beginning with lack of faith,
constitutes the fault of views regarding the factors of enlightenment;
"obscuration" is the term under discussion.
In this context, "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Its seven factors of awakening—consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity—are called "factors" because they arise at the time of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.

However, if they were called "factors" merely because they are conducive to awakening, then it would follow that the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth would also be factors of awakening.
How is it that the fault of [wrong] view is an obscuration regarding the factors of enlightenment? To this he says:
"Because they are brought forth by the path of seeing.
The meaning is: because they are established by the path of seeing.
What, then, is this fault of views?

It consists of the five imagined views, doubt, ignorance, and the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as attachment and so forth, together with their associated mental factors, which take those [views] as their objects.
But are not doubt and the others also obstructions here?
Let there be an obstruction.
However, since here the instruction regarding the faults of views is intended to refer to the primary [factor], it is not contradictory that those [other factors] are not explicitly mentioned.

Furthermore, it is precisely the seed residing in the *ālayavijñāna* of those views and so forth that is called their "obstruction," because they are to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Regarding the factors of the path—namely right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration—it has been stated that the fault of *dauṣṭhulya* (inner corruption) is an obscuration.
He states the reason for this very point:
"Because those factors of the path are brought forth by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
Because it is established as belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

What is that fault of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*)? In detail, it consists of the innate view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), together with their associated mental factors; and the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, which have those views as their objects and also take external objects as their focus, together with their associated mental factors.
The seed residing within their storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is that which constitutes *dauṣṭhulya*.

In brief, however, it is the other contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors, distinct from those to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavya*), as they reside within the storehouse-consciousness; this is *dauṣṭhulya*.
And because it is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is established as an obscuration with respect to the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Thus has been explained the obscuration regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

Immediately following that, the obscurations regarding the perfections (pāramitās) must be explained; therefore, he says: "The obscuration regarding the perfections is the obstruction to sovereignty, to a happy rebirth, and to the non-abandonment of sentient beings."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Here, regarding the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the obscuration of whichever perfection is indicated by its respective fruit is explained as the obscuration of that perfection.

What is the reason here for stating that stinginess (*mātsarya*) and so forth—which in reality exist as obstacles to giving (*dāna*) and the other perfections—are described as obscurations to their fruits rather than as obscurations to the perfections themselves?
Because everything proceeds from giving and the other perfections for the sake of that fruit,
the obscuration to the fruit is mentioned for the purpose of generating diligence toward the abandonment of stinginess and so forth;
it is not called an obscuration to the perfections.

Alternatively, obscurations such as stinginess are called "obscurations" because they act as obstacles to results such as sovereignty; being the opposites of sovereignty and so forth, they produce results such as poverty.
What is their result?
In that regard, the primary result of the perfection of generosity is sovereignty and dominion.
From the perfection of ethical discipline comes a favorable rebirth;
from the perfection of patience comes the non-abandonment of sentient beings;
from the perfection of vigor comes the decrease of faults and the increase of virtues.
Through the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), one causes sentient beings to enter the teaching;
through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one liberates that teacher;
and through the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*), by means of the dedication toward awakening, there is the inexhaustibility of virtue.
The uninterrupted continuity of virtue is the perfection of aspiration;
the bringing forth of wholesome qualities is the perfection of power;
and [the mastery of] phenomena is the perfection of knowledge.
There is also enjoyment and the ripening of sentient beings.
Regarding "the obscuration of sovereignty and lordship," therein, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the abundance of wealth and requisites;
lordship (*adhipatya*) is mastery over their enjoyment.
The obscuration of both of these is the obscuration to the perfection of generosity, because it is the result thereof.
What, then, is that? It is stinginess.
Regarding "an obscuration to a good rebirth": a good rebirth refers to excellent states of existence.
Humans and gods:
its obstruction is an obstacle to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), because that [perfection] has that as its fruit.
Furthermore, that immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) is contemptible action of body and speech.
"Non-abandonment of sentient beings" means embracing even those beings who cause harm, just as one embraces those who are helpful;
this is the fruit of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). Anger is the obscuration to that.

The decrease and increase of faults and virtues consists in the abandonment of faults that have arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen—these being applied toward harming oneself or others—which constitutes the decrease of faults;
and the further development of virtues that have arisen and the arising of those not yet arisen—these being directed toward benefiting oneself and others—which constitutes the increase of virtues.
Furthermore, what is the obscuration in this regard? It is laziness.
Regarding the "obstruction of introducing those to be trained":

this refers to the introduction of those to be trained into the teaching, because it is accepted as the cause for attaining heaven and liberation. When reverence arises through such an approach, sentient beings enter the teaching effortlessly by means of the power of their resolve.
And here, distraction is an obscuration;
"obscuration to liberation" refers to liberation, which is the abandonment of the afflictions,
and that occurs through instruction.
And instruction is by means of wisdom and not otherwise; therefore, liberation is the fruit of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Its obscuration is afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭaprajñā*), delusion (*moha*), or poor wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).

Regarding "the obscuration to the inexhaustibility of generosity and so forth": that which is an obscuration to the inexhaustibility of generosity, ethical discipline, and the rest is the obscuration to the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*).
Furthermore, as to how that inexhaustibility of generosity and the other perfections comes about, he says:
"Because of its inexhaustibility through dedication toward enlightenment."

The roots of virtue, such as generosity, when dedicated toward great enlightenment, are not exhausted, just like Buddhahood itself. Regarding its obscuration, some say it is the lack of knowledge regarding the method characterized by dedication toward great enlightenment; others say the obscuration is the grasping at the three spheres due to a lack of skill in means.
"The obstruction to the uninterrupted engagement in virtue throughout all births" means that virtue is practiced without interruption day by day or moment by moment;
and this is the fruit of the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
To explain how this is so, he says:
"By means of the power of aspiration, through the undertaking of rebirths favorable to that [practice].
For by the power of aspiration, one undertakes a rebirth conducive to the continuous practice of giving and the other perfections.
Its obscuration is the lack of aspiration for a rebirth favorable to giving and the rest.

"The obscuration to the certainty of that very same virtue" means that certainty (*niścaya*) is the state of making [the mind] one-pointed day by day and moment by moment. He states the reason for this very point:
"Because one is not overcome by opposing factors through the two powers of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In this context, the power of analytical discernment is wisdom (*prajñā*) accompanied by steadfastness (*dhairya*);
furthermore, steadfastness is a conventional (*prajñapti*) phenomenon.
Because the triad of vigor, concentration, and wisdom is present innately (*sahaja*), there is analytical discernment.

The power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*) consists in engaging in giving and the other perfections without effort through habitual practice; because of this, one is not overcome by their opposites, such as stinginess and so forth.
What is the obscuration here?

The weakness of non-analytical cultivation is the obscuration regarding the enjoyment of the Dharma and the ripening of oneself and others. Thus, the result consists of being established within the assembly-circle of the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) and the enjoyment of the profound and vast Mahāyāna Dharma, as well as the ripening of sentient beings through the teaching of the Dharma by means of various forms of emanation-activities.
Furthermore, the obscuration to that [result] is the failure to investigate the meaning of what has been heard as it truly is, and dullness of wisdom.
And here, in substance, there are six perfections;
by name, ten. [97] Wisdom-perfection...
And it is characterized by the four perfections (*pāramitā*).
Among these, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is supramundane non-conceptual knowledge (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
By means of that knowledge, there is the gradual abandonment of all obscurations (*āvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, the perfections of skillful means (*upāya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) are comprised within the knowledge obtained subsequent to the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
If the perfection of knowledge is preeminent, how is it not non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)?
For the perfection of knowledge is indeed non-conceptual knowledge, [and yet] the knowledge obtained subsequent to that [non-conceptual] knowledge.
Having discerned that state awakened by that knowledge, one personally experiences the enjoyment of the Dharma and brings others to maturity;
yet since even this duality does not exist within non-conceptual [wisdom], it is therefore called the perfection of non-conceptual knowledge.
The obscuration of the perfections has been explained.
Immediately following that, it must be explained regarding the stages (*bhūmi*); therefore, he says:
"In the stages as well, in due order, there is the meaning of being all-pervading and the meaning of being supreme."
Thus is the detailed exposition.
In that regard, there are ten stages (*bhūmi*):
the Joyous (*pramuditā*), the Immaculate (*vimalā*), the Luminous (*prabhākarī*), the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), and the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*).

The stages are Abhimukhī (Facing), Dūraṅgamā (Far-Reaching), Acalā (Immovable), Sādhumatī (Excellent Intelligence), and Dharmameghā (Cloud of Dharma). Among these, because of the realization of the meaning of the all-pervading nature and so forth of the dharmadhātu, the specific distinctions of opportunity are called "stages" (*bhūmi*) by way of being the locus for successive attainments and by way of being the basis for the qualities produced therein.

Others maintain that the designation "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the state of remaining within whichever dwelling (*vihāra*) a bodhisattva frequently dwells in, for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the all-pervasive nature of the *dharmadhātu* and so forth.

Furthermore, the formal establishment [of the grounds] by means of the grounds is as follows: in the *pramuditā* (Joyous) ground, because of the arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the bodhisattva realizes the Dharma (*abhisameti dharma*). Having realized the Dharma, on the *vimalā* (Stainless) ground, he accomplishes the excellence of training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*) which flows spontaneously.

Due to the departure from all subtle transgressions and impurities, in the stage of Radiance (*prabhākarī*), one accomplishes the specific training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) characterized by the quality of non-retrogression even in future lives.

In the stages of Blazing Radiance (*arciṣmatī*), Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), and Presence (*abhimukhī*), one accomplishes the specific training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) which has the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*), the truths (*satya*), and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as its objects.
Regarding those very trainings, it should be understood that there is a fourfold fruit in the remaining stages.
Therein, on the stage Dūraṅgamā, he accomplishes the dwelling in the knowledge of the signless accompanied by effort.

On the stage Acalā, he accomplishes the dwelling in the knowledge of the signless without effort, together with the purification of the field. On the stage Sādhumatī, he accomplishes the excellence of the qualities of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
By means of which one becomes a speaker of the Dharma;
and in the Dharmameghā [stage], one accomplishes the excellence of the qualities of meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs.

Regarding the tenfold dharmadhātu, such as the meaning of "all-pervading" (sarvatragārtha) and so forth—it is within the dharmadhātu that the meaning of "all-pervading" and the rest is realized through the ten bodhisattva stages.
In that regard, non-afflicted ignorance constitutes ten kinds of obscurations across the ten bodhisattva stages respectively;
this is because it is their antithesis— that is,
because it is the antithesis of the stages.
For the stages (*bhūmi*) consist in the specific nature of providing scope for supramundane concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
Non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is the adversary because it obstructs their arising.
And here, it is not only non-afflicted ignorance that constitutes an obscuration; rather, other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) do as well.
For it is thus:
on the stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā*), all that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) constitutes an obscuration.
This is because, through the path of seeing which realizes the meaning of the all-pervading (*sarvatragārtha*), all accumulations of misconceptions regarding the truths are abandoned.
Furthermore, those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation are [abandoned] by means of the remaining stages;
however, even though they have not been abandoned, they are as if abandoned,
for they do not cause defilement for Bodhisattvas.
With reference to this very point, the following verse was spoken: "For one who employs great skillful means, affliction becomes a limb of awakening;
even cyclic existence is of the nature of peace; therefore, the Tathāgata is inconceivable. [99]

Since it is stated that on the ten stages (*bhūmi*) the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) become increasingly more excellent in their respective order, it is understood that their opposites, such as stinginess (*mātsarya*) and so forth, are also abandoned in that same order.
If other afflictions (*kleśa*) were also obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), why was it said that on the stages only non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is the obstruction?
Because [ignorance] is unique [to this context].
For this indeed acts as an obstacle to the attainment of nirvāṇa for bodhisattvas alone, but not for śrāvakas and others. To explain:
śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are liberated even while that [obstacle] exists, whereas bodhisattvas are not; therefore, it is unique [to them].

This has been described as an obscuration regarding the stages (*bhūmi*). It is not, however, because that [affliction] alone is the obscuration regarding the stages that it is mentioned; rather, since affliction (*kleśa*) is common to both Śrāvakas and others and Bodhisattvas, there is neither a prescription nor a prohibition of it as an obscuration within the Bodhisattva stages. Thus, even though it is not explicitly stated, its status as an obscuration does not cease. Others say: non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is common to both Śrāvakas and others and Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is specifically designated as an obscuration of the stages.
However, affliction (*kleśa*) is not mentioned [in that context] because it is incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*).
For even affliction is common to Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas and so forth; thus, it would not be considered merely incidental.
Others, however, say:

That which is ignorance regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) constitutes the obscuration for Śrāvakas; being non-afflicted ignorance, it does not act as a hindrance to liberation, because Śrāvakas attain liberation even while such ignorance regarding the stages persists. For Bodhisattvas, however, it is afflicted, as it serves as a cause for obstructing the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
Others say: "This is not so; there is an undefiled tenfold revolution.

For by means of the first stage (*bhūmi*), one penetrates the all-pervading nature of the *dharmadhātu*. In this context, the first stage is the first supramundane wisdom together with its retinue, comprised within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Because the *dharmadhātu*—which is emptiness—is all-pervading, being the same everywhere as it is in one place due to its universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is called "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*).

The statement, "Since no phenomenon exists apart from the *dharmadhātu*," serves as the indicator that the *dharmadhātu* is all-pervasive; "penetrates" (*pratividhyati*) means he realizes it directly. Through that penetration, he attains the equality of self and other, thinking, "Whoever I am, that is the other; whoever the other is, that is I. Because he perceives no difference in emptiness between himself and others, he considers self and other to be non-different. For this very reason, on this stage, the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) becomes preeminent.

Then, in this regard, just as a bodhisattva acts for the sake of others as he does for his own sake—this indeed illustrates the penetration, the counteragent, and the fruit of the counteragent—and these three are to be understood as existing in the other stages as well; by the second stage, one penetrates the supreme meaning of the *dharmadhātu*, which is connected [to the previous statement] because of the vision of its natural luminosity. Therefore, the following thought occurs to him: "Therefore, in our equal accomplishment, we must apply ourselves specifically to the accomplishment of purification in all its aspects.
