Thus he shows the scriptural authority (*āgama*) from the Sūtra:

It has been said that "because" the ten paths of wholesome action, when cultivated through the aspect of wisdom, lead as far as the Śrāvaka vehicle; when purified further than that, they lead as far as the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and when purified even further than that, they lead to the purification of the Bodhisattva stages, the purification of the perfections, and the vastness of conduct.

"Thereafter, they become further purified; because they are purified in every aspect, they conduce even to the power of the ten powers. Therefore, in that case, we have attained [this] through meditative realization," and so forth.
Since this occurs for him on the second stage, the words "therefore, in that case" and so on are used.
Thus, it is understood that by means of the second stage, he penetrates the meaning of supremacy.
*Abhinirhāra* means effort or that which is to be accomplished.
The purification in all aspects refers to the removal of the obscurations of both afflicted and unafflicted delusion within the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) becomes even more distinguished.
By means of the third [verse], which concerns the specific object through its excellence, one penetrates the supreme outflow of that [object] by way of the cause consisting solely of oneself;
"penetrates" is the term supplied from the context.

Because the word of the Buddha is manifested through the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*. For the teaching-dharma (*deśanādharma*) consisting of the sūtras and so forth—which is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmadhātu*—is manifested by the power of the *dharmadhātu*, which is designated as the "Dharma-body completely pure in all its aspects. This is because, due to the supremacy of the *dharmadhātu*, there is supremacy in the teaching-dharma that is its outflow; and because it serves as the cause for the purification of the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, the detailed explanation is: "having understood the supremacy of the heard outflow of the *dharmadhātu*," and so forth.
"By that" means by the dharmadhātu which has negated [all phenomena].
"Of what has been heard" refers to the dharma of the sūtras and so forth that have been studied.
"Having known its supremacy" means having realized it thus within oneself through non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
"For that purpose" means for the purpose of hearing the Buddha’s word.
For it is said in the Sūtra: "One should throw oneself even into a fire-pit as vast as the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
Suppose someone were to say this:

"In this way, I would cause you to hear this verse of the Dharma, brought forth by the Perfectly Awakened One, which purifies the conduct of a bodhisattva, provided that you would cast yourself into a great pit of fire, blazing and become a single mass of flame,
and undergo a great onset of painful sensations with your own body."
It occurs to him:

"I am able, for the sake of even a single word of Dharma brought forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One which purifies the conduct of a bodhisattva, to cast myself from the Brahma-world into a great trichiliocosm world-system filled with fire;
how much more so into an ordinary pit of fire?"

Furthermore, we must indeed seek the Buddha-dharmas even through dwelling in all the sufferings of the hells and the miserable states of existence, let alone through dwelling in the sufferings of the human realm.
For this very reason, on this stage, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) becomes even more preeminent;
for it is indestructible even by the endurance of all afflictions (*kleśa*) for the sake of the meaning of what has been heard.
The fourth [perfection] is for the purpose of [realizing] non-appropriation.
It is connected with the phrase "one penetrates the dharma-realm.
On the fourth stage, because of its equality, one penetrates the non-belonging-to-self nature of the dharma-realm.
Because there is no self whatsoever in the dharmadhātu;
or rather, because it is not the object of any perversion, there is no appropriation by anyone.
Since it is itself free from perversion, there is no appropriation here whatsoever.
For there is a scriptural statement that even craving for the Dharma is turned away.

Thus, through the realization of the dharmadhātu by means of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*) in the Arciṣmatī stage, there is the attainment of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This applies even to the Bodhisattva’s craving for the Dharma such as the Sūtras and so forth.
Others maintain that even the previously mentioned craving for the phenomena of meditative absorption, concentration, and attainment ceases;
therefore, on that stage, the perfection of vigor becomes preeminent,
because one dwells constantly with the factors conducive to awakening, having transcended the discursive speech of body and mind.
By means of the fifth [ground], one penetrates the fact that the continuum of the *dharmadhātu* is undifferentiated; this is the subject under discussion.
One perceives the equality of oneself with the past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and with Bodhisattvas through their successive continua, as being undifferentiated.
He shows the scriptural authority for this by stating, "by means of the ten equalities of the pure mental disposition."
And by the equality of the pure intention regarding the qualities of past Buddhas; and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the qualities of future Buddhas;
and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the qualities of present Buddhas.
And by the equality of the intention for the purification of the mind; and by the equality of the intention for the purification of the mind;
and by the equality of the intention for the purification that removes views, doubts, perplexity, and hesitation.

And by the equality of the pure intention regarding the knowledge of what is and is not the path; and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the knowledge of the abandonment of the [wrong] course;
and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the progressive cultivation of all the factors conducive to awakening.
And by the equality of the pure intention to bring all sentient beings to maturity;
through these equalities, one penetrates the non-differentiation of the mental continua of all Buddhas,
because the Dharma-body, characterized by the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is indivisible.

Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of meditative concentration becomes even more predominant; because of the abundance of cultivation regarding the aspects of the truths from the perspective of ultimate reality,
it is connected with the statement that one penetrates the dharmadhātu for the sake of the non-affliction and purification of the sixth [stage].

Defilement has dependent origination as its characteristic; because it is adventitious, the [mind] is not defiled by nature, and due to its natural purity, it is not purified. Thus, one penetrates the *dharmadhātu* by means of non-conceptual gnosis in the form of self-cognition. To this very point, he shows the scriptural authority:
Because of the penetration that within dependent origination there is no dharma whatsoever that is either defiled or purified,
on the sixth stage the bodhisattva penetrates dependent origination,
yet therein he does not perceive the defilement or purification of any dharma.
Because the dharmadhātu is luminous by nature and because the members of dependent origination are merely defilement,
there exists no other self or anything belonging to a self apart from these, in which either defilement or purification could be conceived.

Therefore, on this very stage, the perfection of wisdom becomes even more preeminent by virtue of the meaning of purification from affliction through the realization of the profundity of dependent origination; thus,
it is established that by means of the seventh [stage], one penetrates the non-differentiation of the *dharmadhātu*.

On that stage, the bodhisattva becomes one who is free from the manifestation of all signs (*nimitta*), because the manifestation of diversity occurs through the gateway of the manifestation of signs;
therefore, due to the absence of the manifestation of signs, it is said that on the seventh stage, one penetrates the non-differentiated nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
"Because, due to the absence of signs (*nimitta*), there is no manifestation of diversity in the characteristics of phenomena such as the *sūtras*.

This means that those signs of phenomena such as the *sūtras* by which one enters the *dharmadhātu* would, by force, manifest as diverse to the two types of knowledge: the knowledge of that entry and the knowledge subsequently attained (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha*).

Up to the sixth stage, however, on the seventh stage, by means of a knowledge that perceives all signs as having a single flavor, one penetrates the signlessness of the dharmadhātu; those signs do not manifest.
Therefore,
on that stage, the perfection of skillful means becomes preeminent;
for one penetrates all signs as being signless, having transcended what is produced by signs.
And it does not contradict conventional usage;
through the penetration of that [reality], one attains mastery over that very [convention].
The eighth [insight] is for the purpose of neither diminishing nor increasing;
it is connected with the phrase "he penetrates the dharma-sphere," because the dharma-sphere is pure by nature.
Because there is no difference between the states of being with stains and being stainless,
it is called *tathatā* (suchness) precisely because it is eternally just so.
There is no diminution whatsoever regarding the sign;
nor is there any increase whatsoever regarding the sign.
For thus, there is nothing whatsoever such that "the sign itself is the signless," because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The reason for this is as follows:

on the eighth stage, because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the bodhisattva penetrates the fact that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is characterized by the absence of increase and the absence of decrease.

There is no quality of diminution in affliction, nor is there any increase in purification, because of the non-arising of any previously non-existent phenomena. There are four masteries: mastery over non-conceptuality, mastery over the purification of the field, mastery over knowledge, and mastery over karma.
In this regard, it should be understood that the dharmadhātu is the basis for mastery over non-conceptual knowledge,
because there is an absence of the manifestation of all signs (*nimitta*) through effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).

Although the absence of the manifestation of signs also occurs on the seventh [stage], the distinction here is that it occurs through the absence of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), whereas on that [seventh] stage it occurs with volitional effort (*abhisamskāreṇa*).
The subject under discussion is that on the eighth [stage], one penetrates the state of being the basis for mastery over the purification of the field (*kṣetrapariśuddhivaśitāśrayatva*).

This state of being the basis for mastery over the purification of the field arises from the attainment of the power to purify Buddha-fields and manifest circles of assemblies (*parṣanmaṇḍala*) at will within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) becomes preeminent,
because of the continuous application of wholesome qualities through the attainment of the non-conceptual mastery over the buddha-field.
It is the subject at hand that one penetrates the ninth [stage] as the basis for the mastery of gnosis (*jñāna-vaśitā*) within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
How is it known that, by means of the ninth [knowledge], one penetrates the state of being a basis for the possession of knowledge?
To this he says:
"Because of the attainment of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)."
For on this stage, one attains the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, meaning, etymological derivation, and eloquence, which are unsurpassed by others;
therefore, it is understood that here the dharmadhātu is realized as the basis for mastery of knowledge.
Consequently, on that stage, the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) becomes even more preeminent.
Because of the possession of a specific power of wisdom,
it is connected that one penetrates the state of being the support for the non-obstruction of karma in the tenth [bhūmi].
How is this understood?
Therefore, it says:
"Because of performing the welfare of sentient beings through emanations according to one's wish.
By this certainty, on the tenth stage, one penetrates the fact that the *dharmadhātu* is the basis for the mastery of activity (*karmavaśitā*).
By that, one attains sovereignty over the activities of a Tathāgata.

For, like the Sugata, through emanation bodies, one performs for sentient beings dwelling in the infinite world-systems of the ten directions whatever is to be done for whomever, in whatever manner, and at whatever time, according to their desire; at that very time, one acts accordingly for them.
Therefore, on this stage, the perfection of gnosis becomes even more preeminent.
"Because of the excellence of the enjoyment of the Dharma and the ripening of sentient beings.

Thus, regarding these aforementioned bodhisattva stages, there exists an undefiled ignorance that constitutes an obstruction to the purification of all aspects of the tenfold realization of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) on each individual stage; the ten bodhisattva stages are established as the antidotes to that.
The distinction between the ninth and tenth stages is illuminated by way of their fruit, and not by way of a distinction in the realization of different objects of focus.
Because that dwelling has reached an indescribable state that cannot be defined;
and because the purpose for establishing the meanings of the "all-pervading" and so forth is the sequential attainment of the specific distinctions of the ten perfections across the ten stages.
Therefore, this has been stated: "The obscuration of the stages (*bhūmi*) is the obscuration to the specific progress of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Alternatively, it is precisely that which is taught in the Sūtras—such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)—distinguished by each successive stage, comprising all aspects, having various final fruits, and serving the purpose of penetrating meanings such as "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*).
[5] Summary of Obstructions:
In order to demonstrate that all the various types of obstructions previously mentioned are included within two obstructions, he says:
"Furthermore, in brief..."
The obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable have been explained.
How is this understood?
Briefly stated, there are only these two; furthermore, there is no third.
Therefore, he says:
"All obscurations here."
The phrase "included herein" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
It is understood that all obscurations are included within the two obscurations; there is no third.

And because all obscurations are included right here, liberation from all obscurations is maintained to result from the destruction of those very two—afflictive and cognitive obscurations—which comprise all obscurations.
The meaning is the abandonment of all obscurations.
If the obscuration to the stage of a Buddha has not been mentioned, how can it be included here?
For inclusion does not occur merely through verbal designation.
Rather, it is by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Moreover, since the term "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) implies pervasion (*vyāpti*), that [intrinsic nature] is already expressed by it as well.
Otherwise, there would be obscuration only of a specific location (*pradeśa*).
Alternatively, in order to include the obscurations to the stage of a Buddha, it is said:
"All obscurations here are included; liberation is held to occur through their destruction.
As long as the obscurations to Buddhahood are not destroyed, there is no liberation."
Therefore, it is established that this too is an obscuration, just like the obscuration of the senses.

However, non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) in its state of extreme subtlety and the latent impressions of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) are said to be the obscuration of the stage of a Buddha.
Thus, it is explained that because of the extreme subtlety of these, they cannot be perceived otherwise.

[The Summary Meaning of the Obscurations: The great obscuration is that which is pervasive—the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable belonging to those of the bodhisattva lineage. The slight obscuration is that which is limited—the obscuration of afflictions alone belonging to those of the śrāvaka and other lineages.
The obscuration to application (*prayogāvaraṇa*) is that which is "excessive," because for those whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth, they have not attained the state of application.
The obscuration to attainment (*prāptyāvaraṇa*) is that which is "equal," because it pertains to those of equal parts (*samabhāgacarita*); for it functions as an obstacle to attainment.

The obscuration to specific attainment (*prāptiviśeṣāvaraṇa*) is that which consists of "taking up and abandoning," because it is an obscuration to specific realization for those belonging to the lineage of the Bodhisattvas.
Non-abiding nirvāṇa is a distinction of realization;
this indeed should be understood as a distinction of the fruit.
The obstruction to correct application consists of the ninefold characteristics of affliction, because of the statement that "the nine fetters are the obstruction."
These constitute the obstructions to correct application (*samyakprayoga*), as has been explained.

The obstruction to the cause (*hetvāvaraṇa*) is that which pertains to the tenfold causes regarding virtue and so forth; for it is called the "obstruction to the cause" because it acts as an obstruction by way of binding the causes of virtue and the rest.
The obstruction to entering reality (*tattvapaveśāvaraṇa*) is that which pertains to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*); for through them one enters into reality.
The obscuration to supreme virtue is that which pertains to the perfections (*pāramitā*), because there is no virtue superior to them.

The obscuration to the progression toward their distinction is that which pertains to the stages (*bhūmi*); for it is the perfections themselves, when they have become the practice of supramundane excellence, that are called "stages.
The obscuration to being gathered is that which...

"In brief, it is twofold" refers to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), since by these all obscurations are subsumed. This statement of the summarized meaning is for the sake of easy grasping and retention;
for that which is condensed is easily grasped and retained.
In the *Madhyāntavibhāga-ṭīkā* following the *Āgama*, composed by the venerable master Sthiramati, the second chapter, "The Obstructions," is completed.
[110] Immediately after the exposition of the obstructions, it is the occasion for the exposition of reality (*tattva*).
Since that was indicated immediately thereafter, he says, with reference to reality: "He says... [as follows].
Furthermore, reality (*tattva*) exists in many forms.
Therefore, because the nature of reality is difficult to comprehend for the sake of understanding its various divisions, [the author], first explaining the classification of reality, says:
"The reality of the fundamental characteristic."
Thus, in detail, there are ten kinds of reality (*tattva*).

Among them, the statement regarding fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating how the other realities are subsumed within it. The statement regarding characteristic reality (*lakṣaṇatattva*) is for the purpose of abandoning faults in one who is engaged in the full comprehension, abandonment, and realization of fundamental reality.
The statement regarding reality free from error is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for generating world-weariness toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
The statement regarding the reality of cause and fruit is for the purpose of showing the departure via the Śrāvaka vehicle for one who has become weary;
for it is by means of the penetration and cultivation of the four noble truths that a Śrāvaka departs.
The statement regarding gross reality is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for practicing the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*).
The statement regarding subtle reality is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for abandoning all obscurations.

And the statement regarding well-known reality is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for teaching the well-established Dharma and for demonstrating the means for refuting all opposing disputants.

Furthermore, although the *dharmadhātu* is uniform, the statement regarding the reality of the sphere of purification is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctions in purification according to the differences in lineage (*gotra*), disposition (*āśaya*), and so forth.
The statement regarding the reality of inclusion is for the purpose of demonstrating the means of entering into all modes of affliction and purification. Beginning with suchness (*tathatā*)... [111]

The statement regarding the reality of differentiation (*prabheda-tattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity to dispel all doubts. The statement regarding the reality of skillfulness (*kauśalya-tattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity to establish selflessness (*nairātmya*) after having dispelled every form of grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*).
Others, however, say that the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*) is unique to the bodhisattva.
In that very context, the second is the reality that serves as the antidote to false application;
the third is the reality conducive to correct application;
and the fourth is the reality common to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The fifth is the reality of the means of practice;
the sixth is the reality common to the world;
the seventh is the reality uncommon to that [world].
The eighth is the reality of the summary of the knowable;
the ninth is the reality of the fundamental nature;
the tenth is the reality of the eradication of the root of affliction.
In brief, these ten principles (*tattva*) serve as the basis for all the intentional teachings (*abhisandhi-vacana*) of the Tathāgatas.
In detail, the reality (*tattva*) is immeasurable.
Regarding this, some say that even conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*) is called "reality" because it conforms to reality.
Others maintain that all these [categories] are indeed real because they are non-contradictory in the ways already described;
for whatever does not contradict in a particular manner is considered real in that way.
[1] Regarding the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*):
since it is not well-known that the fundamental reality consists of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), he says:
"namely, the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)."
Demonstrating the reason why the threefold intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is called the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), he says:
"Because therein other realities are established.
The meaning is that within it, other realities—such as the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*) and so forth—are included. [112]
For what purpose is the threefold nature taught?
Some say it is for the purpose of demonstrating conventional reality, ultimate reality, and their basis.
Others say it is for the purpose of demonstrating error, its cause, and the objective support for its antidote.
Others say that it is for the purpose of liberating bodhisattvas from obscurations and for the purpose of demonstrating the objects of abandonment, thorough knowledge, and realization.
Still others say it is for the purpose of achieving non-erroneous practice regarding the nature of profound wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
For it is thus stated in the *Abhidharmasūtra-gāthādhyāya*:
The teaching on illusion and so forth refers to the dependent nature; the teaching that [things] do not exist refers to the imagined nature;
but the teaching on the perfected nature refers to the fourfold purity.
Purity consists of natural purity, freedom from defilement, the object of focus, and the path;
for these four aspects comprise the nature of purified phenomena.
Thus [it is said].

Others maintain that the three natures (*svabhāva*) exist according to their possibility, in order to demonstrate that they are the objects of mundane, supramundane, and subsequently attained knowledge (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
What is intended here as the reality (*tattva*) within these three natures?
For the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) is the non-erroneous meaning. What, then, is the non-erroneous nature within these three natures?
The intention of the question is: "Because reality resides within the three natures."
"The three natures are indeed eternally non-existent," and so forth, in detail.
The imagined characteristic is eternally non-existent.

For that wherein the attachment of the ignorant to the grasped and the grasper, and to the signified and the signifier, proceeds like a dream—that is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) because it lacks intrinsic reality.
Therefore, because its essence is non-existent and because it is erroneous, the non-existence of the imagined characteristic is [itself] non-existence.
Thus, in the imagined nature, non-existence alone is said to be the reality (*tattva*).
"Because it is non-erroneous" means that here the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) is the non-erroneous meaning; thus he shows that the dependent characteristic (*paratantralakṣaṇa*) exists.
And "not in reality" means that its existence is based on the conventional designations of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth; yet,
because it lacks the nature of the grasped, the grasper, and so on, it does not exist in that way in reality.
Explaining this very point, he says:
"Because it is mere illusion.
This is what is meant:
That which appears exists as the material cause of illusion;
however, it does not exist in the manner in which it appears— namely, in the form of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject—
just like an illusory person and so forth.
Therefore, it is called "error.
That [error] is the reality (tattva) within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
otherwise, it would be the manifestation of that which exists [in itself] under a form that does not exist in its own essence.
Here too, the phrase "because it is non-erroneous" connects [to the previous context], as it is the subject under discussion.
Regarding the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) as the reality of existence and non-existence:
the perfected characteristic is the reality that is both existent and non-existent.
It is existence because its nature consists in the presence of the absence of duality;
it is non-existence because its nature consists in the absence of duality;
and it is reality because it is the objective support for purification.

This is the reality (*tattva*) in the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It is connected [to the preceding] by the phrase "because of its non-erroneousness. The reality of the three natures has been stated, but not their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); therefore, he asks. Alternatively, since the reality of characteristics was mentioned immediately after the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*), and that is not yet established, he asks: "What is the reality of characteristics?"
Therefore he says:
"Regarding the superimposition and denial of phenomena and the person here," and so forth.

The characteristic of reality regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is that knowledge through which the views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) with respect to the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) do not arise.

The view of superimposition is the insistence that the self and phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as objects of apprehension, distinct from the consciousness in which they appear. The view of denial is the [insistence] that they do not exist even conventionally (*vyavahāra*).
Others say:
"The abandonment of consciousness appearing as persons and phenomena is the view of negation (apavāda-darśana).
This [interpretation of] "the rejection of grasping" is to be considered.

The characteristic of reality within the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) is that by discerning which characteristic the views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) regarding the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) no longer arise;
it should be understood as being free from superimposition and denial.
Furthermore, that is reality by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), but not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because, through the realization of the imagined nature, the view of superimposition and denial regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and the person (*pudgala*) does not proceed;
that is to say, it does not arise. This is the meaning.
"The view of superimposition and denial regarding the grasped and the grasper" is the detailed explanation.
If one adheres to the view that the error appearing as the grasped and the grasper— which is apprehended as a phenomenon (*dharma*) or as a person (*pudgala*)— exists in reality,
this is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the grasped and the grasper.
Alternatively, if one adheres to the non-existence of the grasper just as [one does] of the grasped...
Thus, there is the negation of the grasped and the grasper.

That characteristic of which, through knowledge, the views of superimposition and negation regarding the grasped and the grasper do not arise—this should be known as the characteristic of reality within the dependent nature, free from superimposition and negation.
Furthermore, that consists in non-existence by way of the imagined nature of the grasped and the grasper, and existence by way of being the basis for the conventional usage of those [terms].
For through such thorough knowledge, the view of superimposition and denial regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra*) does not arise.
"The view of superimposition and denial regarding existence and non-existence" is the detailed explanation.
Some say:

If one perceives emptiness as being an existent entity, there is thus a view that superimposes existence. Alternatively, if one perceives it as being a non-existent entity, there is thus a view of non-existence.
Both of these are views of existence and non-existence.
That characteristic through the knowledge of which those views of existence and non-existence would not arise is the characteristic of reality within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
And that has a nature free from both existence and non-existence.
For some say that through the knowledge of that, the perception of existence and non-existence does not occur with respect to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Others, however,
say that emptiness as the absence of duality by its own nature is the extreme of the superimposition of existence (*bhāva-samāropa-anta*).
Regarding the state of being free from existence and non-existence,

there is the extreme of the negation of non-existence (*abhāvāpavādānta*) because one superimposes the nature of existence upon that which is free from existence and non-existence— that is, upon the nature of the absence of duality, which is the object of non-conceptual knowledge.

Others maintain that these two explanations are to be considered together, because each [of the extremes] is connected to the views of both superimposition and negation regarding existence and non-existence.
In this context, "existence" refers to the existence of the non-existence of duality.
If one grasps that as mere existence, then one has superimposed existence;
if one grasps it as mere non-existence, then likewise—
It is negated.
Even non-existence, which is the non-existence of duality—if one grasps that as annihilation, then non-existence is superimposed as absolute non-existence;
if, on the other hand, one grasps it as precisely duality, then it is negated.

Because this is characterized by the absence of these two; otherwise, if one were to grasp it as having the nature of an entity (*bhāva*), it would be a superimposition (*samāropita*). Or, if one were to grasp it as being merely non-existent (*abhāva*), then both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) would be negated.
This destruction of the two extremes is the characteristic of reality (*tattva*) in its perfected nature (*pariniṣpannatva*).
But was it not already stated previously that the three natures are characterized by being uncharacterized?
Indeed, they were taught as being [unreal] because of the object, because of the construction of the unreal, and because of the absence of duality.
Thus, in that context "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas here it refers to a sign (*cihna*); therefore, there is no redundancy.
That through the knowledge of which [the two extremes] do not arise is the definition of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*).
The characteristic of the fundamental reality is that view—namely, knowledge—by which the views of superimposition and denial regarding the person (*pudgala*) and so forth do not arise.
[3) The Reality of Non-perversion (Aviparyāsatattva): Immediately after the reality of characteristics (lakṣaṇatattva), the reality of non-perversion must be explained.
Since it was listed immediately following that, he says:
"The reality of non-perversion," and so forth.
For impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness are called the "reality of non-perversion" because they are the antidotes to the perversions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self.
Since it was previously asserted that the other realities are included within the fundamental reality, he asks [the following].
Regarding the question "How [is it] in the fundamental reality? and so forth:
"The aspect of impermanence and so on" means that those modes which are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self are "impermanence and so on."
Its nature is impermanence and so forth.
To demonstrate the inclusion of the reality of non-perversion within the fundamental reality, he says:
"For the meaning of impermanence is the perception of the non-existent."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
For the meaning of impermanence is threefold: the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of arising and ceasing, and the meaning of being with stain and without stain.
That which exists eternally in such a manner is permanent.
That very same [nature] is impermanent from the latter perspective.
Regarding those [three natures], it is said "in their respective order": therein, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is impermanent in the sense that its object is always non-existent.

Others maintain that it should be understood through the method of etymological interpretation (*nirukti*) that "the non-existent is impermanent" means "it is impermanent. The dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) is impermanent in the sense of impermanence characterized by arising and ceasing at every moment; for it arises from conditions and its destruction is without cause.

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), although its characteristic is unchanging, is impermanent by virtue of the adventitious meaning of impermanence, which consists in the characteristics of being both stained and stainless.
"Suffering is called the characteristic of grasping," and so forth.
Suffering is also threefold:
the suffering of appropriation, the suffering of characteristics, and the suffering of connection.
Among these, the imagined nature is suffering by way of appropriation.
Because suffering is appropriated through that which is not fully understood, either in this world or the next, it is called "suffering.
Demonstrating how suffering is appropriated through that which is not fully understood, he says:
"due to the appropriation of adherence to a person and to phenomena."

Through the gateway of grasping at that existence, one adheres to the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*); thus, there is adherence to the person and phenomena. And because it falls into duality, it is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It has been stated that from adherence to the imagined nature, there is the continuity of suffering.
Furthermore, suffering is not merely the imagined nature itself,
because that [imagined nature] does not exist.

Alternatively, the imagined nature is suffering by way of appropriation, insofar as it is appropriated as a real entity through the adherence to persons and phenomena as having an imagined intrinsic nature.
The dependent nature is connected with suffering by way of its characteristic;
for there are indeed three kinds of suffering.
The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned formations—
these three types of suffering are, by their very nature, the suffering of dependence on others; thus they are characterized as suffering.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is suffering by way of connection; the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction.
How is it so by way of connection? To this he says: "because of its connection with suffering.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is suffering, and because that quality belongs even to the perfected nature, it is called suffering due to its connection with suffering.
In this very context of the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), "in due order" means that therein suffering is [the nature] from the perspective of appropriation (*upādāna*),
the dependent (*paratantra*) from the perspective of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) from the perspective of connection (*saṃbandha*).
"Non-existence, the non-existence of that [which it is not], and intrinsic nature are considered emptiness.
Thus, emptiness is threefold:
the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the non-existence of that [which it is not] (*atadbhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
In that context, the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

To demonstrate this, he says: "The imagined characteristic, like the nature of a rabbit's horn and so forth, does not exist as an object of apprehension even by way of a form that is not perceived; because it is non-existent, it is empty.
This is the emptiness of being other than that (*atad-bhāva-śūnyatā*), which pertains to the dependent nature (*paratantra*).

Demonstrating this very point, he says: The dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) does not exist in the way it is imagined by the foolish as having a dual nature, yet it is not non-existent in every respect. And in the way that it does exist, it is perceived by pure mundane knowledge (*śuddha-laukika-jñāna*). Therefore, because it is not that [dual] entity, its emptiness is "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); this refers to the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). For this very reason, he says that the perfected characteristic is of the very nature of emptiness because its essence is the absence of duality;
therefore, its emptiness is its very intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), its very essence (*svabhāva*).

"Because selflessness follows from the absence of characteristics," and so forth. Selflessness is threefold: the selflessness of the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), the selflessness of differing characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), and the selflessness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-nairātmya*).
Among these, because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks any characteristic, its selflessness is precisely the absence of characteristics.

For this very reason, he says that because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), its selflessness (*nairātmya*) is precisely the absence of characteristics; he shows that it is not so by way of any other mode.

The dependent nature (*paratantra*) has a selflessness that is "dissimilar" (*vilakṣaṇa*). This is because the dependent nature possesses characteristics in the form of real entities, yet it does not exist in the manner of duality as it is imagined by the ignorant.

Thus, being "characterized by the opposite of those [imagined] characteristics" means that the selflessness of the dependent nature consists in its dissimilarity to the imagined characteristics through its own dependent characteristics.
Thus, its selflessness is shown by way of its being an imagined self.

As for the perfected [nature], its selflessness is its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); since the perfected nature consists in the absence of the apprehended and the apprehender, it is selfless. Therefore, by stating that its selflessness is its own characteristic, he shows that the perfected phenomenon has selflessness as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*).
What, then, is the distinction between these two—emptiness and selflessness?

Some say that the distinction between these two is as follows: when something is not present in a certain place, that place is empty of it; and when something does not have another as its own essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is without self (*anātman*).

However, in reality there is no difference at all; the distinction exists only through a difference in formal definition (*vyavasthāna*). For, based on the fact that something lacks an intrinsic nature because it is not present in a certain place, one speaks of "selflessness" (*nairātmya*); whereas for the other, based on the fact that it lacks a perfected intrinsic nature therein, one speaks of "emptiness" (*śūnyatva*). [End of fragment].

Within the threefold fundamental reality, three kinds of impermanence are demonstrated in sequence as the counteragents to the extremes of superimposition and denial, and by means of showing adventitious stains:
namely, the impermanence of non-existence, the impermanence of arising and ceasing, and the impermanence of being both stained and stainless.
Thus, up to the threefold selflessness, what has been described is the state of non-perversion.
[4] Regarding the reality of cause and fruit (*phalahetutattva*): immediately following that, the reality of cause and fruit must be explained; therefore, he says:
"[120] The reality of cause and fruit exists within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*)," and so forth. In this regard, first the concise position (*saṃkṣepapakṣa*) is presented.
With reference to the truth of suffering, it is the reality of the fruit;
the truth of origination is the reality of the cause.
Likewise, within the category of purification, the truth of cessation is the reality of the fruit, and the truth of the path is the reality of the cause.
Thus, the four truths beginning with suffering constitute the reality of cause and fruit.
It has been stated that within the fundamental reality (mūlatattva) lie the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
however, it is not yet understood how the fundamental reality has the nature of the truths of suffering and so forth. Therefore, he asks:
How is it that the threefold fundamental reality is the truth of suffering and so forth? To this he says:
because it is characterized by impermanence and the rest.
"From that, the truth of suffering is understood. Thus,

it is impermanent because it possesses the characteristics of the truth of suffering— namely, being suffering, empty, and non-self— and it has been explained in detail that this [impermanence] exists in its entirety within each of the categories, such as the imagined and so forth.
Therefore, the imagined and the other [two natures] are each intended as the truth of suffering.
The fundamental reality is the truth of origination by way of the threefold meaning of origination, respectively.
Since that very origination is not understood, he says:
The meaning of "origination" (samudaya) is threefold:
latent predisposition (vāsanā), emergence (samutthāna), and non-separation (avisaṃyoga).
Thus,
origination is threefold: origination as latent predispositions (*vāsanā-samudaya*), origination as manifestation (*samutthāna-samudaya*),
and origination as non-separation (*avisaṃyoga-samudaya*).
In this context, the origination of latent predispositions (vāsanā) should be understood as the imagined nature (parikalpitasvabhāva).
Therefore, it is said:
"the latent predisposition for attachment to the imagined nature."

For when the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist, worldly phenomena establish the latencies of conceptualization and affliction based on the adherence [to the notion] that "it exists. However, supramundane phenomena are free from such adherence.
Therefore, the imagined nature is said to be the origin of latencies.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) consists of origination and so forth. Origination is the acquisition of self-existence (*ātmalābha*).
That from which something arises is its origination by way of emergence (*samutthāna-samudaya*), because it emerges from that. Furthermore, as to what its nature is, he says:
"karma and afflictions" (*karmakleśāḥ*).
And because they have the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), they are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The origin through non-separation is suchness (*tathatā*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Non-separation from the obscurations" means this:
as long as suchness is not separated from the obscurations, so long does suffering arise.
Or, suchness that is not dissociated from obscurations is the nature of origination; thus, there is the attainment of the name "origination.
The fundamental reality, by means of three kinds of cessation, is the truth of cessation.
Since that is not understood, he says:

Cessation is considered to be threefold: the non-arising of intrinsic nature, the non-arising of the two [natures], and the cessation of stains. Among these, the non-arising of intrinsic nature refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
For because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there is its absolute non-arising, like the son of a barren woman.
The non-arising of the apprehended and the apprehender belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
Since that too is utterly devoid of the natures of the apprehended and the apprehender, its non-arising consists in its being essentially a delusion regarding duality.
The two stains and their cessation constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction.
Since that [perfected nature] is not yet understood, he says:
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is called suchness (*tathatā*).
Defilement is of two kinds:
the obscuration of passion and so forth, and the imagined (*parikalpita*).

In that regard, when the seed has been extracted from its basis by means of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the acceptance (*kṣānti*) consisting in the absolute non-arising of the stains such as passion is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the acceptance consisting in the non-arising of the imagined stain (*parikalpita-mala*) by means of non-dual knowledge whose object is suchness (*tathatā-gocara*) is suchness itself.
For these two constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This threefold cessation should be understood as corresponding respectively to the imagined nature and so forth within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*).

Others, however, state that through the penetration of suchness (*tathatā*), there is the pacification of the two stains—the afflictions and the imagined—whereby suchness is called "the cessation of the two" and "the cessation by nature. [122]
Because of the statement:
"Nature is suchness;
because the mind is luminous by nature."
Therefore, that cessation which has suchness as its object is called "cessation by nature" (*prakṛti-nirodha*).
Cessation by deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is merely the state of having been ceased.
Others maintain that "cessation" (*nirodha*) is so called because one ceases [from defilements] within it; thus it is "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, because cessation has the nature of non-arising, all such points as the non-arising of intrinsic nature are subsumed and termed the "truth of cessation.
The inclusion of the truth of cessation within the fundamental reality has thus been explained.
Immediately following that, however, the truth of the path must be included; therefore, he asks.
How is the truth of the path established within the threefold fundamental reality? To this end, there is the statement beginning with: "thorough knowledge and abandonment," and so forth.
Regarding "the thorough knowledge of the imagined":
since the imagined is absolutely non-existent, there is only its thorough knowledge and not its abandonment;
for the abandonment of that which is non-existent is not logical.

Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra*), there is thorough knowledge and abandonment. For the dependent nature is to be understood as non-existent in the manner in which it appears, yet not non-existent in its entirety like the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
Furthermore, because it consists of the essence of karma and afflictions, it is to be abandoned.

Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), there is thorough knowledge and the realization of attainment. For the perfected nature is to be thoroughly known by way of its characteristic of being free from existence and non-existence, and by way of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

The state of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is to be fully understood through the thought that it must be realized as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) free from [conceptual] constructs. Cessation (*nirodha*) is to be realized through the realization of attainment.
Others, however, maintain that both [cessation and transformation] are to be realized in both ways.
For thorough knowledge is twofold: thorough knowledge as cognition and thorough knowledge as abandonment.
Among these, the first and the third are to be thoroughly known through cognition;
the second, however, is to be thoroughly known through both.
Realization is also twofold: realization through knowledge and realization through attainment.
Among these, all three are to be realized by means of realization through knowledge.
But by means of the direct realization of attainment, it is indeed the third [truth].
Thus, in this fundamental reality, the truth of the path should be understood as being established through thorough knowledge, abandonment, and direct realization;
however, it is not because of its inclusion within those [other two truths].
And here, by means of the four truths, that which is affliction, that from which it arises, the purification of those two, and that from which it arises, are fully elucidated;
their sequence, however, is according to the order of realization (*abhisamaya*).
[5] The Reality of the Gross and the Subtle:
There is the gross reality and the subtle.
The gross reality is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), while the subtle reality is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Since one first matures sentient beings through the coarse [method] and subsequently liberates those who have been matured through the subtle,
the coarse comes first and the subtle later;
the statement is expressed in reverse order for the sake of conforming to the verse (*kārikā*).
In this context, conventional truth (*saṃvṛttisatya*) is the gross reality because it is the object of non-concentrated cognition;
ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the subtle reality because it is the object of concentrated cognition.
Alternatively, it is gross because it is the object of [ordinary] consciousness.
It is subtler than the object of knowledge.

Since it has been asserted that all principles (tattvas) are included within the root-principle (mūlatattva), he asks: "How is that to be understood in relation to the root-principle? To this, he says:
Designation is the state of practice;
thus is the subsequent elucidation.
Designation, practice, and manifestation are to be understood as the coarse reality within the fundamental reality;
explaining this very point, he says:
For it is said in detail that "convention is threefold.
The establishment of the form of a non-existent object as a jar or a cloth is the convention of designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛtti*).

Others maintain that the verbal expression of names (*nāmābhilāpa*) according to the specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) of form, feeling, perception, and so forth, is conventional designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛtti*).

Some hold that whatever is conventionally expressed in dependence upon verbal expression—such as "form" or "feeling"—is conventional designation. Because it does not exist as a real entity like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), its nature is merely imagined (*parikalpita*).

The conventionality of apprehension (*pratipatti-saṃvṛtti*) is that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by which form and so forth, as well as pots and so forth—which, though not external to the manifestation of consciousness, appear as if they were external—are adhered to as real entities according to their conventional establishment; that conceptual construction is the conventionality of apprehension. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the conventionality of disclosure" (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti*) has the sense of conjunction. The conventionality of disclosure is the demonstration of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), which transcends even the state of being conceptual construction, through such synonyms as emptiness, suchness, the stained, and the stainless.

Through these three types of concealment (*saṃvṛti*), the nature of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) should be understood as applying to the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) in their respective order.
Conventional truth is linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).
"Designation" (prajñapti) means a verbal expression.

Conventional usage based on mere verbal expression in the absence of an objective referent is "conventional designation" (prajñaptisaṃvṛti). Precisely because the object does not exist, that which is conceptually constructed through conventional designation is conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
Adherence to an object when no such object exists is apprehension (*pratipatti*).
Conventional usage based on that is the conventionality of apprehension (*pratipatti-saṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, that is the conceptual construction of adherence (*abhiniveśa-vikalpa*).
Therefore, through the conventionality of practice, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
That which indicates the ineffable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) by means of terms such as "suchness" (*tathatā*) is manifestation (*udbhāvanā*).
The conventional usage of the realm of phenomena by means of that [manifestation] is the conventionality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti*).
Therefore, by way of the conventionality of manifestation, the perfected nature is conventional truth.

In this regard, the status of conventional truth as the conventionality of manifestation through designation should be understood as a systematic arrangement for the sake of inclusion within the context [of discourse], but not as existing by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Having thus explained conventional truth, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) must now be stated; therefore, he says:

"But the ultimate is from one [aspect]" means that while the imagined and dependent [natures] are ultimately impossible as reality, the perfected nature should be understood as reality from one [aspect]. Furthermore, for what reason is that perfected nature called the "ultimate"? To this he says:
"For the ultimate is considered threefold by way of object, attainment, and practice."

Thus, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indeed threefold: the ultimate reality as object (*arthaparamārtha*), the ultimate reality as attainment (*prāptiparamārtha*), and the ultimate reality as practice (*pratipattiparamārtha*). Among these, the ultimate reality as object is *tathatā* (suchness). For it is "supreme" (*parama*) because it is supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*), and it is called "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) because it is the object (*artha*), that is, the domain (*viṣaya*) of that [knowledge]. This is like the case of sense objects (*indriyārtha*). Demonstrating this very point, he says: "because it is the object of supreme knowledge. The meaning is that it is established by way of being the objective support (*ālambana*). Since it is not separate from knowledge, at that time no objective support exists, just like the appearance of mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*).
For example, for those who accept that there is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there are no appearances of form and so forth apart from the mere representation of form and so forth.

Nirvāṇa is the ultimate attainment, characterized by the revolution (*parāvṛtti*) of having attained the utterly pure suchness (*tathatā*). How is it the ultimate? To this he says: "Because it is the supreme object. Since it is both supreme (*parama*) and an object (*artha*), it is the ultimate object (*paramārtha*).
In that regard, it is "supreme" because it is the foremost among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, and because it is the purpose of the path.

The path has purpose as its nature; for the path has the attainment of nirvāṇa as its aim, and nirvāṇa is the purpose because it is free from all faults that cause harm, since that which is accompanied by faults is called "that which is not the purpose" (*anartha*). Why is the path the ultimate reality of practice? Because its purpose is supreme (*paramo ’syārthaḥ*);
for "purpose" (*artha*) refers either to the object or the aim, and the object is—

Suchness is the purpose, and Nirvana is called "supreme" by way of its object; how could these not be mutually supportive? If they are mutually supportive, what fault is there? [The objection: There would be no certainty [of their being ultimate]. [The response: It will not be so, because of their mutual support, like the lion and the forest. How can that which is called Nirvana be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while that which is called the Path be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), yet both be called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)? For it has been taught that the perfected nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); however, it is illogical for the Path to be the perfected nature.

It is not because of the absence of prior and posterior parts that the path is not the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), nor is it because it is unestablished that it is included within the ultimate truth; therefore, he says: "The two are established by way of being non-otherwise and non-erroneous."

Alternatively, how can that which is unconditioned and called *nirvāṇa*, and that which is conditioned and called the *path*, be said to have the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)? For the perfected is suchness (*tathatā*), and this is the absence of the two characteristics in the dependent nature (*paratantra*). Thus, it would not be logical for *nirvāṇa* and the *path* to possess the perfected nature. This objection is not tenable, because in that case, the absence of duality is itself the perfected; it is not that the perfected is merely the negation of something other than that absence of duality. Therefore, it is something other than that.

And the two types of perfected nature—namely, the non-alteration and the non-perversion—are also connected with the term "perfected"; these are the unconditioned: nirvāṇa and suchness. The unconditioned [is as follows].

Because it does not become otherwise, the perfected is that which is conditioned and included within the Path by way of perfection through non-transformation; it is not elsewhere, for it is connected with the phrase "perfected by way of perfection through non-perversion. How so? To this he said: "furthermore, because of the absence of perversion regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*). Since one does not again fall into perversion regarding the object of knowledge, the Path is also perfected. And thus, there is no contradiction in stating that both the conditioned and the unconditioned are perfected, as they are intended separately.
[6] Regarding that, the well-known reality (*prasiddhatattva*)...

Since it is impossible for that which is well-known in the world to belong to a single [entity] according to its designation, it must be [the nature] of the imagined alone and not of anything else; however, because its own essential nature is not known, he says:

"Regarding the object," and so forth: "convention" (*saṃketa*) is the knowledge of the connection between a name and the named; "familiarity" (*saṃstava*) is the observation of its repeated application. "By means of an intellect that has entered into that" refers to what is the entry of the intellect into convention and familiarity? It is the recollection of them. This is what is meant: for all worldly people—whether they are learned in the treatises or not—the perception of a certain state as "this is the ground [of such-and-such]" and so forth is the same, by means of an intellect accompanied by the recollection of convention and familiarity. This is the reality established by the world (*lokaprasiddha-tattva*). Worldly... [128]
"Because it is established that it is exactly so, [the category] 'established by reasoning' is based on the threefold [nature];
for reasoning is indeed applied with reference to all three types of intrinsic nature."
Therefore, the reality established by reasoning is determined by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
since that is not understood, [the author], demonstrating it, says:
"That which [is known] by the wise who are experts in the meaning of reasoning," and so forth.
In that regard, those who are virtuous, wise in the meaning of what is logical, the dialecticians, and the investigators—
after [presenting] the basis for the previous explanation, the subsequent statement was spoken.

Alternatively, "the wise" (*santaḥ*) are seekers of what is wholesome, experts in the meaning of what is logical, and skilled in the composition of treatises that do not contradict the fourfold reasoning— namely, dependence, efficacy, proof, and the nature of phenomena;
they are dialecticians capable of investigation and refutation who, by relying on the teachings of the Tathāgata, compose treatises free from error.
Some Mīmāṃsakas, who are experts in their own and others' treatises and are investigators of what is beneficial and what is a fault, do not read the word "mīmāṃsakāḥ";
they speak as follows.
When it is asked, "Who are the 'virtuous' (sat) referred to by this term?", he says: "Those who are wise in the meaning of the yoga.
And they are of two kinds, because they are established on the stage of reasoning (tarka-bhūmi) and the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi).
Therefore they are called "logicians" (tārkika);
and since some among them follow what is well-known in the world, he says:
"Relying on the three means of valid cognition" (pramāṇatraya) means [acting] without contradicting the three means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the three means of valid cognition are direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and scripture (āgama).
Among these, direct perception consists of that which arises from the five sense faculties as well as mental [perception], such as the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Inference is the knowledge of an object to be inferred by means of a logical mark possessing three characteristics; authoritative testimony is the word of a reliable person; moreover, reliable persons are those who are free from the causes of falsehood.

Alternatively, because that which is already established [for oneself] is what is to be proven for another by means of a reason and an example well-known through perception, inference, and scripture, it is said "relying on the three means of valid cognition. In this context, "establishment" (*upapatti*) refers to the logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*), and "established nature" (*prasiddhabhāva*) refers to the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), since it is the means for communicating the object to be proven.
The "means of proof through logical justification" (*upapattisādhana*) is the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), because it establishes that [object] by means of it.
"Reasoning" (*yukti*) is the method (*upāya*) by which, through a specific application, the three features of the logical mark are stated.
Alternatively, "upapatti" (logical proof) is the impossibility of it being otherwise;
"sādhanayukti" (the reasoning of the means of proof) is the connection between the members [of the syllogism].
Thus, the compound is analyzed as "upapatti-sādhanayukti" (the reasoning that constitutes the proof).
Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "upapatti" (logical proof) itself is the "sādhana-yukti" (method of proof).
The term "upapatti" is included for the purpose of excluding other methods of proof (*sādhana-yukti*).

Thus, that established entity which is proven by the method of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*) based upon the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being one of the three natures, is called "established by reasoning" (*yukti-prasiddha*).
The well-known reality has been explained.
[7) The Reality of the Object of Purification: Immediately following that, however, the object of purification must be explained; therefore, he says:
"The reality of the sphere of purification is twofold."
Demonstrating how that [reality] is twofold, he says:
"the sphere of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the sphere of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The purification of the obscuration of afflictions is the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions.

The term *kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñāna* means knowledge for the sake of purifying the obscuration of afflictions, or knowledge regarding the purification of the obscuration of afflictions; the meaning is that its purpose is the purification of the obscuration of afflictions, or that it has that as its cause. "The sphere (*gocara*) of that knowledge which purifies the obscuration of afflictions" means its object (*viṣaya*).
In the same way, the objective domain (*gocara*) of the knowledge that purifies the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhijñāna*) must also be explained.

In that regard, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consists of all the primary and secondary afflictions to be abandoned through the paths of seeing and meditation; therefore, the reality of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—which is the object of the knowledge of seeing, meditation, and their associated applications—is called the truth of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
That is the purification of the obscuration of afflictions.

The object of knowledge (*jñāna*) is that which is to be known (*jñeya*). It consists, in its entirety, of the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*); these are, moreover, called inner science (*adhyātma*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), logic (*hetu*), medicine (*cikitsā*), and all the fields of arts and crafts (*sarvaśilpakarmasthāna*).
Among these, non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) that acts as an obstruction to knowledge is the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The purification of that [obscuration] is comprised of the stages included within the practice of the path that accords with supramundane knowledge, specifically the eleven stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*).
It also includes the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Furthermore, this [knowledge] exists within the mental continua of Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas, and its object of focus is suchness (*tathatā*) by way of its meaning as being all-pervading and so forth; therefore, suchness is the reality that is the domain of the knowledge purified of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Since both types of the sphere of purification have already been indicated by the statement of the reality of cause and fruit and by the statement of subtle reality, their further prescription would be redundant.
It is not redundant;
for that reality of cause and fruit and the subtle [reality] were stated from the perspective of the formal establishment of things (*vastuvyavasthānata*).
However, in this context, it is taught how the obscuration is purified;
therefore,
this twofold sphere of purification is proclaimed as belonging solely to the one perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
He states the reason for this very point:
"For no other intrinsic nature (svabhāva) can be the object of pure knowledge.
What is the reason? Because the unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) is defiled by the stains of depravity (dauṣṭhulya), and because that which is imagined (parikalpita) does not exist.

However, because the reality that is the object of purification is, by its very nature (*dharmatā*), the object of the two kinds of knowledge, it is established as belonging to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) alone.
Thus, the reality of the sphere of purification has been explained.

Immediately following that, the reality of inclusion (*saṃgraha-tattva*) must be discussed; therefore, he asks: "How is the reality of inclusion to be understood within the threefold fundamental reality? Demonstrating how the reality of inclusion is subsumed within the threefold fundamental reality, he says:

"The sign, conceptualization, and name are subsumed within the two"—this is the detailed explanation. "Within the two" means they are subsumed within the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita*). Since the reality of subsumption consists of the five categories (*pañcavastu*), he says: "beginning with the five categories as appropriate. It should be understood that the five categories are subsumed within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) according to their respective applications, and not necessarily in sequential order. Furthermore, the five categories are: [the imagined, the dependent, the perfected, the dharma-realm, and the path].

The sign (*nimitta*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—because all objects of knowledge are subsumed within these five kinds of entities, these five entities are called the "reality of inclusion" (*saṃgraha-tattva*). Among them, the sign consists of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*); they are called "signs" because they exist as mutual signs for one another. Furthermore, the "name" (*nāma*) is the verbal expression that indicates that very sign—even though the sign is inexpressible—just as the winking of an eye indicates something.

Discriminations (*vikalpa*) are the minds and mental factors associated with the three realms that conceptualize the specific characteristics of the nature of signs as previously described. Emptiness, suchness, and supramundane right knowledge have suchness as their object. Furthermore, the sequence of these is as follows: first, the sign (*nimitta*), which is the basis for the designation of affliction (*saṃkleśaprajñapti*), because it is the basis for the designation of affliction; immediately after that, the name (*nāma*), because one conceptualizes the basis for the designation of affliction according to its name; immediately after that, discrimination, which is that very affliction; and finally, suchness, because that affliction is ceased by supramundane right knowledge of suchness. Thus, suchness comes last.
And some say it is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Delusion has its cause in delusion, and its cause is *dauṣṭhulya*.
Therefore, error is its cause,
and therein knowledge is the natural tranquility.
According to others, by this verse the meaning of these five kinds of entities is expressed:

therein, the cause of the delusion comprised within the internal consciousnesses of the eye and so forth is the external and internal delusion comprised within objects such as form and the sense faculties such as the eye.
The cause of that external and internal error is *dauṣṭhulya* (disquietude);
furthermore, that is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) in the *ālayavijñāna*.
The cause of that latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is precisely that same external and internal delusion;
therefore, verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) functions therein,
and by the power of verbal expression, [the predisposition arises].
And the persistence of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
"Quiescence by nature" refers to suchness (*tathatā*),
because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is by nature undefiled.
And therein, "knowledge" refers to that knowledge which has suchness as its object and is comprised within the Path.
Therein, the two types of conceptualization regarding signs are comprised within the dependent nature because they are produced by causes and conditions;
[conceptualization] regarding names is comprised within the imagined nature.

Just as, because the object does not exist [apart from] the name, the name is included within the imagined nature (*parikalpita*), so too is the inclusion by way of function (*adhikāra-saṃgraha*) through the imagined nature; it is not an inclusion of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the name.
As it has been said:

Because it is established as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is not included among the five things beginning with the "sign" (*nimitta*); thus, there is no contradiction.
This is because, in that context, what is intended to be expressed is its inclusion within the [other] natures.
[133] Regarding the reality (*satattva*) of correct knowledge (*saṃyagjñāna*):
Thus, that which is always excellent— the reality (*tattva*), true reality (*satattva*), suchness (*tathatā*),
and non-dual gnosis having emptiness as its object— as well as the subsequently attained pure mundane right gnosis,
are subsumed under the single perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because suchness and right gnosis are respectively perfected through their perfection as being immutable and non-erroneous.
Thus, the reality of compendium has been explained.

Now, regarding the reality of differentiation, since it is not understood how many types there are and how they are subsumed within the fundamental reality, he asks: "How is the reality of differentiation to be known within the fundamental reality?"
Therefore, he says: "The reality of differentiation is sevenfold.
To the question "How so? he replies: "The reality of engagement (*pravṛtti-tattva*), the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tattva*), and so forth," as explained at length.

That which was taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* as the sevenfold suchness—from the suchness of engagement up to the suchness of correct practice—is precisely what is here called the sevenfold reality of differentiation, namely, from the reality of engagement up to the reality of correct practice.

Therein, the reality of occurrence (*pravṛtti-tattva*) is the beginningless and endless nature of saṃsāra; that itself is the suchness of occurrence (*pravṛtti-tathatā*), because it never possesses a state of being "first.
The reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tattva*) is the selflessness of persons and phenomena; it is the fourfold suchness of characteristics due to its non-alterability.
The reality of representation (*vijñaptitattva*) is the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) regarding phenomena;

it is non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Others say that it is the reality of representation because it serves as the basis for representation, and because it does not undergo change into something else.
The reality of cognition (*vijñapti-tattva*) is said to be the reality of representation (*jñapti-tattva*).
The reality of configuration (*saṃniveśa-tattva*) is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*),
because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are situated within suffering.
And that very suchness is "always just so" (tathatā).
The reality of false practice is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
Furthermore, this refers to the engagement with those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of perceiving them as possessing qualities.
The reality of purity (*viśuddhitattva*) is the purification of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, that is both suchness (*tathatā*) and the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Others maintain that its nature as the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is the nature of cessation, is indeed the truth of cessation itself.
The reality of correct practice is the truth of the path. The reality of representation is appropriate application.
Others maintain that both the reality of correct practice and the reality of representation are simply the truth of the path.
These three realities are also eternally just so; thus, there is the expression "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Among them, the reality of phenomenal activity (*pravṛtti-tattva*) is twofold.

It should be understood that within the fundamental reality (mūlatattva), there are the imagined (parikalpita) and dependent (paratantra) characteristics. Among these, "activity" refers to the beginningless continuum of living beings. Since that [continuum] does not exist [in itself], it is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
However, for those who possess that continuum, because it is produced by causes, it is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Thus, for those [phenomena], whatever their activity is, that is designated as the reality of activity (*pravṛtti-tattva*).
Alternatively, the beginningless arising of afflictions, karma, and birth is called the activity of *saṃsāra*.
And since that [activity] is produced by the adherence to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), therefore—
The reality of manifestation is twofold;
it is called the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*). Thus...
"Disposition is wrong course.
This means that false practice is the wrong course.
