In the same way, the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) is twofold. Because suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are produced by causes and conditions and because they have the imagined (*parikalpita*) as their object, the reality of the arrangement (*sanniveśa*) and the reality of wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti*) are subsumed within these two; one [is subsumed] in the representation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇavijñapti*), and purity (*śuddhi*) is correct realization (*saṃpratipannatā*).

The reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), the reality of representation-only (*vijñaptitattva*), the reality of purity (*viśuddhitattva*), and the reality of correct practice (*samyakpratipattitattva*): these four realities constitute a single fundamental reality, namely, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Among these, the perfected nature consists of the reality of characteristics and the reality of purity because they are established as being non-erroneous; the reality of representation-only and the reality of correct practice are perfected through the perfection of non-perversion (*aviparyāsa-pariniṣpatti*).
Here, the equality with sentient beings is shown by means of the three [realities]—the reality of engagement, the reality of manifestation, and the reality of false practice;
the equality with phenomena is shown by means of the reality of characteristics and the reality of representation;
and the equality with enlightenment is shown by means of the reality of purity.
The equality of wisdom is demonstrated by way of correct practice; thus it is said:
"The equality of sentient beings is proclaimed through three [factors], while the equality of phenomena is shown through two."
Thus, the equality of awakening and wisdom has been demonstrated individually;
this is the reality of skillfulness (kauśalyatattva).
Immediately after the reality of differentiation, the reality of skillfulness was indicated;
therefore, demonstrating that, he says:
"The reality of skillfulness is tenfold, consisting in the negation of the view of self. [135]

Furthermore, since it is not known how the tenfold view of self (*ātmadarśana*) occurs with respect to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, he asks: "In what way is this tenfold view of self? To this, he says:
"In being a single cause, being an enjoyer, being an agent, and exercising control; in being the object of sovereignty and leading, and in being the basis for affliction and purification."

Regarding the statement "the view of self occurs in these," it is connected with "in the aggregates and so forth. This, however, is called the "tenfold grasping at a non-existent self"; because the self does not exist, it is called "grasping at what is non-existent. [An objection: If the self does not exist, how can this grasping—which is dependent upon an object—proceed without an object?

[The reply: It is not that this [grasping] lacks an object; rather, it proceeds with respect to the aggregates and so forth. Therefore, as an antidote to those [views], the tenfold skillfulness regarding the aggregates and so forth has been taught.

Furthermore, why is it that this grasping at a self occurs only with respect to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, and not because a self exists as a reality? For when one examines [the matter] through reasoning, no self distinct from the aggregates and so forth is found; moreover, whatever constitutes the nature and activity of a self according to those who propound a self, all of that proceeds only with respect to the aggregates and so forth. Therefore, it is understood that the aggregates and so forth alone are the basis for the grasping at a self.

The grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) proceeds through these ten types of adherence to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*) and not by others; therefore, skill regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth should be understood as the antidote to all grasping at a self. For instance, "grasping at oneness" arises from grasping at a collective self within the five aggregates of clinging; its antidote is skill regarding the aggregates. "Grasping at causality" is the grasping at a self as a cause because one perceives the eyes and so forth as being the instigators [of experience].
Skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*) serves as the antidote to that.
In this same manner, the relationship between the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) should be stated for the others as well.
Alternatively, the notion that "everything proceeds because of a self" is the grasping at causality (*hetutva-grāha*).
The notion that the self (*ātman*) is the cause of whatever desirable or undesirable fruit arises from one's wholesome or unwholesome karma in this life is the "grasping at causality.
It is also called the "grasping at being an experiencer," as in:
"The self is the experiencer because it is conscious."
The manifest and the unmanifest are, however, the "food," because they are insentient.
Alternatively, the grasping at being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvagrāha*) is the notion that he alone who arises through wholesome and unwholesome actions is the enjoyer of their fruits.
Regarding the "grasping at agency":
it is the grasping that the self alone is the agent of good and evil deeds;
or, the grasping that the self is the agent who, endowed with instruments and so forth, performs various actions—this is the grasping at agency.
The "grasping at independence" (svatantratvagrāha) is the grasping that the self is that which possesses autonomy (svairavacitva)— that is, the authority (adhikāra) known as the self—
or it is the grasping at independence in the sense that this [self] possesses the autonomy for the production of a fruit that conforms to its cause.

The grasping at lordship (*adhipatitva-grāha*) is the notion that "the one who is the sovereign, the master, the lord— that is the self," or alternatively, the notion that "lordship consists in the performance of actions corresponding to their fruits— that is the self. The grasping at permanence (*śāśvatatva-grāha*) is the notion that "even though the self is impure due to the fivefold causes and so forth, it is nonetheless eternal."
Otherwise, however, there would follow the arrival of what was not done and the destruction of what was done; likewise, the absence of memory and recognition would result.
It is called "the grasping of affliction and purification" because it serves as the basis for affliction and purification.
Regarding the term "the yogi's grasper": yoga is the fixing of the mind upon the self, or the restraint of both breath and mind.
Yoga is a specific kind of conjunction between the self and the mind.
One who possesses that [yoga] is a yogin. "The grasping at being unliberated or liberated" refers to the conceptual construction that the self has been released from its prior bondage.
How does this tenfold skillfulness (kauśalya) subsume within the fundamental reality?
For skillfulness is proficiency regarding the aggregates (skandha) and so forth;
how, then, is it subsumed within the three natures (svabhāva)?
The question arises for one who does not understand [this]:

since those aggregates and so forth are included within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), this skillfulness (*kauśalya*) is proclaimed by the word "object of skillfulness" (*kauśalyaviṣaya*); it is not, however, that skillfulness itself is [identical] to that [object].

Therefore, it should be understood that the reality of skillfulness (*kauśalyatattva*) is also included therein by way of its functional scope (*adhikāra*), but not by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For example, it has been stated that the reality of cause and fruit (*phalahetutattva*) and the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) are included within the [three] realities.
Yet, even so, it is not clearly understood how they are included; thus, it was asked: "In what manner are they included?"
And therefore he says: "In that regard, for you, there are [two aspects]: the object imagined by conceptual construction and the object that is the true nature (dharmatā)."

It is established that those aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are included within those three natures (*svabhāva*). Among these, since they have already been taught, the inclusion of the aggregates within [the first nature] must be clarified before the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth. Furthermore, among those [aggregates], it is the form (*rūpa*) that is addressed; therefore, he says:
Form is threefold. How so? It is imagined form, discriminated form, and the form of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā-rūpa).
In that regard, what is the imagined nature?
It is that which is the imagined intrinsic nature of form.
Furthermore, that existence of an object which is imagined in a place where it is not perceived elsewhere is called "imagined" (parikalpita) because of its absolute non-existence.
"Discriminated form" (vikalpitaṃ rūpaṃ) refers to the dependent nature (paratantraḥ svabhāvaḥ) of form; the meaning is that it is bound by causes and conditions.
But for what reason is this called "conceptualized form" (*vikalpita-rūpa*)? To this he says:
"In that regard, conceptualization of form is performed.
This is because, in the consciousness in which form appears, those who have not seen reality do not fully understand it, and thus, due to the perception of form, they perform an adherence to form.

Just as there is the grasping at a self in the aggregates (*skandha*), so too, within the dependent nature (*paratantra*), that which is called "imagined form" (*vikalpita-rūpa*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of form, which is its true reality (*dharmatā*). This is emptiness, whose essence is the absence of both imagined form and the form conceptualized by imagination.

Just as "form" (rūpa) is—having been divided into three ways—included within the three natures (svabhāva), so too should feeling (vedanā) and the others, as well as the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and so forth, be applied. Thus, the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the elements and sense-bases (āyatana); the factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); the bases and non-bases; the faculties (indriya); the three times; the four truths; the three vehicles (yāna); and the conditioned and unconditioned—all these, beginning with feeling and the elements, are each individually imagined (parikalpita).
By dividing it threefold according to the distinctions in the intrinsic nature of the conceptualized dharmas, it should be subsumed within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Among those, regarding the appearances of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, that state of grasped and grasper which is absolutely non-existent—just as the state of being a grasped object is conceptually constructed (*parikalpyate*) in the appearances of form—that is "conceptually constructed sensation" up to "conceptually constructed consciousness.
That in which conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is performed by means of the grasped and grasper is the "conceptualized [nature]."
Feeling, up to and including conceptualized consciousness, [are the imagined nature].
The feeling of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the perfected nature of feeling.
In this same way, it should be understood for everything up to the consciousness of the true nature of phenomena.
In this same way, it should be explained in detail for the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the directions as well, according to their respective possibilities.

Whatever entity is denotable by a name—from form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) up to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—that too should be understood as having the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures.
How so?
In this context, it is the *parikalpita* (imagined) because it is designated as having the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth;
it is the *paratantra* (dependent) because it is the basis for designation and because that very basis is dependent upon conditions;
and it is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) because it is the absolute absence of the existence of form and so forth.

Is it not the case that it is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra*) that is designated by names as the entity of form and so forth, and not the imagined nature (*parikalpita*); thus, the conceptualization of the imagined is entirely purposeless?
It is not purposeless, because the intrinsic nature of form and so forth is superimposed upon that [dependent nature].
For in whatever way a name functions with respect to an object, in that very same way it does not exist; yet the foolish adhere to its being the intrinsic nature [of that object].

And that is a false determination, for it does not correspond to the actual reality anywhere. Why is this so? Because whether there is similarity or dissimilarity between the name and the object, the relationship of signifier and signified is excluded.

If words such as "tree" and their referents were of an identical nature, then, because the name would not be distinct from the form of its referent, its status as a signifier would be excluded— just like the referent itself. Furthermore,
because the referent would not be distinct from the nature of the name, its status as the signified would be lost, due to the absence of any restrictive cause.
Alternatively, it would follow that there must be another denoter for the name and another denoted for the object, leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, if one object has many names, or if one name has many objects, it follows that they would possess multiple forms;
however, it is illogical for a single entity to have multiple natures. [141]
Furthermore, for words denoting non-existence, there is non-existence [of the word] just as there is existence [of other words], because their referent is of the nature of non-existence;
or else, even that referent has existence, because the name exists.
This is the case when there is a difference in form (*vairūpye*).
Even so, there is no cognition of an object corresponding to the word;
for in that case, it is the word itself that is the "tree," not the object, while the object is neither a tree nor a non-tree.
Therefore,
the referent of the word "tree" does not possess a commonality with both trees and non-trees, because that referent is by nature not a non-tree.
And the exclusion of such [commonality] constitutes the cessation of the relationship of signifier and signified between the word and its referent.
Furthermore, if there were a difference [between word and meaning], the restriction between the signifier and the signified would not exist,
due to the absence of any cause for such restriction. Moreover, a name could neither produce an object nor manifest it.

In that regard, it is not something to be produced, because a name is applied to an object that has already arisen. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even what has already arisen must be produced again and again,
since the name is applied repeatedly.
Nor does it manifest [the name],
because a name is created after having grasped an object, and it is not logical for that which has already been grasped to be manifested.
It is not logical that by that very same downward slope another who does not know it should not grasp that same object;
nor is it logical that this very [slope] should be both the manifestor and the non-manifestor of that same object.
Manifesting agents such as lamps do not manifest their manifested objects in dependence upon linguistic convention;
nor is there a restriction regarding the manifesting agent with respect to manifested objects such as jars or cloths.
If it were seen that every object is manifested by every name,
then there would be no restriction regarding smell and so forth;
for it is accepted that things such as the *kuthāra* and *jāṭa* possess the capacity to produce smell and other qualities.
But it is not [their] manifesting nature (*vyañjakatva*).

Therefore, it is understood that the adherence to the expressed and the expresser (*vācyavācakābhiniveśa*) is indeed of an unreal object (*asadartha*), just like the adherence to the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakābhiniveśa*).

Thus, because the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are included within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the tenfold reality of mastery (*kāñcalyatattva*) should be seen as being within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) itself.
This instability regarding the aggregates and so forth has been taught as the antidote to the view of a self.

However, the meaning of the aggregates and so forth—in which sense this instability serves as the antidote to the opposing view of a self—has not yet been stated; therefore, that is now being explained.
The meaning of non-multiplicity, condensation, and delimitation is presented from the beginning.
The word "from the beginning" (āditaḥ) is connected with the phrase "is stated at the outset. First of all, the aggregates (skandhas) are stated;
and they are to be understood by way of three kinds of meaning.
It has multiple meanings, namely whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;

gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near. Thus, because the word "aggregate" (*skandha*) denotes many substances, such as those of the past, future, and so forth, it possesses multiple meanings.
Because they are summarized by way of expression, "aggregate" (*skandha*) is used in the sense of summary;
"summarized" means made into one.
And it is connected with the sense of delimitation as well: "aggregate."
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction;
it serves to combine both meanings: the sense of multiplicity and the sense of condensation.
He states the reason for this here:
Because the aggregates are established as distinct from the characteristics of feeling and so forth by means of the characteristic of form;
"distinct" (*pṛthak*) and "separately delimited" (*paricchinna*) are synonyms.
What is the reason here that the meaning of the aggregates is established by these three factors?
For the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is indeed the meaning of "heap" (*rāśi*); it is for this reason that it is established in this way.
This is also seen in the world:
in the world as well, it is observed that whatever consists of a collection of many things and is delimited is called a "heap."
Just as it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so too should the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and the others be understood.

In that regard, as a counteragent to this grasping at a single self— such as the notion that "this person alone is all that has been and all that is to be"— it was stated how one should act with respect to the meaning of the aggregates.
How so?
Because the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*) is made by subsuming under a single unity those things like form that are distinct from the self (*ātman*) and so forth.
Furthermore, this establishment of the three types of aggregates is for the purpose of counteracting the threefold delusion.
Delusion is threefold: delusion regarding unity, delusion regarding conventional reality, and delusion regarding the confusion of characteristics.
(b) Regarding the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*): after the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements are enumerated.
Therefore, immediately after the meaning of the aggregates (skandha), he states the meaning of the elements (dhātu):
"Another [meaning] is considered to be the sense of the seeds of the grasper, the grasped, and the grasping thereof."
In this context, the word "other" (apara) refers specifically to the elements (dhātu), because they were mentioned immediately after the aggregates (skandha).
For this very reason, the author of the Commentary also says: "Which is the other?
The elements."
The meaning of "element" (dhātu) is the meaning of "seed" (bīja).
For example, when gold exists, it is called the "gold element";
it is understood as the "seed of gold."
And that [consciousness] is divided into three types according to the difference in its results:
the subject-element (grāhakadhātu) and the object-element (grāhyadhātu).
And there is the element of the grasped (*grāhya*).
In that context, the meaning of the seeds of the grasper (*grāhaka*) refers to the eye-element and so forth.
Those beginning with the eye-element and ending with the mind-element are "the eye-element and so forth."
And because they serve as the basis for grasping objects such as visible form, they are "graspers" (grāhaka).
Because they are the causes of their own kind, such as the eye and so forth, they are called "elements" (dhātu).
The meaning of "seeds of the graspable" refers to the elements beginning with the element of visible form (rūpadhātu) and ending with the element of mental phenomena (dharmadhātu).
They are "grasped" (grāhya) because they are the objects of the visual consciousness and the other [sensory] consciousnesses.
Furthermore, they are called "elements" (dhātu) because they likewise serve as the causal conditions for their respective homogeneous [phenomena], such as visible form and so forth.
The objects to be grasped by those [consciousnesses] are the eye-consciousness element and so forth.
Because they have the nature of apprehending form and so forth, the graspers of form and so forth are the eye-consciousness and the others, up to the mind-consciousness.

These too are called elements—the eye-consciousness element and so forth, up to the mind-consciousness element—because they serve as the causes for their respective homogeneous eye-consciousnesses and so forth.
Others, however, say: the *ālayavijñāna*, perfumed by the karma of attachment to the eye and so forth, is the seed of the eye and so forth respectively;
likewise, the *ālayavijñāna*, perfumed by the karma of attachment to form and so forth, is the seed of form and so forth respectively;
and likewise, the *ālayavijñāna* itself, perfumed by the karma of attachment to the visual consciousness and so forth, is the seed of the visual consciousness and so forth respectively.
Thus, it must be considered that only the *ālayavijñāna* is denoted by the term "element" (*dhātu*), and not the eye and so forth.

The "element" is established in the sense of a threefold seed for the purpose of eliminating confusion regarding agent, action, and object. In this context, the preceding eyes and so forth are themselves the causes of the subsequent eyes and so forth; no other self or external cause exists therein. Thus, through skill in the elements, the grasping of a cause in relation to a self is eliminated.

Immediately after the meaning of the elements (dhātu), the meaning of the sense-bases (āyatana) must be stated; therefore, he says: "In the discernment of the objects of knowledge, the state of being a gateway for the arrival of experience is the supreme [meaning of the sense-bases]."

Thus, because there are many [topics] following the elements (*dhātu*), such as the bases (*āyatana*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and because the word "other" (*apara*) is a general term, the question arises: "What is other? In order to make it known that—since it was mentioned immediately after the elements—the word "other" refers in meaning specifically to the bases, he says: "The base. Among these, the six internal bases are for the purpose of the experience of feeling; they are "bases" in the sense of being doors for the experience of the discernment of objects. The six external ones are for the purpose of the arrival [of the object]; thus, the meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) is the meaning of a door for arrival (*āya*).
Influx (*āya*) means arrival (*āgama*).
They are called "bases" (*āyatana*) because they extend (*tanvanti*) the experience and the discernment of objects.
There is a distinction between internal and external bases based on the difference between the door of the experience of what is felt and the door of its enjoyment.
For that which is felt—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is experienced;
thus it is called "enjoyment" (upabhoga). The meaning is that it is experienced.

The internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāny āyatanāni*) alone have been taught as the gateway for that enjoyment of feeling (*vedanopabhoga*). Although the objects (*viṣaya*) are also gateways for its arising, the eyes and so forth are designated as "primary" because they are unique [to each sense]; they are primary by virtue of being the basis for benefit and harm, and by virtue of their capacity or incapacity for that [enjoyment]. For when the eye and so forth exist, there is the enjoyment of feeling through those gateways, but not when they do not exist. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the discernment of the object (*arthapariccheda*).
Because it consists in the grasping of the signs of objects,
and because it consists in the comprehension of those very objects, it experiences the object-field.
The external sense bases are called "bases" (*āyatana*) by virtue of being the gateways for its arising.
But they are not internal.

For even though they possess the status of being doors of entry, when there is an absence of objects, there is an absence of the experience of discerning the object, despite the presence of the internal bases such as the eye.
These must be understood as *āyatanas* because they serve as the doors of entry for both feeling and the discernment of objects, along with their associated mental factors.
For the apprehension of the two is primary.
This primacy of apprehension, moreover, is due to the experience of the fruit of karma and because it consists in the discernment of objects.
Since the conceptualization of an experiencer proceeds by way of experiencing the discernment of objects, the bases (*āyatana*) are established through these two kinds of objects.

In this way, the section on the sense bases (*āyatana*) shows that the sense bases are the experiencer and the owner, while the external sense bases are the object of experience; thus, the grasping at a self as an experiencer among those who are not the experiencer does not cease.
As for the claim that because of the benefit or injury to the sense bases such as the eye, the conventional designation of "experiencer" applies only to their substrate—that is incorrect.

Even in the case of the relationship between producer and produced, the status of object and subject is established because the presence or absence of consciousness does not deviate from the presence or absence of those two;
for, by the example of the non-difference between the appearance of form and its cognition, there is primarily no similarity [between them],
not merely through the metaphorical attribution of difference.

For example, because it serves as the basis for the conceptual construction of the grasped and the grasper, consciousness—such as that of dreams, illusions, or cities of the Gandharvas—is established as if divided into the forms of the grasped and the grasper through the relationship of object and subject (*ālambya-ālambaka-bhāva*), even though in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) it is undivided; likewise, there is no contradiction in other cases as well. Moreover, the relationship of object and subject is merely a figurative designation (*upacāra*) everywhere and does not exist in a primary sense.
For consciousness, whether arisen or unarisen, does not take an object as its support.
Because it perishes immediately after arising, because it does not persist at the time of the act of apprehending its object, and because it is non-existent;
an object— whether arisen or unarisen— is unfit to serve as an objective support (*ālambana*) in either case,
since that which has arisen does not persist and that which has not yet arisen is non-existent.
For an act of apprehension without a basis is not tenable.

Even for one who posits the relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject as being merely the causal relationship [established by] mere existence, the status of the present consciousness as an object of apprehension becomes meaningless;
it is established as having that very nature.
Even for that which is in the process of arising, [consciousness] is purposeless because of its non-existence.
It is not purposeless for that which is in the process of arising,
because when an object exists, consciousness acquires a self-nature that manifests as that object.
If the appearance of an object in consciousness were caused by an external entity,
then in the case of past, future, or dream objects and the like, consciousness would be devoid of form;
or else, due to the absence of such an object, it would be non-existent.
An effect is not produced by incomplete conditions,
because that would lead to an over-extension;
nor is it [produced] by those that are absent.
Therefore, [their] status as conditions is logical.
Furthermore, external objects are not the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for consciousness,
because consciousness exists even without them.
Therefore, it must be admitted that all consciousness, such as that of those suffering from ophthalmia, is entirely independent of external objects as its objective support.

Immediately after the meaning of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) must be explained; therefore, he says: "The meaning of dependent origination is, moreover, [defined] by the absence of superimposition and denial regarding cause, fruit, and effort."
The meaning is that [phenomena] arise from conditions that are effortless, impermanent, and efficacious.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "When this exists, that comes to be;
from the arising of this, that arises—namely, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth in detail.
And demonstrating that this dependent origination is intended as the negation of the superimposition and denial of causes, effects, and activities, he says:
"The meaning of dependent origination is the absence of superimposition and denial regarding causes, effects, and activities.
By the word *āyāsa*, however, activity is expressed.
In that regard, there is the superimposition of a cause (*hetusamāropa*),
because one imagines Puruṣa, Īśvara, Anupradhāna, and so forth to be the cause, having set aside ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links of dependent origination].
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
This is because [the opponent] postulates an unequal cause for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, ending with old age and death.
For the meaning is that an eternal entity such as the *puruṣa* is an unequal—that is, dissimilar—cause for the impermanent formative forces and so forth.
Alternatively, a cause is observed to depend on a modification of its own nature, as in the case of seeds and the like being the causes of sprouts and the like.
Furthermore, there is no modification of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that which is eternal.
The imputation of a cause (*hetusamāropa*) consists in the conceptualization of causality where there is no actual cause.

The negation of a cause (*hetvapavāda*) consists in the conceptualization of causelessness; for by asserting that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth arise without a cause, the status of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest as causes of the formative forces and so forth is sublated.

The superimposition of a fruit consists in the conceptualization that conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth—which possess a self—proceed with ignorance (*avidyā*) and other conditions as their causal basis.

Some maintain that while conditioned factors and the like proceed with ignorance and other conditions as their basis only when a self exists, they do not do so when a self is absent; thus, this is the superimposition of a self onto the fruits such as the conditioned factors.

Others hold that the superimposition of a fruit consists in the conceptualization that conditioned factors and the like, which possess a self either by being inherent in the substance of a self or by being the agents of its benefit and injury, proceed with ignorance and other conditions as their basis.

Denial of the fruit consists in the conceptualization that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth do not proceed with ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links] as their conditions; for example, the denial by those who repudiate good conduct, bad conduct, and the next world, saying: "There is no good conduct, there is no bad conduct, and there is no next world. Superimposition of activity consists in the conceptualization that ignorance and the others possess an active function (*vyāpāra*) in the production of the formative forces and so forth.
If it were imagined that ignorance and the other factors produce a real entity as a distinct thing during the arising of the formative forces and so forth,
this would be the superimposition of activity (*kriyāsamāropa*).
The negation of activity (*kriyāpavāda*) results from the conceptualization of [the factors] as being devoid of causal capacity.

For, although the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are capable of being produced by the mere existence of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links], one imagines them to be devoid of such capacity; thus, there is a denial of activity (*kriyāpavāda*).
It should be understood that because of the absence of that [denial], there is neither superimposition nor denial.
That is to say, it should be understood as "neither superimposition nor denial" because of the absence of superimposition and denial regarding its causes, fruits, and activities.

Thus, this skill in dependent origination should be understood as the antidote to the grasping at agency— whether attributed to a self or to something else— which occurs apart from ignorance and the other factors.
For herein, there is no self or anything else, distinct from ignorance, that acts as the agent of wholesome or unwholesome karmas.

There is no agent of consciousness other than the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). This should be stated accordingly in all cases: [consciousness arises] from ignorance and the other factors, which are causeless, impermanent, and efficacious.
The arising of formative forces and so forth.
Since the meaning of the possible and the impossible must be explained immediately after the meaning of dependent origination, he says:
"Of the undesirable, the desirable, and purification."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
It should be understood that "the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*) is to be known by way of seven kinds of dependence (*pāratantrya*).
In this context, "possibility" (sthāna) is the reason (hetu),
while "impossibility" (asthāna) is the absence of a reason.
As it is said in a verse:
One should speak the truth, one should not become angry, and one should give when asked, even if one has little;
by these three means, one shall go to the assembly of the gods.
It is understood as "by means of reasons.
Alternatively, *sthāna* means possibility;
*asthāna* means impossibility.
Furthermore, non-existence;
skill in that is skill in what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
The state of being dependent is dependence (*pāratantrya*).
The meaning is "dependence on another.
And although that [dependence] is sevenfold, it is subsumed within the three types of dependence on others: karma, afflictions, and birth.

Regarding the phrase "therein, dependence upon others [is found] in what is undesired": the "undesired" refers to the miserable destinies (*durgati*). Demonstrating that going there is dependent upon misconduct (*duścarita*), he says:

Because one goes to an unfortunate rebirth (*durgati*)—even against one's will—by means of misconduct (*duścarita*) consisting of physical, vocal, and mental actions such as taking life, along with their preliminary applications (*prayoga*) and subsequent consequences (*pṛṣṭha*); for the unfortunate rebirths are the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, and since they consist exclusively of suffering, no one has a desire to go there. Because karma is powerful and because misconduct is the cause of an unfortunate rebirth, one goes there by the power of karma alone, even against one's will. Regarding the dependence on others in what is desired: "By means of good conduct (*sucarita*), one goes to a happy rebirth (*sugati*)," for a happy rebirth is what is desired.
A good rebirth consists of the states of gods and humans.

Good conduct (*sucarita*) refers to abstaining from killing and so forth, along with their preliminary and subsequent stages; performing acts such as giving, honoring, and showing respect; and specific virtues such as loving-kindness and compassion toward teachers, preceptors, and those endowed with excellence.
Dependence (*pāratantrya*) means that for those who seek [a good rebirth] otherwise, without good conduct, there is no attainment of a good rebirth.
The arising in a happy rebirth is strictly dependent upon good conduct.

Regarding the statement "dependence regarding purification," the detailed explanation is as follows: purification is the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*). There are five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*): sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
When sloth and torpor are combined as one, and restlessness and remorse as another, there are five [hindrances].
They are called *nivaraṇas* (hindrances) because they obscure the side of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) without distinction.

When distinguished, however, they obscure respectively: the delight in the life of renunciation (*pravrajyābhirati*); the correct practice of one who has been properly exhorted by fellow practitioners regarding bodily and vocal actions corresponding to that [renunciation];

lack of laxity at the time of calm abiding (*śamatha*); non-distraction at the time of exertion (*pragraha*); and spontaneous flow at the time of both calm abiding and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, they are called *nivaraṇas*.

"Without having abandoned them, without having relinquished them, up until not having cultivated the seven factors of awakening"—by the mention of the limit "up until," there is also the inclusion of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), and the powers (*bala*).

"Because one does not bring about the end of suffering": the end of suffering is that wherein suffering no longer exists, which is *nirvāṇa*; "not bringing it about" means its non-attainment; the meaning is that one does not attain *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, "the end of suffering" means that because of this suffering, no further suffering is joined to it; thus, it does not produce such suffering, meaning it does not produce suffering that leads to rebirth (*pratisandhika*). Dependence regarding purification refers to being bound by the abandonment of the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*). Dependence regarding simultaneous arising refers to the two—the Tathāgata and the Cakravartin—being neither prior nor posterior, meaning they arise together.

"Because two Tathāgatas and a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin) do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system. Some maintain that for the two Tathāgatas, the intended world-system is the trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasra-lokadhātu), whereas for the Wheel-turning Monarch, it is the four-continent system (cāturdvīpaka).
Others maintain that for two Tathāgatas as well, it is only within a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*).

For the Blessed Buddhas, by virtue of their sovereignty over the *dharmakāya*, manifest both perfect awakening and final nirvana through their *nirmāṇakāya* in each of the four-continent world-systems within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
This is because the purpose of Bodhisattvas—namely, the undertaking of death and birth among Tuṣita gods and among humans—occurs within a single four-continent world-system.
This is the same for all other sets of four continents as well.

Therefore, they believe that the Blessed One, having attained perfect enlightenment in the Akaniṣṭha heaven itself, displays through his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) everything— including his birth in the Tuṣita heaven, his passing away from there, and his taking of birth among humans— within all the sets of four continents contained within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

In that regard, there is dependence on others (pāratantrya) concerning coexistence, because the arising of a Buddha or a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) is contingent upon karma conducive to such an occurrence;

and there is dependence on others concerning sovereignty, because a woman cannot exercise the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch and so forth, since karma conducive to being a Universal Monarch has the capacity to yield its maturation (*vipāka*) only within a complete physical form (*ātmabhāva*).
Indeed, a woman is not capable of enjoying the precious jewels, such as the [wheel] jewel and others.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the nature of being a wheel-turner and other such qualities are included.
Dependence on another regarding attainment refers to a woman's realization of individual enlightenment (pratyekabodhi) or unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttarabodhi).
Attainment is the realization of the state of a Buddha or a Pratyekabuddha.
In that regard, dependence belongs to the man, not to the woman;
for she lacks association [with others] like a sword, and because she cannot move through the three worlds, respectively. Furthermore, she is accessible to all types of rogues.

And because of their limited wisdom, they are unfit for awakening without a teacher. Regarding active manifestation, there is dependence on another because [wrong] views do not manifest in one who is endowed with right view, whereas they do manifest in an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); thus, "one endowed with right view" refers to one who has seen the truth.
Harm refers to the taking of life;
by the word "and so forth," taking what is not given and other such acts are included.
These, beginning with harm, have the nature of actions of body and speech.
They do not manifest in one who is endowed with right view,
because through the path of seeing, the afflictions that give rise to such misconduct as harming others have been abandoned.
They do, however, manifest in an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Because that has not been abandoned;
and its non-abandonment is due to the fact that the path which serves as its antidote has not arisen.

Thus, skill in abiding—which conforms to dependence upon the undesirable and so forth—is the antidote to the grasping at independence in [theories such as] a primal person (puruṣa) or a Lord (īśvara).
For if anyone were independent, they would not go to a miserable rebirth because of misconduct;
the same should be said for other cases as well.
Immediately after the explanation of the meaning of the possible and the impossible, the meaning of the faculties (indriya) must be stated;
therefore, he says:
"The faculty is of two kinds."
From the faculty of the eye up to the faculty of one who has already known;
here, moreover, the meaning is that of predominance.
The meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*).
To the question, "Of what, then, is there sovereignty over what? he says:
"In grasping, abiding, connecting, and enjoyment; [they have] the nature of the two purities."
Thus it is said.

And here, regarding the phrase "the state of being the sovereignty over the two," one should understand that the word *ādhipatya* (sovereignty) has been elided for the sake of conforming to the meaning of the verse.
Therefore, the author of the Commentary says:
"Because of their predominance over those," and "in the sense of grasping."
In this context, the word "artha" (object) signifies purpose;
it shows that the sense organ is the cause for the purpose of apprehension.
In this way, it should be stated elsewhere as well, according to the appropriate application.
"In those" refers to the apprehension of objects and so forth.
"Sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) means superior power; thus, "sovereignty" has the sense of being a cause (*hetutva*).
From form (*rūpa*) up to phenomena (*dharma*), these are the objects such as form and so forth.
The apprehension of these is the consciousnesses of the eye and the other [senses].
In this context, there is sovereignty over the six [faculties], beginning with the eye.
Because the eye serves as the basis for the cognition of all varieties of form without exception, it possesses superior power over forms and so forth; thus, it is called an "indriya" (faculty).
However, a blue form does not become the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition of yellow forms and so on.
In the same way, this should be explained in detail for the ear and the other [faculties] as appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)," the life-faculty is that which— impelled by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of prior karma— possesses the capacity for reconnection (*pratisaṃdhi*) in subsequent moments that are similar to each preceding moment within the continuum of maturation (*vipākasaṃtāna*), provided there is no cause for its interruption.
The life-faculty has sovereignty over maintenance; this is precisely as stated [in section 155].

He states the reason: "Because [beings] do not die through its predominance. Non-death is the continuation of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) projected by prior karma. Although food and so forth are causes for the maintenance of sentient beings, they do not possess the status of a faculty (*indriya*), because even when they are present, there is no continued existence once the life-span (*āyus*) has been exhausted. Furthermore, in the form and formless realms, continued existence occurs solely through the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) even in the absence of physical food (*kavaḍiṅkāhāra*). Nor is it logical for contact (*sparśa*) and the other [nutriments] to have predominance over continued existence in those realms, because the continued existence of sentient beings is possible even in the absence of contact and the rest during the states of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñīsamāpatti*), and among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*).

The female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*) have sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over the continuity of the lineage (*kulasaṃdhāna*). This means they function in the production of offspring and in the non-cessation of the lineage; thus, the "continuity of the lineage" refers to the production of offspring. Demonstrating this very point, [the author] says: "because of sovereignty over procreation. A certain specific portion of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) itself receives the designation of "female faculty" or "male faculty" due to a particular sovereignty. Where the female and male faculties exist, there is the establishment of the lineage; by their power, the lineage does not cease. Furthermore, even among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), as long as the female and male faculties exist, the establishment of the lineage persists. For the *gandharva* and others do not possess sovereignty in that regard; even when a *gandharva* is present, if one is a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*) or similar, the female and male faculties are absent, and thus there is no capacity for the production of offspring. Moreover, food and other such factors are not counted as faculties because, although they possess sovereignty, they lack that specific quality.

It has been stated that the faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*) have sovereignty over experience. To the question "In what way?", it is said: "Because of the experience of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma. The faculties of feeling are the five: pleasure, pain, mental joy, mental grief, and equanimity. For it is by these that the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma is experienced, because their nature is that of direct experience (*anubhava*). Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) does not have this sovereignty, because it is merely the equipment for feeling; and its status as equipment is due to the fact that feeling is the primary element within the maturation (*vipāka*). [156] Worldly purification is the abandonment of worldly afflictions.
Regarding the phrase "therein, of faith and so forth":
it refers to the five faculties (indriya) of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The term "sovereignty" (ādhipatya) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
Because they are produced by the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) as the antidotes to lack of faith and so forth;
others say, "because they are produced by the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

Regarding the supramundane purification (*lokottaraviśuddhi*), the term "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) applies to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others.
The abandonment of afflictions by means of the supramundane path is supramundane purity.
In that regard, the three faculties— the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known"— exercise sovereignty,
because they are respectively subsumed within the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.

In that regard, with respect to their occurrence according to the specific basis— such as the *anāgamya* stage— the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), along with mind (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), mental happiness (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), these nine faculties constitute the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
and the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). However, according to the Yogācāras, the arrangement is otherwise: within the two faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*)—there are ten faculties.
By adding *daurmanasya* (mental distress) to the nine previously mentioned, there are ten;
however, the *ājñātāvīndriya* (faculty of one who has already known) consists of only nine.

In that regard, during the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) consisting of the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one should understand that there is the faculty of mind (*manaindriya*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and whichever is appropriate among the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity—depending on the specific basis such as the *anāgamya*—as well as the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*). Furthermore, at the time of preparation, this [faculty of mental distress] is to be understood as being comprised by the longing for higher liberation following upon the stages conducive to penetration.
Thus, this faculty is of ten kinds according to its occurrence.
Because it is engaged in the task of knowing what is not yet known, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
That same tenfold faculty—

From the sixteenth moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), within this path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), it is called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*). Because there is no longer any state of something previously unknown that must be known, on this path of no-more-learning, the remaining [faculties]—excluding the faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyendriya*)—are obtained under the name of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvindriya*); thus, the faculty of "having known" is called the faculty of "one who has known."
Thus, for one who is skilled regarding the faculties (*indriya*), that grasping at a supreme lord among Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, Īśvara, and so forth, is turned away.
Regarding the meaning of the time periods (*adhvan*):
since the meaning of the three time periods must be explained immediately after the meaning of the faculties, he says:
"Because of the utilization of fruit and cause, and likewise because of experience. In this context, the cause is the reason for birth, while the fruit is that which is comprised within birth.
The utilization of the cause is the giving of the fruit; the utilization of the fruit is the exhaustion of what has been experienced.

Such a type of past [phenomenon] consists of both the cause and its fruit; therefore, the past time-period (*adhvan*) is so called in the sense that the fruit and its cause have already been utilized. Likewise, the future time-period is so called in the sense that the fruit and the cause have not yet been utilized. As for the present time-period, it should be understood as follows: because the present birth has already yielded its fruit to the cause, it is characterized by the utilization of the cause; and since the fruit of that [cause] continues to follow along with the present birth, it is characterized by the non-utilization of the fruit.

Furthermore, the establishment of the time periods (*adhvan*) should be understood as being based on the momentariness (*kṣaṇatva*) of entities, insofar as they exist as cause and effect at every moment.
In this regard, the utilization of the cause consists in the production of its own fruit.
The utilization of the fruit (*phalopayoga*) occurs because the fruit perishes immediately after its arising.

Thus, it follows that the past time period is defined by the sense of having utilized both the fruit and the cause, while the future time period is defined by the sense of not yet having utilized the fruit and the cause; this is the subject under discussion.
It should be understood that there is no utilization of the fruit and the cause in the future because the effect has not yet arisen, and for that which has not arisen, there is no destruction.
"By way of the utilization of the cause and the non-utilization of the fruit": there is utilization of the cause because it produces an effect;
there is non-utilization of the fruit because the effect is not destroyed.
In this way, for one who is skilled in the [three] time periods, the grasping at a permanent self is turned away.
Because nothing else is perceived apart from the temporal paths (adhvan).
Regarding the meaning of the Four Truths:
immediately after the meaning of the three time periods, the meaning of the Four Truths must be explained; therefore, he says:
"By way of sensation, its cause, its object, and the practice directed toward that object."
Thus it is with regard to craving. It is well-established in the world that feeling has the sense of suffering;
and in the treatise as well, because of the statement: "Whatever is felt, all that is here [regarded] as suffering."

Demonstrating that, within the established framework of the truths, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) sensations—whether accompanied by signs (*sanimitta*), pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are the meaning of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) says:
"In that regard, the truth of suffering is [defined] by way of sensation together with its signs.
From what [source] does it follow that "all sensation is suffering"?
Therefore it is said:
"Because of the statement, 'Whatever is felt, that here is suffering.

And that feeling is suffering according to its occurrence through the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
Or rather, it is suffering by way of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Furthermore, the "cause of feeling" (*vedanā-nimitta*) should be understood as those phenomena that serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā-sthānīya*);
that is, phenomena to be experienced as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant are the bases of feeling.
Thus, the five aggregates have been explained as the truth of suffering.
The truth of origination is [defined] by way of practice directed toward that [suffering].
By the word "that," the truth of suffering is referred to.
The practice by which suffering is produced is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

Furthermore, that practice consists essentially in the agitation of body, speech, and mind, preceded by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) directed toward feeling and those phenomena that serve as the basis for feeling.
In brief, it is said that karma which brings about the arising of existence is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
And by the phrase "of those two," the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is meant; "of those two" refers to the truths of suffering and origination.
"By the sense of cessation" means by the sense of non-arising.
And thus, because it is characterized by the non-arising of suffering together with its causes, cessation is said to be twofold:
that which is with a remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣa*) is [the cessation] by the sense of the cessation of the origin (*samudaya*).
It is called "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) in the sense of the cessation of suffering.

The truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering and its origin, in the sense of being the antidote to those very two previously mentioned factors, suffering and its origin.

Thus, for one who is skilled in the truths, because they have understood mere affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), the grasping at affliction and purification as substantial entities is overturned.
Because of its non-existence.
[1] Regarding the meaning of the three vehicles:
since the meaning of the three vehicles is to be explained immediately after the meaning of the truths, he says:
"by means of knowledge that discriminates between qualities and defects."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
The word "knowledge" (jñāna) is connected with both:
namely, with the knowledge of virtues and faults, and with non-conceptual knowledge (avikalpa-jñāna).
Alternatively, it should be understood that the word "vikalpa" (conceptualization) is elided in the middle [of the compound].

In that regard, one must explain by distinguishing between "from another" and "by oneself" through the knowledge of qualities and defects; whereas [in the case of] "without conceptualization," it is "by oneself alone. For this very reason, he says in the *Vṛtti*: "according to what is appropriate."
In this context, "by means of knowing the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra," the term *nirvāṇa* includes both the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*),
just as the word "tranquil" (*praśānta*) does.

In that regard, knowledge of cessation through its aspects such as peace (*śānta*), and knowledge of the path through its aspects such as leading to deliverance (*nairyāṇika*), constitutes the knowledge of the qualities of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is also characterized by the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

In that regard, knowledge through the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, as well as through the aspects of origin and conditions, constitutes the knowledge of the defects of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Having heard from others" means having heard from Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others about the qualities of nirvāṇa and the aforementioned defects of *saṃsāra*.
"For the sake of departure" means for the sake of exiting from *saṃsāra*.

The Śrāvaka vehicle is so called because it leads to liberation by relying on the voice of another. This indicates its distinction from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. The Pratyekabuddha vehicle is so called in the sense that one attains liberation by oneself—without hearing [the teaching] from others, such as Buddhas or Bodhisattvas—through the knowledge of the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra.
"Having not heard from another" distinguishes it from the Śrāvaka vehicle.

"By means of non-conceptual gnosis" refers to non-conceptual gnosis because of the penetration of the ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. It is the Mahāyāna in the sense of departing by oneself alone, without having heard from another.
For here, indeed, there is a distinction from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle by virtue of [this] knowledge.
Others, however, say:

the Śrāvaka vehicle is the departure [from saṃsāra] after having heard [the teaching] from another, by means of a knowledge that has the selflessness of the person as its object and which involves the conceptualization of qualities and defects.

The Pratyekabuddhayāna is the self-attainment of liberation independent of hearing [the teachings]. The Mahāyāna is said to be the self-attainment of liberation through non-conceptual gnosis that has the selflessness of phenomena as its object and which brings about non-abiding nirvāṇa. This explanation contradicts the commentary (bhāṣya).
In this way, for one who is skilled in the three vehicles, through the vision of mere yoga, the grasping at a self as the yogin is turned away.
[j) The Meaning of the Conditioned and the Unconditioned] Now, explaining the meaning of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he says:
"That which is together with designation and together with cause. [161]

The sign (nimitta), the question, and the meaning were revealed only later; therefore, what is this "later enumeration" (paścād-uddeśa)? To this he says: "the conditioned and the unconditioned," because these are enumerated last of all. Among those, the conditioned [is explained] from that which is designated (saprajñaptika).

Furthermore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established by way of its cause, its sign (*nimitta*), and its meaning. To demonstrate that [sign] through ignorance regarding the cause of designation (*prajñapti*), he says: "In this context, 'designation' refers to the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth. Since the intrinsic nature and specific qualities of phenomena are designated by means of the sets of names and phrases, the sets of names and phrases constitute "designation. The set of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), however, is also a "designation" because it manifests both of those. Furthermore, the "cause" is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as comprised of seeds.

And that [seed], entering into the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), has not yet yielded its fruit and is subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). For this very reason, in order to distinguish it from that which has already yielded its fruit, he says it is "subsumed under the seed. It is further described as being "subsumed under the signs (*nimitta*) of the locus, the body, and objects of enjoyment," which refers to the *ālayavijñāna*—this being the subject under discussion. The "subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses" refers to the mind (*manas*), the grasping (*udgraha*), and the conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Among these, the "locus" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*); the *ālayavijñāna*, appearing as that [world], is subsumed under the aspect of the locus.

Thus, "comprised within the basis" means that the body—the physical frame together with the sense faculties—and the *ālayavijñāna* which appears as that [body], are comprised within the body; the meaning is that they are apprehended as being the self of the body. "Comprised within experience" refers to what was stated subsequently; these two constitute the pair.

The remaining consciousnesses experience [objects] as sovereign objects (*adhipativastu*), and thus they are "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). Alternatively, the objects such as food and drink are enjoyed, and thus they are "enjoyment. Consciousness appearing as those [objects] is subsumed under enjoyment. This sign (*nimitta*)—together with its designation (*prajñapti*), its cause (*hetu*), and its associated mental factors (*saṃprayoga*)—is to be understood as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Furthermore, the "associated" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*); that which is conditioned is not merely [the sign alone].
He shows that it is indeed that [which is the cause]. But for what is that the sign (*nimitta*)?

It is the sign for the sets of names and so forth (*nāmakāya*), because they indicate their own specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*); and it is the sign for the mind and mental factors—designated as mind (*manas*), apprehension (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—which, following those [names], adhere to those specific intrinsic natures.
Some maintain that the signs of the *ālayavijñāna* consist of the grasping and conceptualization of persons; this is because [those signs] nourish the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) therein.
Others, however, think as follows:

Because it designates the specific nature [of things], perception (*saṃjñā*) is the cause (*nimitta*) of conceptual designation (*prajñapti*), according to the statement that "perception consists in the grasping of signs.

The storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which comprises the basis for existence and the common enjoyment of objects, is the causal sign (*nidānanimitta*) because it nourishes the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, the mind (*manas*), the grasping (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) constitute the objective sign (*ālambananimitta*) in the sense that they take the object as a sign.
And the state of being the sign of both the object and the subject is due to the formation of signs in both ways.
In that regard, the mind (*manas*) is that which has the constant mode of activity of mentation (*manana*);
that which constantly conceives "I" or "mine" is called the mind.

And that [mental consciousness] is associated with the view of self, the attachment to self, and the pride of self regarding the self; and with the five omnipresent [factors]: feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention.
"Apprehension" refers to the five bodies of sensory consciousness, because their characteristic is the grasping of the specific nature of objects.
Because it cannot be described as "self-cognizable," it is called "apprehension" (*udgraha*).
"Conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) refers to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
because that [consciousness] consists of the conceptualization of the specific and general characteristics of phenomena (*dharma*).
All this—the sign (nimitta) together with its conceptual designations (prajñapti) and its causes—is conditioned (saṃskṛta), because it is produced by karma and the afflictions (kleśa).
Furthermore, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) consists of cessation (nirodha) as tranquility (praśama) and suchness (tathatā) as the object of that tranquility.
It is logical that cessation has the nature of tranquility, because it is characterized by the pacification of suffering along with its signs.
How is suchness said to have the meaning of "quiescence"?
Because it is the object of quiescence.
But is it not [the case that] suchness is [identical to] cessation?

What connection exists such that *tathatā* (suchness) has the meaning of "quiescence"? Because the path has *tathatā* as its object. Furthermore, how is the path itself quiescence? Because it brings about quiescence. Nirvāṇa is quiescence; because it is quiescence, and because this [path] brings about quiescence, the path is quiescence. Thus, through a distinction in grammatical analysis (*vigraha*), both nirvāṇa and the path are grasped by the single term "quiescence" (*praśama*). As for the truth of the path, is it conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? It is conditioned, because it is something to be produced. If one were to say it is conditioned because it is not constructed by karma and afflictions, and because it is characterized by the unconditioned, there would be no fault.
In this sense, knowledge regarding the aggregates and so forth should be understood as skill in the aggregates and so forth;
thus, the meaning of multiplicity, condensation, and delimitation should be explained in detail everywhere from the beginning.

[The Compendium of Reality (Tattvasamāsa): The summary of the meaning of reality is as follows: in brief, reality is of two kinds; in detail, it is said to be of ten kinds. Therefore, he states that in brief it is twofold:
the mirror-like reality (ādarśatattva) and the object-of-vision reality (dṛśyatattva). Among these, the fundamental reality (mūlatattva) is the mirror-like reality.

Furthermore, regarding those three natures: for what reason is that called the reality of the mirror? Because the remaining [realities], such as the reality of characteristics and so forth, are seen therein.

As for the ninefold reality of the visible—which was previously specified as the reality of characteristics and so forth—for what reason is it called the reality of the visible? Because it is seen within the fundamental reality; thus, the reality of the visible is the reality of characteristics, which is free from conceit.
Therefore, one becomes free from conceit regarding the person and phenomena, the grasped and the grasper, and existence and non-existence, because of being neither superimposing nor denying.

This reality of the object of vision, which serves as the antidote to error and is characterized by non-perversion, is indeed the antidote to errors such as [the notion of] permanence. This reality of the object of vision for the departure via the Śrāvaka vehicle consists of both cause and fruit; it constitutes the departure of the Śrāvaka through the cultivation of the penetration of the four noble truths.

The reality of what is to be seen as the departure via the Mahāyāna consists of the subtle and the coarse realities. Because one brings sentient beings to maturity through the coarse conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti-satya*) and liberates them through the subtle ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one departs by means of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the reality of what is to be seen as the refutation of opposing disputants and the reality of what is established, [the text] asks "How so? and therefore says: "By means of reasoning, based on an example, because of the refutation. In this context, the "refutation" refers to an example well-known in the world; the "reasoning" refers to that which relies on words established by logic. The reality of what is to be seen as the illumination of the Mahāyāna is the reality that is the domain of pure gnosis (*viśuddhi-jñāna*).

For that [Mahāyāna] is the illumination of other scriptures regarding the sphere of knowledge purified of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable; furthermore, it is the Mahāyāna, which is the reality of what is to be seen through entry into all that is knowable, and it is the reality of summary. And that consists of five entities. Among them, because of the entry into all that is knowable, there is the reality of the vision of the illumination of non-erroneous suchness (*avitatha-tathatā*). There is also the reality of differentiation (*prabheda-tattva*), for by means of it, the non-erroneous suchness and the otherwise-suchness of phenomena are illuminated.

And the reality of the visible object (*dṛśyatattva*), which is the entry into all intentions regarding the basis for the grasping of a self (*ātmagrāhavastu*); this is the reality of skill (*kauśalyatattva*). For by means of all the intentions concerning the basis for the grasping of a self, one enters [into that reality], as previously stated: through the ten intentions, the statement of the summarized meaning of reality (*tattvapindārthavacana*) regarding the aggregates and so forth—which proceeds from the occurrence of the grasping of a self—is drawn out from the text according to its meaning for the sake of easy retention, and for the sake of non-confusion and lack of weariness; for when the beginning, such as the subject matter (*adhikāra*), and the end are clearly perceived, neither weariness nor confusion arises.
From the instruction according to the enumeration, the characteristic arises;
thus has reality been explained.
The third chapter, "The Investigation of Reality," in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable master Sthiramati according to the tradition of the Āgamas, is completed.
[166] Following the exposition of reality, the cultivation of the antidotes must be explained,
as well as the stages therein and the attainment of the fruit.
Therefore, the fourth chapter is commenced for the purpose of explaining that.

Because it was mentioned immediately after reality (*tattva*), and because it serves as the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) to the cultivation [of the obscurations], there is a mention of its stages and the attainment of the fruit.
He says this in order to demonstrate that the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are accepted as the counteragent in the Sūtra.
The cultivation of the counteragents is the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
For when they are cultivated, they are capable of abandoning the aforementioned adverse obstructions; thus, they are called "counteragents.
Furthermore, they are thirty-seven in number.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the noble eightfold path—

cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇā*), establishment (*āropaṇā*), practice (*abhyāsa*), and frequent exercise (*bahulīkriyā*) are synonyms for these. This [cultivation] must now be explained.
Because it was listed immediately after the [four] truths.

What is the reason that the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) alone is mentioned first, and not the cultivation of any other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)? He says:
In that regard, first of all, the detailed explanation begins with "caused by the craving for heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulyatṛṣṇāhetuka*).
Therein means: in the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*).
The word "first" (tāvat) indicates sequence;
first, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness is taught,
and afterwards, that of the others as well.

Because they do not understand the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, the foolish, through their attachment to formations as being pleasant, pure, and a self, take delight in the enjoyment of existence and feel terror toward the goal of nirvāṇa.

This lack of understanding regarding virtues and faults, as well as this attachment to pleasure and so forth, is turned away by the vision of the truths; therefore, for the sake of causing revulsion toward saṃsāra and for the sake of turning one toward nirvāṇa, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness and so on are taught at the beginning for the purpose of entering the four truths.
By means of the body, corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) is manifested; thus, corruption is a state of being ill-situated.
For in this way, since the body undergoes transformation as it is conditioned day by day, corruption is manifested through the body;
and from that, through the thorough investigation of the body, one enters into the truth of suffering.
To the question "For what purpose is this? he says:
For the characteristic of that [body] consists of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) that are always characterized by corruption (*sadauṣṭhulya*).
Since the conditioned factors of the truth of suffering are its characteristic— that is, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)— and corruption is manifested through the body,
one enters into the truth of suffering by means of the thorough investigation of the body.
Since it is not understood what "dauṣṭhulya" (corruption) is, he says:
"For dauṣṭhulya is the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Here, *saṃskāra* refers to the arising of phenomena.
And that is the basis of all ruin; it is *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption), and because it is repugnant to the Noble Ones (*ārya*), it is suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
As it has been said: "This birth is a misfortune, for when there is birth, there exist enemies such as old age, death, disease, calamity, slaughter, and bondage.
Those misfortunes would not exist if there were no destruction and no arising."
If the tree had not arisen, there would be no falling away of fire, wind, or forest fires;
"by that" refers to the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
and not to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) or the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Because those two do not pervade [all conditioned phenomena], and because they lack the characteristic of the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
the Noble Ones perceive every contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing as suffering, but not that which is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Because the truth of the path is the antidote to the arising of birth,
whereas ordinary beings do not abandon the accumulation of perversions;
it is also said in the Sūtra:
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Others say that the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is inflexibility (*akarmanyatā*);
others say it is not inflexibility, but rather corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*).
What is the reason?
Because it is unworkable (*akarmanyatā*) due to being associated with outflows (*sāsravatva*), its state of having outflows must necessarily be admitted as arising from a causal seed.
However, that [unworkability] may at times occur even without a seed in the continuum of an Arhat, due to the improper application of nutriment and so forth.
And this [transformation] cannot be *dauṣṭhulya* because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, the seed of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) residing in the *ālayavijñāna* is designated as *dauṣṭhulya*.
This body, accompanied by pleasure, pain, and neither-pleasure-nor-pain, is its fruit.
Therefore, that *dauṣṭhulya* is manifested— that is, made known— by means of the body which arises moment by moment and provides the occasion for pleasure and so forth;
just as, for example, a seed within a granary hole is manifested by its sprout.
Therefore, through the examination of the body, one enters into the truth of suffering.
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Because that which has such characteristics consists of conditioned factors accompanied by functional rigidity (*sadauṣṭhulya*)."
The meaning is: because they consist of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) together with seeds.

Indeed, the suffering of formative forces (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is so called because it is permeated by both the corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), and because it is the cause [of those two], it is termed "corruption."
