For this very reason, because of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the Noble Ones have viewed every contaminated thing as suffering.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to the body, one enters into the Truth of Suffering.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the cause of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This is because it is intended [to refer to sensation] born of contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja*).
Since that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is not caused by that [ignorance],
pleasant sensation therein is [characterized by] non-separation from its conjunction.

Craving is the cause of suffering. The craving for non-union with and non-separation from that [suffering] is the cause of suffering. The state of neither-suffering-nor-happiness is the cause of the craving for delight in that state and the craving for union with and non-separation from it in certain meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Because of the statement that "one touched by painful feeling delights in sensual pleasure," even a painful feeling becomes a cause for craving for pleasure. Through the investigation of that [feeling], one enters into the truth of the origin [of suffering].
For he, examining feeling (*vedanā*) by way of its intrinsic nature, its cause, its effect, its impermanence, and its suffering, enters into the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*).
The meaning is that he understands craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its effect.
For craving is stated in the Sūtra to be the truth of the origin.
What is the origin of suffering?
It is recited as "craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion," and so forth.
In this way, one enters into the truth of the origin through the application of mindfulness to feelings.
The mind is the objective basis for the adherence to a self;
because there is no other self characterized by qualities such as permanence, the mind alone is the focal object of that adherence to a self.
Therefore, through its thorough investigation, one enters into the truth of cessation as peace.
He states the reason for this very point:
"Because of the disappearance of the fear of the annihilation of the self.
For when there is a thorough investigation of impermanence and so forth regarding the mind, attachment to a self is turned away and the perception of suffering proceeds.
Therefore, because the fear of the annihilation of the self has vanished and because there is the cessation of mere suffering, one enters into the truth of cessation as peace.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to the mind, one enters into the truth of cessation.
Through the investigation of phenomena, because of the absence of delusion regarding defiled and purified phenomena, one enters into the truth of the path.
In this context, the defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*) are the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);

whereas the purifying phenomena (*vyāvadānika*) are those that serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the primary and secondary afflictions, such as the [four] immeasurables (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.

Having understood the relationship between the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) among those phenomena that are defiling and those that are purifying, one becomes oriented toward the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), which is the means for the absolute abandonment of all calamities.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of the Path.
Here, "entry" (*avatāra*) refers to the awakening to the specific characteristics of truth within each individual truth.
Therein, the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body is also by way of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
by way of its nature as consisting of many impure substances; and by way of its impure seed.
Also from the outflow of impurity;
also from the cause of the persistence of impurity;
also from the transformation of impurity; also from the lack of solidity like a mass of foam; also from its being discharged; also from its source.

Furthermore, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena is [contemplated] by way of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; also by way of their specific characteristics, causes, results, realms, stages, and destinies; also by way of being wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; and also by way of the discordant factors and their antidotes.
For Bodhisattvas, however, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness is likewise performed by way of non-apprehension for the purpose of abandoning conceptual construction.

Although the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have wisdom as their intrinsic nature, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" because these wisdoms are established through the power of mindfulness.
[b) The Four Right Efforts] Immediately after the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, the cultivation of the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) is taught.
What is the reason for this? To this he says:
"Because when the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) are fully understood," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthānabhāvanayā*):
although it is stated without qualification, it should be understood here as referring specifically to the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By means of the elements (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and locations (*avakāśa*), through aspects such as the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, and likewise through aspects such as the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) realms and stages, the learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), and so on; and by means of the various distinctions between the contaminated and uncontaminated realms, stages, learners, and those beyond learning—with both the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) being thoroughly known in all their modes—for the sake of the removal of the adverse factors: here, the removal of the adverse factors consists in the severing of the continuity of those already arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen.
And for the sake of the attainment of the remedies: the attainment of the remedies consists in the continuation of the continuity of those already arisen and the arising of those not yet arisen.

"Vigor proceeds in four ways" means that vigor functions in four ways according to the distinction between arisen and unarisen factors, both in terms of the discordant side (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
The detailed explanation—"for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states," and so forth—demonstrates through scripture that vigor itself proceeds in these four ways.
By mentioning "the detailed explanation," the connection to the remainder of the text is indicated.
In this regard, the remaining text is as follows:
"He generates desire for abandonment, he exerts himself, he arouses vigor, he uplifts the mind, and he correctly applies himself.
Thus, he generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states," and so forth.
"In this way, he generates desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen," and so forth.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, and takes hold of the mind for the stability, increase, non-confusion, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
He exerts himself correctly:
for those [wholesome states] that have arisen, there is their maintenance so as not to let them decline;
there is their increase through continuous production.
"Attainment through fulfillment" means reaching the highest excellence; "generating desire" shows the perfection of diligence applied with reverence.
"Exerting oneself" means directing the body and mind toward [the goal] in order to abandon laziness. "Arousing vigor" is for the purpose of removing lethargy and agitation.

How does one initiate [the effort]? One uplifts the sunken mind through mental attentions (*manaskāra*) toward phenomena that are to be felt and gladdened; one correctly applies the agitated mind to that very same object, which means one sustains it through mental attentions toward phenomena that are to be felt and gladdened. In this way, it is made known that the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) consist essentially of vigor (*vīrya*), for by these one correctly sustains body, speech, and mind; thus they are called "right endeavors" (*samyakpradhāna*).
The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the workability (*karmanya*) of stability therein.
Thus is the detailed explanation; "therein" refers to that cultivation of vigor for the removal of adverse factors.

Workability (*karmaṇyatā*) is the fitness for the accomplishment of all goals through the stability of the mind. And that workability arises through the predominance of desire (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*); therefore, it is said: "Workability is the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). "Success" (*ṛddhi*) is the accomplishment (*samṛddhi*) of every goal, such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth. In the sense of being their foundation, they are called "bases of psychic power," which means they are the causes of psychic power. For this very reason, it is said: "Because they are the cause of the accomplishment of all goals. Furthermore, these are: the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*); the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of vigor accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment. In that regard, "concentration of desire" is when, through the predominance of desire, one proceeds with reverence in the cultivation of vigor and touches upon one-pointedness of mind. "Concentration of vigor" is when, while exerting vigor, one touches upon one-pointedness of mind through continuous application. [173] Mind... [text continues].
Concentration (*samādhi*) is when, having come to the seed of previous concentration, one touches one-pointedness of mind while holding the mind within the mind itself.
The concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*) is when, through thorough examination, one touches one-pointedness of mind.

Here, "stability" (*sthiti*) should be understood as the stability of the mind, which is concentration; the inclusion of the term "concentration" is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the [four] characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

Since the pliancy of mind (*citta-karmaṇyatā*) arises for one who has initiated vigor (*ārabdha-vīrya*), and since the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*) result from that, the bases of psychic power are taught immediately after the right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, as to what the purpose and cause of that pliancy are, it is said: "It should be understood as following from the cultivation of the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) for the sake of abandoning the five faults.
Here, "following" (*anvaya*) means "cause" (*hetu*).
And since those five faults are not understood, he asks, "What are these five faults? and, demonstrating them, says: "Laziness, lack of faith, forgetfulness, lethargy, and excitement."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Since these are indeed six faults, he says: "In that context, lethargy and excitement are treated as a single fault; thus there are five.
Among those, laziness is a fault at the time of application, because one fails to apply oneself due to it.
For one who is striving, the loss of the instruction is a fault, because of the absence of mental concentration (*cittasamādhāna*).

For one who is concentrated, laxity and excitement (*layauddhatya*) are faults, because of the absence of mental pliancy (*cittakarmaṇyatā*). When laxity and excitement have been stilled, non-application (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is a fault; non-application here is equanimity (*upekṣā*), for by it there is the pacification of that state.
The phrase "exertion is a fault in [the state of] tranquility" applies here.
Exertion is volition; because sinking and excitement have departed and equanimity has been attained, it is called "tranquil."
[The Eight Formative Forces of Abandonment] The formative forces of abandonment are the formative forces for the sake of abandonment.
For the abandonment of what?
For the sake of abandoning the five faults just mentioned,
if that is so, one must state how the eight formative forces of abandonment are established for their abandonment.
In that regard, there are four— zeal, exertion, faith, and pliancy— for the abandonment of laziness.
In this context, *chanda* is aspiration;
*vyāyāma* is vigor;
and *śraddhā* is firm conviction.
Pliancy is serviceability.
But how are these established for the purpose of abandoning laziness? To this he says:
"And they should be understood in their respective order."
"The basis, that which is based upon it, its cause, and its fruit. Thus,
he shows that because these are mutually influenced, they lead to the abandonment of laziness.
The basis of exertion is aspiration; exertion is dependent [upon it],
because aspiration is preceded by exertion.
Faith is the cause of that desire for the basis.
To explain how this is so, he says: "Because there is longing when there is conviction.
For one who possesses faith, there arises a longing for action regarding the causes and their fruits.
The fruit of that exertion which is based upon it is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because one who has initiated vigor attains a specific state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."
For the attainment of a specific state of concentration is the sign of pliancy;
therefore, it is said that for one who has initiated vigor, pliancy is the fruit of exertion because of the attainment of a specific state of concentration.
For thus, in one who has initiated vigor, joy arises from the departure of the defects of dysphoria and conceptualization;
from the joy of the mind, there is pliancy of body and mind, characterized by functional flexibility;
and from that, there is the attainment of a distinguished state of meditative concentration.
Thus it is said.
And here, vigor— along with its cause and its fruit— is taught as the antidote to laziness.

The antidotes to the four faults are, respectively: therein, mindfulness is the antidote to the loss of instruction; clear comprehension is the antidote to lethargy and excitement; volition is the antidote to [unintended] formative activity; and equanimity is the antidote to formative activity—here, "equanimity of formation" is what is to be understood.

Furthermore, with the intention of explaining the characteristics of mindfulness and the other [faculties], he says this: "Moreover, those beginning with mindfulness are to be understood in their respective order.

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is non-forgetfulness regarding the object (*ālambana*). This has been explained in detail: "The object" means that which is to be established in the mind; the meaning is that which is expressed as the subject matter of instruction (*avavāda*).

Clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) consists in the recognition of laxity and excitement when mindfulness is not lost; for one whose mindfulness is established necessarily possesses clear comprehension. Therefore, it says "when there is no loss of mindfulness. The meaning is that, having recognized laxity and excitement, one proceeds effortlessly through the union of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

"Equanimity" (upekṣā) means the non-activation of other objects; this is what is meant: one whose mindfulness is well-established correctly understands, according to reality, whether the mind is sunken or excited during the instruction, and applies effort toward the removal of that sinking and excitement; and through the removal of sinking and excitement, one practices equanimity.
Thus, there is for him the pliancy and serviceability of the mind.

And here, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used in its own sense [to denote the state itself], as in the case of "being one's own chest" (*svapeṭatva*) and so forth; this is what is meant by "abiding in serviceability. [176]
It is connected thus: immediately after the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*) beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) were taught.
In what manner are they established? By what sense?
This is the intended meaning.
Therefore, he says:
"When the factors conducive to liberation have been planted, through the predominance of aspiration and application."
Thus is the detailed explanation.

By the phrase "it continues as 'by way of predominance' (*adhipatyataḥ*)," he shows that the word *adhipatya* used here in the expression "by way of the predominance of desire and application" (*chanda-yogādhipatyataḥ*) also carries over in what follows.

By means of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), for one whose mind is made pliant through the planting of roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), the root of merit conducive to liberation gains a firm foundation within the continuity of that pliant mind.
This occurs through the sovereignty of desire (*chanda*) up to the sovereignty of investigation (*pravicaya*).
But it does not belong to one whose mind lacks pliancy;
and that mental pliancy arises through the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Therefore, immediately following the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are established on account of their sovereignty in planting the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*vimokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Regarding the phrase "by the sovereignty of zeal" (*chandādhipatyataḥ*), faith itself is expressed here by the word "zeal" through the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause.
It is, for example, like curdled milk and the *trapuṣa* fruit [in the case of] a sudden fever.
Alternatively, the definition of faith (*śraddhā*) consists of conviction, clarity, and aspiration, directed respectively toward existence, qualities, and capacity.
Therefore, by the mention of "desire" (*cchanda*) here, it is faith (*śraddhā*) characterized by longing that is intended, and not mere desire itself.
Regarding the phrase "by mastery over application" (*prayogādhipatyataḥ*), it is applied.
"Application" (*prayoga*) refers to practice; by the word "application," vigor (*vīrya*) is intended.
"By the predominance of non-forgetfulness regarding the object" means by the predominance of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
The faculty of mindfulness has the characteristic of grasping and verbalizing [the object].
"By virtue of the sovereignty of non-diffusion" means by virtue of the sovereignty of the faculty of concentration.

Non-distraction is indeed the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), because its characteristic is one-pointedness of mind. And "by way of the predominance of investigation" means by way of the predominance of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), because the faculty of wisdom has the nature of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). By the word "and," he shows that the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are to be understood respectively as the predominance for planting the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*vimokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

For one who possesses faith exerts vigor for the sake of escaping the prison of *saṃsāra*. For one who has exerted vigor, there arises the accomplishment of the three qualities: the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, respectively.
Thus, on the stage of application (*prayoga-bhūmi*) for the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the predominance of the faculties is maintained.

Others, however, say that the status of faith and the other [faculties] as "faculties" does not arise from their sovereignty in planting the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

What then? Once the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) have been planted, these are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because of the predominance (*ādhipatya*) of aspiration and the other [factors].
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "By virtue of the predominance of aspiration, faith possesses the nature of a faculty"—this is how it is connected.
"Application" (*prayoga*) means activity (*vyāpāra*).
Non-forgetfulness is the non-loss of the object;
non-diffusion is non-dispersal;
discernment is thorough investigation.

Because they exercise sovereignty over application (*prayoga*), non-forgetfulness (*asammoṣa*), non-distraction (*avisāra*), and discernment (*pravicaya*), these mental factors—namely vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are designated as "faculties" (*indriya*).

However, it must be stated here that once the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) have been planted, there is no distinct intrinsic nature (*viśiṣṭasvabhāva*) for faith and the others, apart from their state of being planted, such that they would possess sovereignty over desire and so forth.
For it is on account of that sovereignty in that particular state that their status as faculties is established.
Those very same factors, faith and the others, when they have become powerful, are called "powers" (*balāni*), as distinct from the previously mentioned "faculties" (*indriyāṇi*).
But why are they powerful? To this he says:
"Because of the thinning away of their opposites. (178)

Thus, because the opposing factors have been completely subsumed, he says "when those" in order to demonstrate this very point: when the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) are not intermingled with their opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), namely lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), indolence (*kausīdya*), forgetfulness (*vismṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)—which are the opposites of faith and the rest—the meaning is that they are not mixed because, due to extreme attenuation, there is no intermittent manifestation; at that time, they are the powers (*balāni*).
They are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they are interspersed with their opposites; this is because those opposites have not yet been eradicated.

If the faculties have not conquered their opposites, how is it that the state of being a faculty of faith and the others is taught in the context of the reality of skillfulness (*kauśalyatattva*), by virtue of their sovereignty over mundane purification?

For in that [other context], the faculties were intended without distinction, whereas here it is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctions among the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Therefore, there is no contradiction; for this very reason, it is said here: "These very same faculties are called powers (*bala*)."

For one who has faith in cause and effect initiates vigor, thinking: "This is the cause of this very fruit, and this is the fruit of this very cause. Thus, through faith in the fruit, one initiates vigor toward its cause; and for one who has initiated vigor, mindfulness becomes established because of that single-minded devotion; and for one whose mindfulness is established...

Due to the absence of distraction, the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed; one whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are. Wisdom supported by concentration becomes clear. Having explained the faculties conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), those conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) follow immediately after. Since the powers (*bala*) follow immediately after the faculties, it must now be stated: are the factors conducive to penetration to be understood as being in the state of the faculties or in the state of the powers?
Likewise, are the factors conducive to penetration [to be considered as] faculties and powers?
Are they of a different nature, or rather of a nature not distinct from that? To this he says:
"The two pairs of aids to penetration are the faculties and the powers."

Alternatively, just as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are characterized by the cultivation of the antidotes or are characterized by faith and so forth, so too are the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Therefore, it is said:
"The faculties of one who has planted the factors conducive to liberation have been explained," and so forth.
Therefore, he says:
"Each pair [of the aids to penetration] is [so called]," and so on for all of them.
The "heat" stages (*uṣmagata*) and the "summits" (*mūrdhan*) are called faculties (*indriya*) because these wholesome states are weak and thus unsuitable [to be called powers].
The "patiences" (*kṣānti*) and the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) are powers (*bala*),
because these faculties are absent from them due to their being of the highest degree.

For faith and the other faculties are of three kinds according to the distinction of weak, medium, and intense. Among these, the weak and medium are the faculties (*indriya*), while the intense are the powers (*bala*).
Those that are weak are the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*);
those that are middling are the summits (*mūrdhan*).
Furthermore, those that are superior are divided into four types.

In that regard, the weak, medium, and intense [levels] are, respectively, the weak, medium, and intense patiences (*kṣānti*). The intensely intense levels are the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
All these aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) have the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), together with their associated mental factors (*saṃprayoga*).
In this context, "heat" (*uṣmagata*) refers to the stage of heat.
Just as, from the friction of fire-sticks, heat first arises as a sign of the forthcoming production of fire capable of burning them,
so too, because it is the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path— which is capable of burning the fuel of all afflictions— that is "heat."
Thus it is said: it is called the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) because one has ascended to the peak from among the fluctuating roots of merit;
it is called a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) because it is a momentary state regarding the meaning of the truths.
Furthermore, they are called "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharmāḥ*) because they are the most excellent among all other mundane dharmas.
Their supremacy, however, consists in the fact that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises immediately after them.
Moreover, these [supreme mundane dharmas] are momentary, whereas the remaining aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) possess continuity.
In this context, the roots of virtue conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) should be understood as functioning by way of destroying the power that manifests cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*);
whereas those conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) function by way of establishing the capacity for the arising of untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).

The seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) follow immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma), because the path of seeing (darśanamārga) arises thereafter and is characterized by those factors of enlightenment; thus it is said that "immediately after that, the factors of enlightenment."
"How are these established?"—this implies the question, "For what purpose is their establishment?
Therefore, he says:
"The member of the basis, the member of intrinsic nature..."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
On the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the factors of enlightenment are called the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
"Seeing" (*darśana*) refers to the initial observation of reality (*tattva*) that has not been seen before.
Because it leads to the attainment of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), it is called the "path" (*mārga*); therefore, it is termed the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*).
For during the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the truths are perceived as if veiled by a thin cloth;
whereas during the stage of the path of seeing, they are perceived as if that veil has been removed.

In that context, the perfect awakening to reality is the non-conceptual gnosis of enlightenment (*bodhi*). Among these, the six factors beginning with mindfulness are its "limbs" (*aṅga*) because they are conducive to enlightenment; however, the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is enlightenment itself, because its essential nature is that of realization.
And the others are factors because they serve as its auxiliaries.
Another, however, says:
the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) as apprehended by the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga) is a factor of enlightenment.
However, that which is comprised within the path of liberation is awakening (*bodhi*).
In this context, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the limb of the basis for awakening, because through the power of mindfulness there is no distraction from that object.
The investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is the limb of its essential nature, because awakening has the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Vigor is the factor of departure, because by means of vigor one transcends the stage of ordinary beings. Joy is the factor of benefit, because by means of it there is assistance to body and mind.
The factor of non-affliction is threefold: serenity, concentration, and equanimity, because these serve as the antidotes to affliction.

Alternatively, [one might ask]: "Since they differ in terms of their cause (*nidāna*), basis (*āśraya*), and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for what purpose has the factor of non-affliction (*asaṃkleśāṅga*) been taught in three ways? The intention here is: "In what sense has it been taught in three ways?
To this, he says: "It is taught here by way of its cause, its basis, and its intrinsic nature."

Thus, pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) is the cause of non-affliction (*asaṃkleśa*), and non-affliction is purity. It is the cause, the reason. How is it the cause? To this he says: because affliction has "unwieldiness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) as its cause, and because [pliancy] is its antidote.

This is what is meant: it is the cause of non-affliction because it serves as the antidote to the cause of affliction. Unwieldiness is the lack of serviceability of body and mind; when that exists, one-pointedness of mind is impossible, and thus there is mental distraction.
In one whose mind is distracted, the afflictions such as passion certainly arise;

thus, *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness) is the cause of affliction. How is it that *prasrabdhi* (serenity) is the antidote to that *dauṣṭhulya*? It is because through *prasrabdhi*, one brings about the pliancy (*karmanyatā*) of body and mind.
In this way, serenity is established as the cause for non-affliction;
its basis is meditative concentration. When body and mind are assisted by serenity, the mind becomes concentrated.
When the mind is concentrated, one knows things as they truly are. Through seeing things as they truly are, the afflictions are abandoned.

Thus, for that which is without affliction, concentration is the basis and equanimity is the intrinsic nature; this is because [equanimity] serves as the antidote to mental unevenness, mental agitation, and the state of mental effort that are conducive to afflicted dwelling.
Thus is equanimity.
Its intrinsic nature is non-affliction.
Others, however, say:

when the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned through the paths of abandonment, that wisdom which arises—being liberated from the connection to those afflictions, pure by nature, comprised within the path of liberation, and well-ascertained regarding the object of knowledge—is here called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because one has accomplished what was to be done, and because one exercises equanimity toward destruction upon destruction;
following the factors of enlightenment are the factors of the path.

How are they established? The path of cultivation follows immediately after the path of seeing; and since the factors of the path are contained therein, the factors of the path are said to follow immediately after the factors of enlightenment.
For what purpose are they established? To this he replies:
"For the sake of discernment and for the sake of attainment."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
By way of being the antidotes to wrong view and so forth, up to the antidote to wrong concentration, there is the sequential establishment of the eight path-factors beginning with right view.
Furthermore, their sequence follows the order of the verses in the context of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and so forth.
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is so called because it is cultivated through the cultivation of repeated practice (*niṣevaṇabhāvanā*).
On that path of cultivation, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the limb of discernment for the attainment and cultivation of what was previously cultivated on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is "mundane" (*laukikī*) either because it is worldly or because it involves conceptualization (*savikalpa*).

Because it acquires the capacity for that [result] to arise, that state is established even for one who has entered the supramundane path. However, because it serves as the basis for right view while being non-conceptual, it is called "right view" despite being non-conceptual itself.
For this very reason, he says: "attained subsequent to the supramundane.
The meaning is that it is attained—that is, produced—by means of the power following after (*pṛṣṭhena*) the supramundane path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, as to what its object is, he says: "by which one's own realization [is determined].
It delimits the realization of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) by means of the thought, "Thus have I realized. Because the path of seeing is its object, it is called right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).

"Being a factor for causing others to attain" means, in detail: because one causes others to attain the reality determined by that right view through right speech and right intention, right intention and right speech are factors for causing others to attain. For this very reason it is said: "Because of causing its attainment through speech together with its origination. For right intention is the origination of speech, as stated in the Sūtra: "One does not utter speech without having applied thought (vitarka) and without having applied investigation (vicāra)."

Even one who is concentrated (*samāhita*) is endowed with those two [right speech and right action], because their arising is obtained; however, one who is concentrated does not form intentions or speak.

Regarding how the factors for inspiring confidence in others (*parasambhāvanāṅga*) are threefold—namely, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—it is said: "By means of those [three], right speech, right action, and right livelihood, there is considered to be the communication to others regarding view, morality, and austerity (*saṃlekha*), respectively."
"Right speech," and so forth, refers to discourse, which is the teaching of the Dharma;

"determination through discussion" is the formulation of objections and their refutations with others concerning realization (*abhisamaya*). Through this determination of discourse and discussion, there arises in others confidence in one's wisdom, because they conclude by necessity: "This person has realized reality, for these words of his are connected with tranquility, possess well-determined and non-contradictory meaning, and have a clear sense.
By means of right action (*samyakkarmānta*), there arises confidence in one's ethical discipline (*śīla*); [the phrase] "there arises" carries over from the previous context.

To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of not doing what should not be done. For right action is the opposite of misconduct; therefore, because of that connection, one does not do what should not be done even for the sake of one's life. Thus, there arises the conviction: "This person possesses the morality beloved by the Noble Ones. Right [action]... [184]
The phrase "there arises the expectation of self-discipline through the life-force" (*jīvena saṃlekha*) is thus connected.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of seeking robes and so forth according to the Dharma and in moderation."
Right livelihood is the conduct of body and speech for the sake of the requisites of life, free from defects such as hypocrisy and the like.
Through it, there arises a conviction regarding austerity; for by certainty, his craving for requisites is abandoned, since he maintains the physical basis [of life] solely for that purpose.
He seeks robes and other requisites only in the proper manner and in moderation.
In this regard, through right view, he does not become conceited,
because he thoroughly understands their flavors and qualities as they truly are.
With speech motivated by right intention, he roars the lion’s roar;
through right speech, right action, and right livelihood, he brings his own vow to fulfillment.
In that regard, the factors of the counteragent to the discordant side are threefold;
however, since they are not known, he says:
"right effort, mindfulness, and concentration."
And as to which adversary they are the counteragents for, he says:
furthermore, they are, respectively, the counteragents to the adversaries consisting of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the lack of mastery (*vaibhutva*).
Thus, in that context, "right effort" refers to the first;
for the affliction to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is the first adverse factor (*vipakṣa*).
Right effort is its antidote. To explain how this is so, he says: "By that."
Because the path is cultivated through right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*).
Right effort is vigor that is embraced by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), free from lethargy and restlessness, and established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Through that, there is cultivation.

Because one cultivates the path that serves as the antidote for the sake of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are to be abandoned, right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) is said to be the antidote to the first [hindrance], through the accomplishment of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). In that very cultivation of the path... [185]
This right mindfulness is not the antidote for the second secondary affliction, characterized by lethargy and excitement; this is the subject at hand.
To the question "How so?", he says:
because lethargy and excitement are absent when mindfulness is well-established upon the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and the other [signs].
The word "etcetera" (ādi) should be understood as referring to the cause for exertion (*pragraha*) and the cause for equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Among these, *śamatha* arises from the subsiding of the cause of distraction;
[likewise] the cause for *śamatha* and so forth.
The practice of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth. In that regard, when the mind is agitated or suspected of being agitated,
mental attention toward an object that inspires spiritual urgency (*saṃvejanīya-vastu*) is the sign of calm abiding (*śamatha-nimitta*).
When the mind is prone to laxity, the mental engagement with an object that inspires joy is the sign of exertion (*pragraha-nimitta*).

When the path is exclusively oriented toward tranquility (*śamatha*), exclusively oriented toward insight (*vipaśyanā*), or proceeds as a union of both, and is untainted by the secondary afflictions of those two, the mental engagement characterized by effortlessness is the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*).
Regarding the mastery that is the intrinsic nature of qualities such as the superknowledges (abhijñā),
its opposite is the non-afflicted ignorance consisting of the hindrance to meditative attainments (samāpatti-āvaraṇa).
It is established that right concentration (samyaksamādhi) is the antidote to that third [hindrance].
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because through the accumulation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there is the actualization of qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
For meditative concentration is the basis for the actualization of all the most distinguished qualities.
Thus, this is the antidote to the obscuration of meditative concentration, which is the adversary to the actualization of qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
In this way, through right effort, it demonstrates the dissociation from the obscuration of the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Through right mindfulness, one attains the purity of concentration;
through right concentration, one transcends what is uneven due to the hindrances to meditative attainment. [h) Summary of the Cultivation of Antidotes]
This cultivation of the counteractive measures should be understood briefly as threefold,
according to the distinctions of its commencement, attainment, and completion;
however, in detail, it is of many kinds.
How are they "concordant" and "perverted"?
This is the detailed explanation.
In that regard, [the wisdom] that is concordant with non-perversion is "perversion" [in name],
because non-perversion is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
since its object is reality (*tattva*).
Because it is concordant with that [reality], it is concordant with non-perversion;
yet this cultivation of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) is perverted because its object is not the ultimate reality,
since the afflictions of an ordinary person have not been abandoned without remainder.
How does that which is inverted become conducive to non-inversion?
It arises from hearing and reflection, which are the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
and that [wisdom] extends from the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the cultivation of the powers (*bala*).
It is non-erroneous and free from the persistence of error;
this indeed is the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment for those in training.
And there is the cultivation of the path.
Because its object is reality, it is non-erroneous;
yet because defilements to be abandoned through cultivation still exist, it is accompanied by error.
Being non-erroneous and free from the persistence of error—
this is the cultivation of the path of one beyond training.
Because it has reality as its object, it is non-erroneous;
because of the abandonment of stains without remainder, for Arhats it is free from the persistence of error.
Now, in order to demonstrate the distinction of the bodhisattvas' cultivation of the counteragents (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) compared to that of the śrāvakas and others, he says:
"But for the bodhisattvas..."
"It is distinguished by its object, by its mental attention, and by its attainment.
Regarding this, its distinction by way of the object is as follows: for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas...
The body and so forth belonging to one's own continuum are the objects; these being the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
For Bodhisattvas, however, the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena belonging to both their own and others' continua are the objects.
For what reason is the object of focus different?
Because for the śrāvakas and others, the engagement in the cultivation of the antidote is undertaken solely for their own benefit.
Furthermore, for Bodhisattvas, it is with reference to the welfare of both themselves and others;
"by means of aspects such as impermanence" refers to the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Why do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas apply their mental attention in this way by means of [contemplating things as] impermanent and so forth?
It is for the sake of generating revulsion toward them;
for one who is not revulsed cannot be dissociated from them.

Those bodhisattvas [practice] "by way of non-apprehension" (anupalambha-yogena); this means by way of the mode of non-apprehension of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva). For what purpose do they attend to [the body] in this manner? It is for the sake of abandoning all conceptual constructions (vikalpa), for this is said to be their specific distinction. They do not attend to it solely by way of non-apprehension; rather, they also attend to it through aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*). Through such a distinction in mental attention, there is excellence up until the dissociation from the body and so forth. Dissociation from the body and so forth is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) and the abandonment of the afflictions that have those [bodies] as their objective support.

Bodhisattvas do not [practice] for the sake of dissociation, nor for the sake of non-dissociation. Why? Because if they were exclusively dissociated from the body and so forth, or if they were not dissociated at all, they would be incapable of acting for the benefit of sentient beings, like those whose afflictions are exhausted or like other ordinary beings. If it is neither for dissociation nor for non-dissociation, then for what purpose do they cultivate the antidote? To this he says: "They cultivate it solely for the sake of non-abiding nirvana."

What is that non-abiding nirvana? First, during the stage of a bodhisattva, by relying on mastery over karma and rebirth, one takes birth in saṃsāra out of compassion; yet, through the power of wisdom, one remains undefiled therein. This is what is prescribed as the non-abiding nirvana of the bodhisattvas.

Even while remaining in *saṃsāra*, he does not exist as one defiled like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); nor is he like the *śrāvakas* and others who enter a *nirvāṇa* without substrate (*nirupādāna*). Thus, even in the state of a *tathāgata*, because of the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, he is not established in *saṃsāra*. Nor is he established in *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), because the *dharmakāya* is never interrupted and because the *sāmbhogika* and *nairmāṇika* bodies continue to act for the sake of others as long as the world endures.

Thus, this cultivation of the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*) of the bodhisattvas is said to be superior to that of the śrāvakas and others by way of distinctions in objective support (*ālambana*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), and fruit (*phala*).
Having thus explained the cultivation of the counteractive measures, the state therein (*tatrāvasthā*) was mentioned immediately after; therefore, he asks: "What is the state therein?"
Regarding the word "therein," it refers to that cultivation of the counteragent; therefore he says,
"called the entry into the stage of the cause," and so forth.
In this context, "the state of the cause" refers to the person who abides in the lineage (*gotra*); here, "lineage" means the cause or the seed.

Among those, the one intended here as "abiding in the lineage" is one who remains within the lineage itself and has not yet [proceeded] to the production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and so forth.
Furthermore, that [lineage] persists through subsequent states and does not cease.
Some describe that lineage (*gotra*) as having the nature of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*);
for indeed, certain roots of virtue themselves are called the *śrāvaka*-lineage,
and likewise, up to, certain others are called the *bodhisattva*-lineage.
Beginning from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the differentiation of the faculties (*indriya*) is called the lineage (*gotra*).
Others also say that the lineage is the capacity of the seed of the mind (*cittabījaśakti*).
When that exists, it is called the *śrāvaka*-lineage during the stages of an ordinary person and a learner (*śaikṣa*), up to the *bodhisattva*-lineage.

However, in the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), one is called a "Hearer" (śrāvaka) or a "Solitary Buddha" (pratyekabuddha). That lineage (gotra) does not belong to that [state of] culmination. Furthermore, it is divided into three types according to the distinctions of Hearer and so forth.
In terms of the distinction between the definite and the indefinite, there are six types.

The stage of entry belongs to one who has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); and that [stage] becomes threefold according to the lineages of the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and *tathāgatas*, due to the generation of the thought for the awakening of a *śrāvaka*, a *pratyekabuddha*, or a perfectly complete Buddha, respectively. Because it is the state resulting from application (*prayoga*), once it has arisen, it is called "entry through application"; thus, its arising is termed the "state of entry through application."

The stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*) is that which follows the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) but has not yet attained the fruit. For one who has generated the thought of enlightenment, the undertaking of roots of virtue beginning with generosity and ethical discipline and ending with the cultivation of the powers (*balabhāvanā*) is the means (*upāya*) that brings about the first fruit; this is called "application."
How is the stage of the introduction to the causes called the stage of the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening?
Because it is their cause.
For this very reason it has been said:
The successive fruits [beginning with] the lineage, the production of the thought of enlightenment, and so forth;
when the first fruit among these fruits has been attained,
one indeed applies oneself for the sake of the subsequent fruit.
Therefore, following the stage of application is the stage of the fruit.
For the one in training (śaikṣa), this is the stage characterized by the presence of effort;
because his fruits are not yet fully perfected, it is called the "fruit."
Because there exists a counteragent to the attainment of those [defilements];
and because for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there is no state of things to be done.
For one beyond training is free from passion regarding the three realms.

Because he has fully attained those fruits, and because there exists nothing further to be accomplished for the sake of attaining another fruit, this is the state of having nothing more to do (*akaraṇīyāvasthā*).
Regarding the phrase "endowed with the specific qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) in this state":

when one is considered to have attained *arhatship*, it means being endowed with specific qualities such as the superknowledges; thus, it is a distinguished state, characterized by a state perfected through specific qualities such as the superknowledges that distinguish it from others.

It is explained: the subsequent state belongs to the Bodhisattva who has extensively traversed the stages (*bhūmi*), whose activity concerns the welfare of both self and others, and who is supramundane, as distinguished from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because of the attainment of the realization of the selflessness of both [person and phenomena] on this path, it becomes superior to other vehicles;
thus, that state is called the "higher state," while the state beyond that is the "unsurpassed state."
Of what? For what purpose? To this he says:

"Beyond that, because there is no further state," means that the Buddha is so called because he is the locus of the intellect that has reached the ultimate limit of the increase and decrease of all virtues and faults.
Beyond that, no other distinct state exists; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). Although this much has been stated, the state of the Bodhisattvas remains entirely inexpressible.

Furthermore, for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctions of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), the states beginning with the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukticaryā*) and ending with the state of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are stated again.
However, for the purpose of showing the distinctions of the three bodies (*kāya*) of the Buddhas, three further states beginning with the state of attainment (*prāpti*) are specified.
In this context, the causal stage (*hetvavasthā*) of a bodhisattva should be understood as being common to others.

Therein, the stage of resolute belief (*adhimuktyavasthā*) for bodhisattvas occurs throughout the entire stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*). This refers to the period from the generation of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) until the entry into the [first] stage; during this interval, although they have not yet perceived reality (*tattva*), they act as if they have perceived it. Through their resolute belief in the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they engage with phenomena by way of the three natures (*svabhāvatraya*).

Because one engages in the accumulations for the accomplishment of Buddhahood—such as the difficult acts of giving, morality, and so forth—for the sake of other sentient beings, this stage is called the "stage of practice through resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā*), since it is characterized by the power of resolute belief.

And that lasts for an incalculable eon or more. It is called the "stage of entry" because, upon the first bhūmi, one is no longer bound by the lack of self-awareness regarding reality, due to the non-conceptual knowledge of the three natures; thus, it is termed the stage of entry.
This very [state] is the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The state of departure (*niryāṇāvasthā*) consists of the six stages following that, because one reaches the culmination of the abandonment of the attachment to signs and self—which are to be abandoned through cultivation—and because one reaches the culmination of effortful application (*sābhoga-prayoga*). These stages are called the state of departure.

The state of prophecy (*vyākaraṇāvasthā*) is on the eighth stage; because of the complete disappearance of all notions of signs and effort in every respect, one becomes fixed in the certainty of Buddhahood on the eighth stage, and is thus prophesied by the Blessed Buddhas with a face-to-face prophecy.

The stage of being a preacher (*kathikāvasthā*) occurs on the ninth [ground]; that is, on the ninth ground, one attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) which are superior to those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and thus becomes an unsurpassed great preacher of the Dharma.

The stage of consecration (*abhiṣekāvasthā*) occurs on the tenth ground; for on the tenth ground, the Bodhisattva, having reached the culmination of the path, is consecrated by the rays of light from the Blessed Buddhas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions.

The state of attainment (*prāptyavasthā*) of the Buddhas is the *dharmakāya*. Because of the abandonment of all obscurations and the accumulation of the seeds of untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) which are their antidotes, it consists of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). Being sovereign over all phenomena and free from attachment (*anālaya*), it is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas. It is called the "state of attainment" because, through it, one reaches the ultimate realization of the penetration of phenomena (*dharmapratīvedha*).
Others, however, describe the *dharmakāya* as the *dharmatākāya*, which is the utterly pure *dharmadhātu* itself due to the removal of the entire web of adventitious defilements.

Others maintain that the *dharmakāya* is the knowledge characterized by sovereignty in its unattached and unimpeded operation regarding all objects of knowledge. That which exists in the state of excellence is the *saṃbhogika* [body].

The "body" (*kāya*) refers to the *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body), that body established in which one attains perfect enlightenment. The *sāmbhogikakāya* (enjoyment body) is that body by means of which one experiences the communal recitation of the Dharma within the circle of the assembly together with the Bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate goal. The *nairmāṇikakāya* (emanation body) is the state of performing activities; it is the emanation body accumulated from the *svābhāvikakāya*, which, observing the inclinations of sentient beings, manifests in infinite varieties by its very nature for the sake of those to be trained when [the essential body] does not engage [in activity]. All these various states, when summarized, should be understood as threefold within the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus [it is asked]: "How so? To this he says:
"Impure, impure-pure, and pure, as is appropriate."
Therein, the "impure state" refers to the stages beginning from the causal state up to the stage of application;
that is, the states of the cause, the entry, the application, and the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) are included.
These states are called the "impure state" because the stains of the *dharmadhātu* have not been abandoned without remainder.
Regarding the phrase "the impure-impure state of those in training" (*śaikṣa*),

this refers to the states of having attained the fruit, having further duties to perform, the distinction of excellence, entering higher stages, the departure [from saṃsāra], receiving the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), being a preacher, and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Even in these states, it is called the "impure-impure state" with reference to the fact that some afflictions (*kleśa*) of the *dharmadhātu* have been abandoned while others have not.

The state of purity (*viśuddhāvasthā*) belongs to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It is called the state of purity because it is the stage of practicing for the attainment of the unsurpassed, which is characterized by the absence of anything further to be done; this is due to the complete and total abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) by those beyond training.
These stages are established for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
And since it must be explained how their manifold classification is to be understood, he says:
"Therefore, the classification of the person (pudgala) is considered according to its appropriate application."
"According to what is appropriate" means according to what is possible.
"Therefore" means because of this distinction of states;
that is to say, [the distinction between] "this one abides in the lineage" and "this one has entered," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," this [term] is applied:
the stream-enterer (śrotaāpanna),
the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmī).
The non-returner; the arhat;
the one adorned with ornaments.
A bodhisattva;
a Tathāgata;
one who practices through resolute conviction.
One who practices with a pure resolute intention; one who is setting forth; one who has received a prophecy.
The states have been described as: the preacher of the Dharma, the consecrated one, the one who has attained awakening, the enjoyer, and the benefactor of others.

[3] Since the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*) is preceded by the state (*avasthā*), he asks about the attainment of the fruit in order to explain it immediately after the state: "What is the attainment of the fruit? To this, he says:
"It is receptivity (*bhājanatva*), known as maturation (*vipāka*)."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Briefly stated, this fruit is fivefold:
receptacle-ness, power, inclination, increase, and so forth.

In this context, "being a vessel" refers to that maturation which is conducive to the wholesome. Furthermore, it is the abandonment of the eight inopportune births (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), consisting of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that are tainted (*sāsrava*) yet undesirable, and which is the maturation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). It is called a "vessel" because it serves as the basis for the arising of all wholesome dharmas;
or, it is a "vessel" by virtue of its sovereignty over being a vessel.
The meaning is that the excellence and fullness of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) is based on the weakness of the basis, the afflictions, and rebirth;
this is called "power" (*bala*).

"Inclination" (*ruci*) refers to the inclination toward virtue through prior practice; that is, due to the practice of wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*) in past lives, there arises in the present life an intention for wholesome phenomena according to the analogy of the flow of a river—this is inclination.
Increase (*vṛddhi*) is the arising of unprecedented, distinguished wholesome factors through the practice of presently arisen wholesome roots;
the intended meaning is the nourishment of the wholesome roots.
This is the specific excellence of the increase of power.
For "strength" (*bala*) is firmness in relation to the ripening of weak wholesome [roots].
"Increase," moreover, is the progressive excellence of the wholesome.

Others, however, consider that what is intended here is the nourishment of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of distinguished wholesome dharmas, which they call the "nourishment of the roots of the wholesome" (*kuśalamūlapuṣṭi*).
Purity is the abandonment of obscurations.
In this regard, for those belonging to the lineages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, purity is the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
For those belonging to the lineage of the Bodhisattvas, purity is the abandonment of both the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

These are the five kinds of fruits in their respective order: the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is that maturation which is concordant with wholesome dharmas; the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) is the excellence of the wholesome resulting from the dominance of the receptacle-world;
and the flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is the inclination toward the wholesome arising from previous practice.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is the nourishment of the roots of virtue resulting from the practice of wholesome dharmas in the present.
The fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) is the abandonment of hindrances.
This is the detailed classification of these five kinds of fruits as summarized above.
It has been taught in brief as "the subsequent, the preceding, and so forth"; this is the detailed explanation.

The progressively higher fruits should be understood through the aforementioned succession of stages, beginning with the arising of the thought of enlightenment from the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), and from the arising of the thought of enlightenment, the application (*prayoga*), and so forth.
The initial fruit is the first attainment of supramundane dharmas, which is the realization of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The fruit of practice (*abhyāsaphala*) and the state of the one intent on that (*tatpara*) refer to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) within the state of the learner (*śaikṣāvasthā*), which is characterized by five types of persons and is preceded by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because it consists of the preparatory (*saprayoga*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is the fruit of practice.
The factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) have completion as their fruit;
furthermore, these— namely right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—
are called "having completion as their fruit" because they abide at the final limit of all fruits.
The fruit of conformity should be understood as the progressively higher fruits by way of being the *upaniṣad*; thus,
the state of being the *upaniṣad* is the cause.
In this context, the "arising of the mind" (*cittotpāda*) is so called because it conforms to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); thus, the arising of the mind is the fruit.

It should be understood that the separate teaching of the successive fruits and so forth, as well as the fruits of conformity and so forth, is according to the sequence of the brief statement (*uddeśa*) and the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).
The fruit of the adverse factors is the path of abandonment.
That which is the initial fruit is precisely that. Because the fruit is the adverse factors themselves, it is called the "fruit of the adverse factors."
The path of abandonment is that by which one becomes dissociated from the afflictions.
The "first fruit" is that which was previously described as the initial attainment of supramundane dharmas.
Although the term "adversary" (vipakṣa) [is used here]...
An obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is so called in the sense of being an obstacle to the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*);
however, in this context, it is held that the "adverse factor" (*vipakṣa*) is what is termed the "counteragent."

The term *vipakṣa* (the adverse side) is derived from the analysis [of its components] as "that which belongs to the side of the extraction of obstructions. The fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) consists of the dissociation from afflictions; it is the fruit of practice and the fruit of completion, pertaining respectively to those with vision and those without vision.

The fruit of practice (*abhyāsaphala*) is dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), belonging to the five types of learners (*śaikṣa*), such as those who have entered the path toward the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphalapratipannaka*),
because they still possess a remainder of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The fruit of completion (*samāptiphala*) is dissociation.

For those of the nature of non-falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*) who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no falling away because they have abandoned all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms without remainder.
The distinction is that what was previously stated according to their classification is now stated without such classification.
The "fruit of distinction" refers to the excellence of qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
This too should be understood as being specifically the fruit of the completion of practice.
Why? Because what is intended to be expressed is the attainment of the distinguished qualities of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.
The higher fruit consists of the bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Because they are superior to those vehicles.

For although the bodhisattva stages consist of both the fruit of the initial [realization] and the fruit of repeated practice—since they are of the nature of the paths of seeing and meditation—they must nevertheless be understood as having a superior fruit relative to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because they are non-conceptual, belong to the lineage of the Buddhas, and have great enlightenment as their fruit.
"The fruit of the unsurpassed is the stage of Buddhahood.

This too is indeed the fruit of completion; for because of the abandonment of all afflictions and secondary afflictions along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), and because of the abandonment of non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭajñāna*), and because there is no other stage superior to it, it is called the "fruit of the unsurpassed.
This is another fruit, according to a brief explanation.
"In detail, it is immeasurable" means that the fruits of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and the Perfectly Awakened One (Saṃbuddha), when being established, become immeasurable.
This is the summary meaning of the cultivation of the antidotes (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*):
the cultivation of analytical understanding (*vyutpattibhāvanā*) is the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
It is like the realization of the four noble truths.
The cultivation of erasure is the cultivation of the right abandonments;
it is the erasure of unwholesome dharmas.

The cultivation of the preliminary preparations is the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). In that regard, because it serves as the cause for preparing the concentration (*samādhi*), one practices the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) in order to abandon the five faults. The cultivation of the higher concentration is the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya*).
Because it produces the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*vimokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
it is the cultivation of connection (*śleṣabhāvanā*) and the cultivation of power (*balabhāvanā*),
due to its connection with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The cultivation of entry is the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment;
it is so called because of entering into reality,
or because of entering into supramundane phenomena, or because of entering into the noble path.
Superior cultivation is the cultivation of the path,
because the path of cultivation is superior to the path of seeing.
Initial cultivation occurs during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and may be either conducive or perverted.

Meditation in the intermediate stage occurs during the state of one in training (*śaikṣa*); it is non-erroneous, yet accompanied by the persistence of error. Meditation in the final stage occurs during the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); it is non-erroneous and entirely free from the persistence of error.
Superior meditation belongs to the disciples (*śrāvaka*) and others.

The unsurpassed cultivation of the bodhisattvas is that which consists of the focal object and mental attention. This is the summarized meaning of cultivation; this is the summarized meaning of the stages.
The state of potentiality is the causal state.
The state of undertaking is the application together with the arising of the thought of enlightenment.
The impure-pure state consists of two states.
The state of fruition is the state of having duties to be performed;
the state of purity is the state of having no duties to be performed.
The state with ornaments is the state of distinction.
The state of pervasion (*vyāptyavasthā*) is the subsequent state of the bodhisattvas; it is called the "state of pervasion" because of their pervading the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
And the unsurpassed state belongs to the Blessed Buddhas, because there is no other state superior to that.
Furthermore, this is the state of attainment (*prāptyavasthā*).
The state of benefits and the state of the performance of duties have been explained previously.
The summary meaning of the results is presented by way of their synthesis, their specific distinctions, their prior practice,
and their progressive refinement.
By way of summary and by way of detailed exposition.
The commentator himself provides the explanation for these:
therein, from the perspective of inclusion, the fruit of maturation consists of five fruits.
Because all fruits are subsumed within them;
"the others" are distinguished by way of those [five].
They are simply the subdivisions of those same five.
The remaining [results], beginning with the successively higher fruits, are to be understood accordingly.
Regarding "the ripening fruit from previous practice": this refers to the ripening in the present life resulting from the accumulation of wholesome [karma] in a previous birth.
It is called "from previous practice" because it arises in accordance with what was wholesome.
The other four are established through successive production:

the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*). Among these, power is produced from maturation (*vipāka*).
From strength comes resolve;
from resolve comes growth;
from growth comes purification.
Some say:
because they are characterized by successive explanations, they are said to be "successively brought forth.
From the perspective of their enumeration, there are four, beginning with the successively superior fruits.
The results are the subsequent result, the initial result, the result of practice, and the result of completion.
In terms of their specific designation, there are six, beginning with the result of conformity.
Since these are the designations for those same four [results], the result of conformity is the designation for the subsequent result.
The fruit of the counteractive factors is the explanation of the initial fruit.
The fruit of dissociation is the explanation of the fruit of practice and the fruit of completion.
The fruit of distinction is the higher fruit and the unsurpassed fruit.
And this is an exposition of the fruit of completion alone, because it is precisely therein that the ornament (*śālaṅkāra*) is intended to be expressed.

Others, however, say: the exposition of the "special fruit" refers only to the fruits of cultivation and completion, since even for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) there is the possibility of qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*);
whereas the "supreme fruit" is an exposition of the fruit of completion.

The fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Cultivation of the Antidotes," in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-ṭīkā* composed by the noble Sthiramati according to the tradition of the scriptures, is completed.

[199] Immediately after the enumeration of the six categories beginning with the characteristics and obscurations, the supremacy of the vehicle (*yānānuttarya*) was enumerated; therefore, following that instruction, the instruction on the supremacy of the vehicle is now under discussion. Thus he says: "Now the supremacy of the vehicle must be explained; it is being explained. The word "now" means immediately after the instruction on the sixfold set beginning with the characteristics. The intention is that it was enumerated immediately after those.

Alternatively, the cultivation of the antidotes, the stages, and the attainment of the fruit have been explained as common to the Śrāvakas and others along with the Bodhisattvas. Now, in order to demonstrate that the supremacy of the vehicle (*yānānuttarya*)—which pertains to the Bodhisattvas—is uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others, and is what is primarily discussed here, he says: "The supremacy of the vehicle must now be stated; it is stated. Why is this so? Because there is nothing superior to it; thus, the word *ānuttarya* is a synonym for "excellence" (*viśiṣṭa*). What, then, is this? It is the Mahāyāna. For the Mahāyāna is superior to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and there is nothing more excellent than the Mahāyāna. This is because of the distinction of degrees between cause and fruit. The state of being unsurpassed is "supremacy" (*ānuttarya*). What, then, is that? To this he says:

"Supremacy of practice," and so forth. For the Mahāyāna indeed possesses a threefold supremacy. What, then, is that Mahāyāna? It is precisely this triad: practice (*pratipatti*), objective support (*ālambana*), and full attainment (*samudāgama*). Among these, the supremacy of practice consists in the accomplishment of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). In terms of accomplishing the perfections, the practice of the bodhisattva is called supreme. Furthermore, as for the objective support... [200]

The perfections such as generosity, the Dharma, and the dharmadhātu—by means of this objective support (*ālambana*), Bodhisattvas become capable of accomplishing the welfare of others without exception. Therefore, the supremacy of the objective support consists in its being the cause for the capacity to accomplish the welfare of others.

Why is that? Because that objective support of the Bodhisattvas is called supreme with respect to the attainment of the lineage, the inclination toward the Mahāyāna, the production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and so forth, which are the fruits [of that practice].

That which arises from or is attained from the lineage (*gotra*) and so forth is "attainment" (*samudāgama*); and because there is no other attainment superior to that, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). Therefore, in this context, unsurpassability consists in the state of being a reality that has no other superior attainment.

Furthermore, it is stated here that the practice (*pratipatti*) of Bodhisattvas is the Mahāyāna, which is both shared and possessed of fruit. And this is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) by virtue of the three kinds of unsurpassedness just mentioned.

Alternatively, the Mahāyāna is knowledge free from all conceptual construction and proliferation (*vikalpa-prapañca*), together with its associated mental factors (*sa-samprayoga*), its accumulations (*sa-sambhāra*), its preparatory application (*sa-prayoga*), and its subsequently attained knowledge (*sa-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); it possesses distinguished qualities, has an object (*sālambana*), and has a fruit (*saphala*).
In this context, the object is suchness (*tathatā*), and the fruit is non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*).

Furthermore, the teaching of the sūtras and so forth that expresses this Mahāyāna also becomes the Mahāyāna; thus, the text itself is metaphorically designated by the term "vehicle," just as the slaying of Kaṃsa and the theft of the jewels [are called by those names].
And that [Mahāyāna] is "great" because it is endowed with the seven kinds of greatness.
It is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*) because by means of it one goes to or attains non-abiding *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, it is sevenfold in its greatness: the greatness of the object (*ālambana*), the practice (*pratipatti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), vigor (*vīrya*), skillful means (*upāya*), attainment (*prāpti*), and activity (*karman*).
Among these, the greatness of the object consists in the fact that the path of the bodhisattva has as its object the infinite dharmas of the sutras, such as the *Śatasāhasrikā* and others.
The greatness of practice consists in the practice of all the aims of oneself and others;
the greatness of knowledge consists in the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and phenomena;
and the greatness of vigor consists in the application of many thousands of difficult feats over three incalculable eons.
The greatness of skillful means consists in not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
the greatness of attainment consists in immeasurable and incalculable qualities such as the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the unique buddha-qualities, and so forth.

The greatness of the activity [of the Mahāyāna] arises from its wisdom; as long as saṃsāra exists, one performs the deeds of a Buddha by manifesting awakening. This alone is the unsurpassed Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), because there is no other vehicle superior to it. Its state of being unsurpassed (*anuttarya*) consists of practice (*pratipatti*), objective support (*ālambana*), and realization (*samudāgama*). For it is through connection with these that the Great Vehicle is called unsurpassed. Practice itself is the unsurpassedness; thus, the unsurpassedness of objective support and the unsurpassedness of realization are to be understood.
