This unsurpassedness is established in sequence with reference to the path of the Bodhisattva, its basis, and its fruit. And this much is expressed by the word of the Buddha: namely, practice, objective support, and its fruit.
[2] The Unsurpassedness of Practice

Since practice is preceded by the objective support (*ālambana*), when explaining the sequence beginning with the objective support, practice was mentioned first in order to demonstrate that practice is the very essence for Bodhisattvas. In that regard, as to how there is supremacy of practice, he says: "Supremacy of practice is to be understood from the practice of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). The practice of the perfections is the performance of the perfections; and that practice of the perfections is taught only in the Mahāyāna and not in any other vehicle, thereby showing that the Mahāyāna alone is supreme. Furthermore, demonstrating those modes by which the practice becomes supreme for one engaged in the perfections, he says:
However, practice is sixfold;
thus,
[a] the supreme practice.
Furthermore, since it is not understood how that practice of the perfections (pāramitā-pratipatti) is supreme, up to how it is undifferentiated, he says: "In that regard,
the supreme consists of twelve aspects."
It means that it is supreme, great, and unsurpassed in twelve ways. To demonstrate those ways, he says: "Vastness and extensiveness."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
From the supremacy of magnificence up to the supremacy of completion, these are the twelve kinds of supremacy.
Among them, the supremacy of magnificence is to be understood through its being unworthy of any worldly prosperity and through its excellence.
Attainment is prosperity. It is of two kinds: that which has been attained and that which has not yet been attained. Regarding these, one does not become attached to what has been attained.
He does not long for what has not been attained, because he is devoted to the removal of the suffering of others without regard for his own happiness.
As it is said: "O virtuous one, whatever merit and fruit of merit you have, all that is for the sake of others and not for your own sake.
Its excellence consists in its being the fruit of Buddhahood, which is endowed with the power of abandonment and primordial wisdom.

Alternatively, in the world, only two kinds of person are called noble (*udāra*): one who is liberal in giving (*sthūlalakṣa*) and one who does not seek a reciprocal benefit. Therefore, although a bodhisattva does not seek any of the worldly prosperities, he applies himself to the perfections of giving and so forth in their most intense degrees; thus, this is called the nobility of his practice.
The supremacy of extensiveness;
excellence by way of extensiveness.
Furthermore, extensiveness is the prolonged cultivation of the perfection of generosity and the other perfections.
And since it is not known for how long that [cultivation] lasts, he says:
"Because of cultivation for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
For the cultivation of the perfections, such as generosity, by Bodhisattvas is extremely extensive, as it culminates only after three incalculable eons.

The supremacy of purpose (*adhikāra-paramatā*) is because it aims at performing the welfare of all sentient beings; thus, the engagement of Bodhisattvas in giving and so forth—being indifferent to their own happiness—is for the sake of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. Therefore, it is called "supreme by way of purpose. The supremacy of inexhaustibility (*akṣaya-paramatā*) is supremacy by virtue of being inexhaustible.

Furthermore, from what does this inexhaustibility arise? To this he says: "Because of its absolute non-exhaustion through dedication toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). For acts of giving and so forth, when dedicated toward great enlightenment, do not become completely cut off even after yielding their ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) throughout all states of rebirth; because they bring about the fulfillment of the *dharmakāya*, which is characterized by the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), and because that [body] is inexhaustible, they are not exhausted even in *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). However, through dedication toward the enlightenment of the *śrāvakas* and others, they are completely cut off in the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, because the basis is utterly destroyed in every respect.

Alternatively, through dedication toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), acts such as giving become inexhaustible because their maturation (*vipāka*) is vast; even that which is vast is called "inexhaustible" because it is never completely exhausted by the granting of its maturation. However, this is not the case when there is dedication toward the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others.

Or rather, for Bodhisattvas, the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) dedicated toward great enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings become inexhaustible like the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*); therefore, like the realm of sentient beings, they are never completely exhausted.

The supremacy of continuity consists in the fulfillment of the perfections such as giving toward all sentient beings through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the equality of self and others. For on the Joyous Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because of the realization of the omnipresence of the *dharmadhātu*, the bodhisattva becomes resolutely convinced of the equality of self and others. Having abandoned the conceptualization of self and other through that conviction in the equality of self and others, he attains a mind of supreme joy not only by means of his own giving and so forth, but also by means of the giving and so forth of others. Consequently, moment by moment, instant by instant, and day by day, the perfections such as giving are fulfilled without interruption.

The supremacy of ease is because the perfections, such as giving, are fulfilled by others merely through one's rejoicing (*anumodanā*); thus, Bodhisattvas rejoice with a joyful mind in the roots of virtue, such as the giving, of sentient beings, so that by their mere rejoicing the perfections of giving and the rest are fulfilled.

The supremacy of wealth is because the perfections of giving and the rest are fulfilled through meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as the "Sky-Treasury" (*gaganagañja*); thus, through the cultivation of the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*, Bodhisattvas attain the meditative absorption known as the Sky-Treasury.
By attaining that [samādhi], they fulfill the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) because they satisfy all the intentions of sentient beings;

for through its sovereign power, space itself becomes a treasury (*gañja*). Thus, this samādhi is designated as the "Space-Treasury" (*gaganagañja*), since by the power of that samādhi, all requisites arise from space.
By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of the meditative absorptions (samādhi) recited in sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

It is the supremacy of appropriation because it is appropriated by non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*). For indeed, for Bodhisattvas, non-conceptual gnosis arises from the non-apprehension of the triad of giver, gift, and recipient;
likewise, non-conceptual gnosis arises from the non-apprehension of the triad of knower, object of knowledge, and act of knowing.

How is the practice of giving and so forth, when embraced by that supreme non-conceptual gnosis, [called "supreme"]? Because it conforms to that [gnosis] and has that as its object, it is therefore called "supreme. This refers to the supremacy of the undertaking on the stage of conduct through aspiration, during the highest degree of receptivity (*kṣānti*).
The first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) is called the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

For one who has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) through the power of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and spiritual friends (*mitra*), there is an intense conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nairātmya*) by way of the three natures (*svabhāva-traya*); this is superior patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), which is invincible against opposing factors such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth.
Indeed, this is the bodhisattva’s state of initial undertaking (*ārambhāvasthā*).
Therefore, regarding the highest degree of patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), it is called the "supremacy of undertaking" (*ārambha-paramatā*);

regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is called the "supremacy of attainment" (*pratilambha-paramatā*). For on the first stage, through the realization that the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is all-pervading, one attains the supramundane perfections (*pāramitā*).

However, since those very [perfections] were previously included within the application (*prayoga*) for the first stage, it is said that there is "supremacy of attainment" (*pratilambhaparamatā*) in the first stage.

"Supremacy of outflow" (*niṣyandaparamatā*) refers to the other eight stages; that is, the progressively superior attainment of the perfections attained in the first stage during the subsequent eight stages is the "outflow," and thus it is the supremacy of outflow. Alternatively, the attainment of the first stage through the power of cultivating the perfections on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) is the supremacy of attainment.

For the first stage of the bodhisattvas is comprised within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and by entering it, one is "born" in the lineage of the Tathāgata; this is because of the attainment of those dharmas which are concordant with and of the same nature as that [lineage]. Such is the reading of the Sūtra.
The remaining stages are the "supremacy of outflow" because they are the outflow of the first stage, which is attained through the power of cultivating the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Alternatively, the eight stages are the "supremacy of outflow" because they are the state of being the outflow of the perfections attained on the first stage.

The supremacy of accomplishment (niṣpatti-paramatā): on the tenth stage and the stage of the Tathāgata, there is the accomplishment of the bodhisattva and the accomplishment of the Buddha. For on the tenth stage, the bodhisattva has emerged from all the practices of a bodhisattva; thus, he is consecrated by the Tathāgatas into the position of crown prince (yauvarājya).

Because of the fulfillment of the inconceivable accumulations of merit and wisdom, because of being free from conceptualization regarding all phenomena, and because of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others in every way, this is the supremacy of accomplishment for bodhisattvas.

And because on the stage of the Tathāgata, through the attainment of excellence in abandonment, knowledge, and power, the Blessed One becomes the teacher of the entire world, there is thus "accomplishment by means of the perfect accomplishment of a Buddha.
What, then, is this accomplishment?
It is the complete realization of all aspects of the qualities of a bodhisattva and the qualities of a Buddha.

Alternatively, the excellence of the perfections (*pāramitā*) comprised within the stage of those still in training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) is the tenth stage; therefore, the perfection of the bodhisattva occurs therein. The pinnacle of the perfections comprised within the stage of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*) is the Buddha-stage;

because the perfections exist in their state of being beyond training on that stage, there is perfection through the perfection of the Buddha. Thus, one should understand that the supremacy of perfection consists in the perfection of the bodhisattva on the tenth stage and the perfection of the Buddha on the Tathāgata stage.
Consequently, in the ultimate sense, the ten perfections are so considered.

Thus, because this twelvefold supremacy exists in the giving and other practices of the bodhisattvas, but not in the giving and other practices of the śrāvakas and others, they are therefore called "supreme" (*paramā*). In this sense, by way of etymological derivation (*nirukti*), the ten perfections (*pāramitā*)—beginning with giving and ending with gnosis—are considered to belong to the bodhisattvas alone. Furthermore, the practice of these ten perfections is called "supreme" (*paramā*) according to some; for those who have not even mastered the mere names of these perfections, this is stated in order to explain those names.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge—these are the ten perfections.

It has been stated that their "supremacy of purpose" consists in the aim of performing what is beneficial for all sentient beings; therefore, this question arises: what is the specific function of each of these? To this, he says:

"Benefiting and non-harming, and the endurance of their [reactions]"—this is the detailed explanation. For by means of giving, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings. In that regard, with the desire to honor and benefit them, he relinquishes external and internal things without reservation; and with a volition that is independent of any reciprocal service or karmic maturation, he effects the transfer through actions of body and speech. This is the bodhisattva’s gift of material goods (*āmiṣadāna*);
by removing the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth, he benefits sentient beings through this.

The gift of Dharma consists of teaching those sciences and arts that do not harm sentient beings, which are endowed with skill and preceded by compassion, as well as teaching the path to happy rebirths and liberation;
by this too one benefits sentient beings by removing the sufferings of worldly existence, miserable destinies, and lack of livelihood.
The gift of fearlessness consists of liberating from danger those who are threatened by kings, thieves, heirs, wild beasts, and so forth.
By this [morality] as well, one benefits sentient beings by removing the fear of poison regarding life, enjoyments, children, wife, and so forth.

Through morality, one does not inflict harm upon them; it consists of abstaining from all misconduct of body and speech, and—conforming to worldly conventions—it consists of abstaining from prohibited actions and the performance of prescribed bodily and vocal acts. By being established in this morality, even for the sake of one's own life, one neither personally commits nor causes others to commit harmful or wicked treatment toward sentient beings.

Patience consists in enduring harm inflicted by others with a mind preceded by compassion, characterized by the acceptance and endurance of suffering in all its forms; through it, one endures harm such as injury, binding, and beating inflicted by others, because of the absence of any desire for retaliation. Diligence increases virtues; diligence is the enthusiasm directed toward giving and other perfections.
Through that, growth (*vṛddhi*) is the accomplishment of distinguished qualities resulting from the practice of virtues such as generosity;

by means of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one attracts and causes [beings] to enter [the path] through supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth—the word "and so forth" includes the knowledge of the mental states of others (*cittaparyāyajñāna*);
meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is concentration (*samādhi*), which is the one-pointedness of the mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) consists of traveling through space and so forth;
"introduction" (*avatāraṇa*) is the demonstration of the nature of the teaching's Dharma.
For it is by means of the two miracles of supernatural power and mind-reading—the fruits of meditative concentration—that those who have been won over are able to enter the teaching.
One liberates by means of liberating through the correct giving of instruction via wisdom (*prajñā*).

Wisdom is characterized by the thorough discernment of phenomena in all their aspects, and its function is the correct giving of instruction, which is dependent upon teaching that is the opposite of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the [three] poisons. Therefore, one liberates by means of liberating through the correct giving of instruction via wisdom.

Through the perfection of skill in means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*), one makes generosity and the other perfections inexhaustible by dedicating them toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). That method (*yukti*) which serves for the accomplishment, increase, attainment, or abandonment of a particular phenomenon is "means" (*upāya*) in that context; skill (*kauśalya*) or proficiency therein is "skill in means" (*upāyakauśalya*). Its function is to render the acts of generosity and so forth—performed and accumulated—inexhaustible through dedication to great enlightenment. Thus, the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) dedicated to great enlightenment become inexhaustible, just like great enlightenment itself.

Through the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), by virtue of securing favorable rebirths, one always engages in giving and the other perfections due to delighting in the arising of Buddhas in all births.

Because aspiration consists of various kinds of prayers, "aspiration" here is intended to mean the prayer for a rebirth favorable to the wholesome. Its function is that, through delighting in the arising of Buddhas in birth after birth, one always engages in giving and the other perfections.

Through the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), one engages in giving and the others with certainty, by means of the two powers of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

"Because it is not overcome by opposing factors": analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), while cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated practice of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*). When both of these are not overcome by opposing factors, they are called the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*). Its function is the engagement in giving and the other perfections with momentary spontaneity; for the word "constant" (*niyata*) is a synonym for "continuous.
Indeed, through the power of analytical discernment and cultivation, wholesome qualities such as giving are never overcome by opposing factors.

Through the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*), because one is free from delusion regarding the Dharma according to its literal expression (*yathāruta*), one experiences the enjoyment of the Dharma governed by the perfections such as giving (*dāna*) and brings sentient beings to maturity. Thus, the perfection of wisdom consists of knowledge that has abandoned delusion regarding the literal expression in all the teachings of the Mahāyāna Dharma. Furthermore, what is this "delusion regarding the literal expression" (*yathāruta-sammoha*)? It is that by which, having set aside the intended meaning (*abhiprāyika-artha*), one conceptualizes only according to the literal expression; this is delusion regarding the literal expression.
With reference to giving—that is, taking giving as the object—the Dharma taught in the Sūtras and so forth is "governed by giving" (*dānādhipateya*).
In this way, the sovereignty of morality, patience, vigor, and so forth should be understood.

With reference to the Mahāyāna, the activity of the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*) consists of both the experience of the enjoyment of the Dharma and the maturation of sentient beings; for it is through the Buddha and Bodhisattvas establishing unerring dialogues and determinations concerning the Mahāyāna, and by means of their unerring teaching of the Dharma to sentient beings, that they bring them to maturity.
Furthermore, the instruction of the Dharma in the form of sūtras and other texts is itself manifested by the perfection of wisdom.
[b) The Practice of Mental Attention] Immediately after the exposition of the supreme practice, the practice of mental attention (*manasikāra*) must be explained;
therefore, he asks, "What is the practice of mental attention? and in response, he says:
"Just as the dharma is designated [as] 'the mental engagement of the Mahāyāna,' and so forth"—
this means with reference to generosity and the other perfections, that is, aiming at generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and the rest.

Regarding the phrase "of the dharmas such as the sūtras as they have been designated": herein, the practice of mental attention (*manasikāra-pratipatti*) consists in attending to those dharmas—the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, and so forth—in the very manner in which the Blessed One taught them concerning generosity and the other perfections, according to both their meaning and their phrasing, free from superimposition and denial;
it is not otherwise. This is the Mahāyāna, not the Śrāvakayāna;
for in the latter, generosity and the rest are taught solely for one's own benefit, whereas in the Mahāyāna, they are taught for the benefit of both oneself and others.

Therefore, it is made known that the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) by Bodhisattvas with the dharmas such as the sūtras as they have been taught with reference to generosity and so forth within the Mahāyāna itself is the practice of mental engagement; whereas the mental engagement with the sūtras and so forth spoken with reference to generosity and so forth in the Śrāvakayāna is the practice of false mental engagement, because it relies solely upon one's own self-interest.
Furthermore, those [Mahāyāna teachings] are generally taught with reference to equanimity of mind, non-attachment, lack of pride, and non-apprehension.
In this context, "evenness of mind" is the desire to benefit both those who possess qualities and those who do not equally.

In this context, "non-attachment" is the application to giving and other virtues solely for the sake of others, by one who is free from longing for existence or enjoyments. In this context, "absence of pride" is that by which one does not exalt oneself through giving and other virtues, nor does one despise others.
In this context, "non-apprehension" refers to the purification of the three spheres by way of the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient.
"Frequently" means again and again.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation": therein, the certainty arising from the authority of the words of a reliable person is that which consists of hearing (*śrutamayī*).
That which arises from the investigation of reasoning is the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*); that which arises from cultivation is the wisdom consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmayī*).
Since all activity is for the sake of a result, he asks: by attending to [the object] with these three kinds of wisdom, what quality does one bring about? To this, he says:
This serves for the nourishment of the elements, for entry, and for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
The element (*dhātu*) is the lineage (*gotra*), the seed (*bīja*). Its nourishment is its growth.
Through the nourishment of the element, one becomes possessed of clear and great wisdom in the future.

"He enters into the meaning of that which has been heard with his whole being" means that he enters into the true existence of the meaning of that Dharma heard in the sūtras and so forth by means of the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*), which produces reasoning. Through the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), he attains the accomplishment of the goal; the accomplishment of the goal is the realization of reality (*tattva*). To the question "How is this so?", it is said: "By way of entering and purifying the stages (*bhūmi*). For one enters the stage through the purification of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth; therefore, it is taught that one enters the stage precisely by means of the applications of mindfulness and the rest.

Then, by purifying through wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-prajñā*) the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth—which constitute the entry into the stages—one attains the accomplishment of the goal; this is the meaning of "entering the stage.

Furthermore, this [practice] should be understood as the practice of mental attention (*manasikāra*) together with its retinue, not as it alone. What is that retinue? It is said: it should be known as being conjoined with the ten dharma-practices (*dharmacarita*).
"Thus they are to be understood as 'embraced' means they are 'surrounded. The practices whose nature is Dharma, or which have Dharma as their objective, are the 'Dharma-practices.
Since those are not yet known, he asks: 'What are the ten kinds of Dharma-practices? To this, he says:
writing, honoring, giving,"

Thus is the detailed explanation. In this context, "writing" refers to the Mahāyāna being written down by oneself or by another for the sake of its long-term preservation or for the purpose of hearing and reciting it. "Worship" consists of honoring the Mahāyāna—with flowers, incense, perfumes, and lamps—as is understood from the subject at hand; it also includes the respectful giving of written books and so forth to others who are established in the Mahāyāna, listening with respect when it is being recited by another, reciting it oneself with great reverence, memorizing it, and internalizing it with great faith.

The disclosure or publication of the text or its meaning for those who are worthy through great effort is *svādhyāyana*. The repeated practice of what has been extracted is *cintana*, which is the determination of its meaning by means of reasoning.
*Bhāvana* is the practice performed with concentrated wisdom (*samāhitayā prajñayā*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction.
In this context, bodily action is demonstrated by these four terms: writing, worshipping, giving, and listening.
Verbal action is demonstrated by these four terms: reciting, memorizing, explaining, and studying.
Mental action is also demonstrated by these two: reflecting and meditating.
For that tenfold conduct is indeed an immeasurable mass of merit.

Regarding this tenfold practice of the Dharma that has been described: the mass of merit arising from even a single one of these practices of the Dharma cannot be measured by oneself or by another because of its extreme vastness.

Furthermore, since the explanation of dharmas such as generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration is equal [in all vehicles], why is it that in the sūtras of the Mahāyāna alone the practice of the Dharma is taught to have exceedingly great fruit, whereas in the sūtras of the Śrāvakayāna the practice of the Dharma is not taught to have such great fruit? This is the connection [of the question].
"By two reasons" refers to the statement that in the Mahāyāna, the practice of the Dharma is taught to yield exceedingly great fruit. To the question "By which two?", he says:
"Because of its excellence and because of its inexhaustibility."
Thus [it is said].
Since even this is not understood, he asks: "How is it by way of distinction? How is it by way of inexhaustibility? To this, he says:
"[213] By means of favoring others and by non-cessation."

Thus it is said: for in the Mahāyāna, the singular purpose of Bodhisattvas is taught to be the accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings through the practice of generosity and the other perfections;
whereas in the Śrāvakayāna, one's own welfare is primary.
Therefore, because it is engaged in benefiting others, the Mahāyāna is superior to the Śrāvakayāna.
Thus, first of all, the superiority of the Mahāyāna over the Śrāvakayāna is established by the explanation of its cause:

namely, that its fruit is the inconceivable accumulation of merit and wisdom, which is comprised of the three bodies (trikāya) and is engaged in performing deeds for the welfare of sentient beings for as long as the world endures.

Its inexhaustibility is due to the illumination of the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which does not cease even in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*);
however, it is not so in the Śrāvaka vehicle.
For the fruit of the Śrāvaka’s equipment is declared to be exhaustible, because for those who have entered the nirvana without remainder, there is a total cessation of all things.
Thus, because its fruit continues even in nirvāṇa, the Mahāyāna is superior to the Śrāvakayāna by virtue of its illumination.
Alternatively, the purpose of the Mahāyāna consists of generosity and so forth, which are directed toward the benefit of all sentient beings;
the purpose of the Śrāvakayāna is not like this.
Because śrāvakas are intent upon their own self-interest,
whereas the qualities of bodhisattvas, such as generosity and the rest, have been transformed into an untainted body (*anāśravakāya*) and thus are not severed even in parinirvāṇa,
unlike those of the śrāvakas.
However, because the path is like a raft, they are completely severed at final nirvāṇa; thus, they do not possess inexhaustibility.
Therefore, it is logical that the practice of the Dharma in the Mahāyāna alone yields great fruit, and not so in the Śrāvakayāna.
Immediately after the practice of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*anudharmapratipatti*) must be explained;
therefore, he asks: "What is the practice in accordance with the Dharma? Thus [he asks].
He said:
"It is that which is undistracted, free from error, inclined [toward the goal], and in accordance with the Dharma."
Thus:

practice that conforms to the dharmas to be meditated upon and known, consisting of the cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) that have been entered into, is "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*anudharmapratipatti*).
In that regard:
That which consists of the cultivation of calm abiding is undistracted;
that which consists of the cultivation of insight is transformed by the absence of error.
This is the twofold practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Since this term *ākāra* occurs in many senses, it is not understood how [the mind] is "undistracted"; therefore, he says:
"In that regard, it is undistracted because of the absence of the six kinds of distraction."
Since it is not known how distraction is also sixfold, he says:
"The sixfold distraction consists of natural distraction (*prakṛti-vikṣepa*)."
"External distraction," and so forth.
Even though this has been shown as a mere classification, he asks [the question] because the actual nature of distraction has not yet been revealed.
How is this distraction, characterized by these six aspects, to be understood? To this he says:
"Arising is [distraction] toward an object; essence is [distraction] regarding the object."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
"By the wise one" means by the wise Bodhisattva.
In that context, "emergence from meditative concentration" refers to [occurrence] by means of the five groups of consciousness. For when, in one who is concentrated,
any one of the five consciousnesses— beginning with visual consciousness— arises again, at that time one has emerged from meditative concentration.

And this is natural distraction (*prakṛti-vikṣepa*). Because it functions with its orientation turned outward, and because the five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are by nature distracted, emergence from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by means of the five groups of consciousness constitutes natural distraction.

It is said: regarding the object, "substantiality" refers to outward distraction; that is, when the mental consciousness of one who is concentrated proceeds toward another object against his will, away from the focal point of meditative concentration.
Some say that outward distraction consists in the shifting of the object of focus to something else.

Others say that for one who is concentrated, outward distraction is the shifting of the mental consciousness to another object after having abandoned the object of concentration. Internal distraction, they say, consists in the relishing of concentration, as well as lethargy and restlessness.

If one who is concentrated relishes that very concentration with afflictions such as craving, then there is distraction from pure concentration due to the presence of afflicted concentration. Furthermore, dullness and agitation constitute distraction from the concentration that carries both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Because they are states of non-concentration, these—relishing, dullness, and agitation—are called "internal distractions."

The distraction of signs (*nimittavikṣepa*) is the intention of seeking esteem. It is called the distraction of signs because for one who is engaged in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by means of this sign—the conceit of being esteemed, thinking "this person is a great soul"—there is a dissipation of the mental disposition (*āśaya*) with respect to a wholesome factor, whether already attained or not yet attained. Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "because of the application [of meditation] having made that sign the basis.
This means that, out of a desire to be known, one makes that intention of seeking esteem the sign; that is, because one is engaged in meditative concentration through the conceit of self-esteem.

The state of mental attention accompanied by the notion of "I" (*sāhaṃkāramanaskāratā*) is called "distraction due to corruption" (*dauṣṭhulyavikṣepa*). This is because even one who seeks the qualities of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with such an intention possesses mental attention accompanied by the notion of "I," which is associated with the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), thinking, "I am a meditator. Consequently, he exalts himself and looks down upon others. Why is this considered mental attention characterized by corruption? To this he says: "Because the conceit 'I am' manifests through the power of corruption.
What is meant by this is that distraction produced by corruption is called "distraction due to corruption."

Furthermore, what is *dauṣṭhulya*? It is the nourishment of the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), for by means of that, the conceit "I am" manifests; thus, through its partial manifestation, the conceit "I am" arises.

Others say that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is *dauṣṭhulya*, while others say it is a state of inferior mind and distraction of mental attention. [This occurs] when one belonging to the indeterminate lineage of Śrāvakas and so forth, though engaged in the mental attention of the Mahāyāna, gives rise to that mind of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha due to fear of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, the misconduct of sentient beings, and association with non-virtuous friends.
That mind is inferior because it is intent solely upon its own self-interest;

that is the mind of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because it distracts from the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the Mahāyāna, it is called "distraction of mental application. He states the reason for this very point: "because of the active engagement in that mental application by means of the Hīnayāna."

The Hīnayāna—the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—is so called because it proceeds with the primary aim of one’s own parinirvāṇa. Since the active engagement of mental attention toward that [Hīnayāna] distracts from the mental attentions of the Mahāyāna, the inferior mind is called "distraction of mental attention.
Thus, this cultivation of calm abiding by a bodhisattva should be understood as being free from the six kinds of faults of distraction. [β) Transformed by Non-perversion]

Thus, it is explained how the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*anudharmapratipatti*), which has been transformed through non-perversion (*aviparyāsapariṇatā*), should be cultivated by one who is undistracted. It is "transformed through non-perversion" because it proceeds with non-perversion as its essence.

In this context, non-perversion is the knowledge of a thing exactly as it is established; however, it is not yet known in how many kinds of things that object consists. Therefore, he says: "In this regard, non-perversion should be understood as pertaining to ten kinds of things. To demonstrate the objects of non-perversion, he states: namely—
Regarding the detailed explanation of the two characteristics within the analysis of phonemes, meanings, and mental attention:
now, in order to demonstrate how non-perversion occurs with respect to those entities, he says: "In that regard..."
"Due to conjunction and arising, and due to disjunction and non-arising, the existence and non-existence of the object [is understood]; this is non-perversion regarding the phoneme.
Thus it is said.
"Regarding the phrase 'when there is a conjunction of consonants' (*samyoge sati vyañjanānām*)," conjunction (*samyoga*) indeed means mutual contact (*parasparasamśleṣa*).
And such [contact] does not exist among consonants because of the absence of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*).
It is impossible for consonants to be articulated simultaneously.

In order to dispel the doubt that the preceding conceptualizations do not persist at the time of the utterance of the subsequent phonemes— because they perish immediately after being uttered— he says:
"By way of being uttered without interruption"—
this is what is meant:
here, the utterance is neither erroneous nor delayed.
The conjunction of phonemes (*vyañjana*) is intended, but not the mutual physical contact of phonemes.
"Because of the possibility that 'this is the name of this'" means that if the conventional designation (*saṃketa*) that "this is the name of this object" has been practiced.
Thus, by these two modes, the syllables possess meaningfulness; that is to say, they are signifiers.
"But by the opposite, there is pointlessness.
The opposite consists in the absence of both [factors] or the deficiency of either one.
That which is such a vision is knowledge;
that should be understood as non-perversion regarding the phoneme.
This is by way of conventional truth, but not by way of ultimate truth;
for the ultimate truth is non-conceptual because it is free from error.
Through this absence of error, the bodhisattva penetrates all phenomena as being devoid of both word and referent.

Now, in order to demonstrate the absence of error regarding the object that is the cause for the designation of linguistic expressions, he says: "It appears as a duality, and yet it does not exist in that way."
Thus it is said at length.
It appears as a duality, namely as the grasped and the grasper. What is it that appears?
The dependent nature (paratantrasvabhāva).
Why?
Because it is endowed with the seeds of the grasped and the grasper.
What, then, is the meaning of "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*) here? To this he says: "Because of arising in that form.
Because of arising in the form of the apprehended and the apprehender, it appears as the apprehended and the apprehender; [it does not appear otherwise].
Furthermore, it is like a crystal due to the coloring of an adjacent object;
thus, there is non-existence.
That is to say, it does not exist in the manner in which its appearing form manifests.

Thus, the intention is that the vision of an object which serves as the cause for the arising of deluded consciousness is non-erroneous with respect to that [object], because of the avoidance of both existence and non-existence.
Regarding the statement that the object is "avoided in its existence," he states the reason right here:
"because of the absence of the grasped and the grasper."
The existence of an object (*artha*) is the reality of the apprehended and the apprehender.
It is "devoid of that" because it is empty of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender;
thus, it is devoid of non-existence.
What is the reason?
It is because of the existence of the error of that appearance; the meaning is that it is because of the existence of the error of the appearance of the grasped and the grasper.
This too is called non-perversion from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Because it is free from conceptual construction.
By means of this non-erroneous knowledge, the bodhisattva thoroughly investigates all phenomena as being devoid of the intrinsic nature of grasped object and grasping subject.
Now, in order to demonstrate non-error regarding the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the cause for the appearance of the grasped object and the grasping subject, he says:
Cultivated by that verbal expression, it is mental attention consisting of verbal discourse, and that [discourse] is its basis.
Thus is the detailed explanation.

"Mental activity consisting of discursive speech (*jalpamānaskāra*) cultivated by the discursive speech of the grasped and the grasper" means that regarding an object characterized by the appearance of the grasped and the grasper, whatever verbalizing through speech and mind occurs—thinking "this is the grasped" or "this is the grasper"—that is called "discursive speech" (*jalpa*).
Cultivated by this discursive speech, it is called "cultivated" (*bhāvita*) because it nourishes the seeds for the production of future discursive speech of the same kind.

Because it is cultivated by discursive speech (*jalpa*), this [mental state] is designated as "mental attention consisting of discursive speech" (*jalpamānaskāra*) by applying the name of the cause to the effect.
Here, "discursive speech" refers to the latent predisposition for speech (*jalpavāsanā*).

By treating the container and the contained as non-different, and by employing the term for the container [to denote the contained], it is called "mental attention consisting of discursive speech," since discursive speech exists therein.
Because it serves as the seed-basis for that conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper known as discursive speech (*jalpa*),
and furthermore, because discursive speech arises in dependence upon it, it constitutes its support.
Thus, this "non-perversion regarding mental attention" means non-perverted knowledge.
However, that mental attention in which there is non-perversion is not yet understood; therefore, he asks: "In what kind of mental attention is there non-perversion?
Consequently, he speaks in order to specify that particular mental attention.

The meaning is that [it] consists of a specific state of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which serves as the cause for the manifestation of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
To demonstrate how this becomes the cause for the manifestation of the grasped and the grasper, he says:
For that very mental engagement with discursive speech (*jalpamanaskāra*) is [so called] because it is permeated by the ideation of verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃjñā*).
It is connected [to the statement] that it "becomes the cause for the appearance of the grasped and the grasper" (*grāhyagrāhakaprakhyānakāraṇaṃ bhavati*).
Alternatively, he says this in order to demonstrate that "mental engagement with discursive speech" is the cause for the occurrence of designations (*abhidhāna*).
It is said that "mental engagement with discursive speech" (*jalpamanaskāra*) is so called because it is thoroughly cultivated by the perception of verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃjñā*).
The "perception of verbal expression" is the perception that arises from verbal expression or that gives rise to verbal expression.
Because its own seed is nourished within the mental engagement with discursive speech by means of that perception together with its associated factors, it is said to be "thoroughly cultivated."
This non-perversion also exists only conventionally, not in the ultimate sense.
By means of this non-perversion, the bodhisattva abandons the cause of perversion, which is characterized by the attachment to the grasped and the grasper.
In this way, that state of corruption is easily abandoned.
Now, in order to demonstrate the absence of error regarding the ultimate nature (*avakāra*), he says:
"The non-existence and existence of the object are considered to be like an illusion and so forth."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
As for that which was just stated regarding the non-existence and existence of the object—how was it stated immediately before? It was said:
"The appearance as duality, and likewise its non-existence."
"This non-perversion regarding the object is devoid of both existence and non-existence";
thus it is considered to be like an illusion and so forth.

Like illusions and so forth—meaning "like illusions etc."—he says this very thing to demonstrate it: "Just as an illusion does not exist in its own nature because it appears in the form of an elephant and so on; therefore, while it is said that it does not exist as an elephant and so on, it does not exist in every respect [as non-existent]. What then? It is not that it does not exist at all, because that which is merely an error exists, since there is the existence of that mere error appearing in the form of an elephant and so on; thus, it does not not exist in every respect."
Even that object does not exist in the way it appears as the grasped and the grasper;
yet, because that which is the nature of the mind and mental factors of the three realms exists as mere delusion while appearing in such a manner, it is not non-existent either.

By the word "etcetera," examples such as mirages, dreams, and the moon reflected in water should be understood accordingly: for mirages, dreams, the moon in water, and so forth do not exist in the way they appear as women or men, nor are they entirely non-existent, because they exist as mere delusions.
In this way, the meaning [of the term] should also be applied extensively to each [case].
Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand the city of the Gandharvas, echoes, and so forth.

Thus, that vision which—by seeing objects as being like illusions and the like—is characterized by the non-diffusion and non-distraction of the mind regarding both the positions of existence and non-existence, is non-diffusion (*avisāra*) and non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*).
Others, however, maintain that non-distraction (*avisāra*) is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the middle way.

If this is so, how is there non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*) in non-distraction? To this he says: "Because by means of that, the mind does not stray toward existence or non-existence. By means of this non-perversion, the bodhisattva, being free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, is undistracted with respect to the objective support of emptiness (*śūnyatālambana*).

Therefore, non-distraction is called the absence of error (*aviparyāsa*). Yet even this absence of error exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because the latter is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatvāt*).

Now, in order to demonstrate the absence of error regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), he says: "Everything is name-only (*nāmamātratva*), because no conceptual constructions (*kalpa*) arise. [221]
Thus it is said in detail:
all this is name-only—namely, that which is from the eye and form up to the mind and mental objects.
Therefore, the entire knowable, consisting of the twelve bases, is name-only.
In that regard, there is the designation of the specific nature of names;
yet, neither the object to be designated nor the designation itself possesses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
It is thus imagined by way of that [imagined] self-nature.
And because the imagined nature does not exist,
otherwise there would be a perception as "eye" and so forth independent of names;
yet there is no such perception for one who has not mastered linguistic conventions.

Therefore, because [the eye and form] do not have that nature as their intrinsic being, the knowledge that "eye and form," and so forth, up to "mind and phenomena," are merely names—this knowledge is the antidote to all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This is non-delusion regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Through the gateway of imagined phenomena (*parikalpitadharma*), the activity of all conceptual constructions proceeds toward all phenomena;
hence, it is said that the knowledge which penetrates [them] as mere name is the antidote to all conceptual construction and is non-delusion regarding the specific characteristic.

In this regard, it is not known whether [this refers] to the ultimate specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or to the conventional; therefore, he asks: "In which specific characteristic? To this, he says:
Regarding the ultimate specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa),
this is non-erroneous;
because the ultimate specific characteristic is inexpressible, it is not [so] regarding the conventional (saṃvṛtti).

What is the reason? Because, by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), one does not grasp this as being "mere name," since conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) proceeds toward the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvarūpa*) by means of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).
This too exists only conventionally and not ultimately, because of the conceptualization that it is "mere name.
Through this non-perversion, the bodhisattva becomes skilled in both the conventional and the ultimate.
Now, in order to demonstrate non-perversion regarding the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), he says:
Since no phenomenon exists that is separate from the dharmadhātu.
Thus it is said in detail.

Without the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), no phenomenon whatsoever— whether material or immaterial— is found, because all phenomena have an ineffable and non-dual nature, being devoid of the state of grasped object and grasping subject.

Therefore, because the *dharmadhātu* is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, its existence as non-distinct from all phenomena is called the "common characteristic. Knowledge that it is thus is the absence of error regarding the common characteristic; this is so conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), but not ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*), because it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
Thus, by means of this non-perversion, the bodhisattva becomes skilled in the pure object of focus, because it is the domain of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*).

What is the distinction between the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? The inexpressible nature (*anabhilāpyasvabhāvatā*), which serves as the antidote to the superimposition of an expressible intrinsic nature (*abhilāpasvabhāvasamāropitatva*), is the characteristic of ultimate reality (*paramārthalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*)—which is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena—is the general characteristic.
Thus, there is a distinction based on the difference in perspective, but not in terms of the actual object.
Now, in order to demonstrate the absence of error regarding the purification and non-purification of the *dharmadhātu*, he says:
"The transformation consisting in the non-abandonment of erroneous mental activity."
Thus it is said in detail.
The non-abandonment of distorted mental activity is the impurity of that dharmadhātu;
its abandonment is its purity. In this context, distorted mental activity refers to the conceptualization of error, which is the cause of the ālayavijñāna.

The non-abandonment of that [perversion] is the impurity of the *dharmadhātu*; its abandonment is its purity. Such knowledge as this is, respectively, non-perversion regarding both impurity and purity. Thus, "the non-abandonment of perverted mental activity is the impurity of that *dharmadhātu*" refers to non-perversion regarding the impurity of the *dharmadhātu*. "Its abandonment is purity" refers to non-perversion regarding purity.
What is the reason?
Because the dharmadhātu is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions.
This too is non-perversion only conventionally, not from the perspective of ultimate reality.
And by means of this non-perversion, the bodhisattva understands that the obstructions of the *dharmadhātu* have not been abandoned [in reality], yet they are abandoned [in appearance].
Now, in order to demonstrate the non-perversion regarding the adventitious nature of both the impurity and purity of the *dharmadhātu*, it is said:
"Because the *dharmadhātu* is pure by nature, like space, [impurity and purity are adventitious]."
Thus it is said in detail.
Furthermore, because the *dharmadhātu* is naturally pure like space, both of these—impurity and subsequent purity—are adventitious.
In that regard, impurity is said to exist because the *dharmadhātu* is defiled by unreal conceptual construction (*abhūtavikalpa*).
And subsequently, through the arising of the counteragent, there is purification by means of the abandonment of that [defilement]; both of these are adventitious to the *dharmadhātu*.
Why? Because the *dharmadhātu* is pure by nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), like space.
For one that is pure by nature, impurity would be adventitious; but as for purity itself, since it is eternally pure, how could it be adventitious?
The purity intended here is that which consists in the removal of stains; thus, there is no such fault.
For this very reason it was stated here: "And purity occurs later.

This is precisely the non-perversion regarding the adventitious nature of both the impurity and the purity of the *dharmadhātu*, [which is realized] through knowledge of the *dharmadhātu* in this manner.
This too exists conventionally, but not in the ultimate sense.
And by means of this non-perversion, the bodhisattva understands the artificiality of the states of affliction and purification within the dharmadhātu.
Now, in order to demonstrate the absence of perversion regarding fearlessness and lack of pride, he says:
For there is neither affliction nor purification of either phenomena or persons.
Thus it is said at length:
there is neither defilement nor purification for the person (pudgala),
nor indeed for phenomena (dharma).
"Defilement and purification" continues [from the previous context].
Regarding this very point, he states the reason:
"Because neither a person (pudgala) nor a phenomenon (dharma) exists"—the word "exists" (asti) follows [from the previous verse].

There exists no such person (pudgala) who exists apart from affliction (saṃkleśa) and purification (vyavadāna), for whom it would be logical to conceive of affliction or purification, or by whose distinctness there could be decrease or increase; this is because such a person is not an object of direct perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna). Furthermore, a phenomenon (dharma) that possesses an imagined nature (parikalpitātmaka) does not exist at all.
Since multiple conceptual constructions arise regarding a single entity, yet it is not logical for a single thing to possess a manifold nature,
there is neither affliction nor purification for either the person (*pudgala*) or phenomena (*dharma*), as both are non-existent like the son of a barren woman and so forth.
Furthermore, even for the dependent nature (*paratantra*), which is the object of pure mundane knowledge, neither affliction nor purification is admitted.

What is the reason? Because its nature is inexpressible and non-dual. If these two [stains and purification] are not admitted even for the dependent nature (*paratantra*), to what would they belong? Since that [dependent nature] does not exist, the effort toward the removal of affliction and the attainment of purification would be futile; yet, the defilement and purification of the *dharmadhātu* do occur—this is not a fault.

These two [states] are established as being non-identical with the *dharmadhātu* itself; for they are adventitious within the *dharmadhātu*, and because the *dharmadhātu* is immutable like space, there is no loss whatsoever on the side of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*), nor is there any excellence on the side of purification (*vyavadānapakṣa*). Therefore, since there is neither fear nor pride, this is the absence of error regarding non-fear and non-arrogance.
Others, however, say: "There is no loss of anything on the side of affliction, nor is there any excellence on the side of purification, because there is nothing whatsoever that possesses both."
Since those very things are thus [non-existent], why does fear arise there, thinking "this is not mine"? Why does pride arise, thinking "this is my excellence"?
Others, however, think as follows:
To begin with, the person (pudgala) does not exist at all; nor does the phenomenon (dharma) exist at all—
that which experiences the two states and for whom these two might be conceptualized.
Rather, this defilement and purification is merely dependent origination;
this too is from the perspective of conventional reality,
but not from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Through this non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*), one penetrates the unchanging nature of the *dharmadhātu* due to the absence of decrease or increase;
through this non-perversion, others maintain that one abandons all obscurations and emerges free from obscuration.
Alternatively, by means of this non-perversion regarding the ten [points] which consists of the conventional, the non-perversion regarding the ultimate is indicated here;
for otherwise, its exposition would be untenable.
Yet another says:

These [eight] non-perversions— concerning the phoneme (*vyañjana*), the meaning (*artha*), mental attention (*manaskāra*), non-distraction (*avisāra*), the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), impurity (*aśuddhi*), purity (*śuddhi*), adventitiousness (*āgantuka*), fearlessness (*atrāsa*), and non-arrogance (*anunnati*)— are taught with reference to the three natures (*svabhāvatraya*). Among these, the non-perversions regarding the phoneme and the meaning refer here to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
because the meaning— which consists of that which is conjoined and that which falls into duality— is imagined.
Even though its object is not the ultimate reality (*atattva*), such being the case, its effect is indeed non-erroneous (*aviparyāsa*).
Non-erroneousness is *tathātva* (suchness);
thus, there is non-erroneousness in mental attention (*manaskāra*).
With reference to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
there is the mental engagement of discursive speech (*jalpa-manasikāra*).

Because this [nature] is by its very nature the essence of the *ālayavijñāna*, there is no error regarding its non-dispersal with respect to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Why is this so? Because non-conceptual gnosis is free from distinctions between existence and non-existence, and because it is comprised within the perfected nature through the perfection of non-error. There is no error regarding specific and general characteristics precisely within the *dharmadhātu*, for its own nature transcends the domain of conceptual construction. There is no error regarding impurity and purity; since the *dharmadhātu* exists in different states, error pertains only to adventitious factors within the *dharmadhātu* itself. For that which is naturally pure like space, both of these—mental affliction and mental purification—are established as adventitious. There is no error regarding the absence of fear and pride precisely within the *dharmadhātu*, because, like space, it is unconditioned and lacks decrease or increase. Thus, these ten non-errors are to be understood within the three natures.
[The Ten Vajra-Points] These ten non-perversions just mentioned should be applied respectively to the ten vajra-points taught in the Sūtra. What are the ten vajra-points? They are:

the non-perversion of existence and non-existence; the basis; being like an illusion; the state of being without conceptual construction; the state of natural luminosity; affliction and purification; likeness to space; and the absence of deficiency or excellence.

In this context, "vajra" is like a diamond because it shatters all distortions (*viparyāsa*) and cannot itself be shattered by them; thus, it refers to the non-distorted knowledge (*aviparyāsajñāna*) just mentioned.
That diamond is "realized" or "comprehended" through these [terms], which is the meaning of "vajra-words" (*vajrapada*), i.e., the explanation of the diamond.

Alternatively, if the words "pada" refer specifically to the phonemes, meanings, mental attentions (*manaskāra*), and so forth, then the meaning is that the "words" of the diamond are its objective supports (*ālambana*).
Alternatively, because they are as indestructible as a diamond (*vajra*), these very points are called "diamond points" (*vajrapada*).
Here, the presentation of the diamond points is for the purpose of connecting the absence of errors with the sūtra;
or rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that this commentary is presented by way of the ten kinds of non-error regarding the diamond points.

In that regard, the existence and non-existence of the meaning within the phonemes constitutes their "existence and non-existence"; therefore, the absence of error regarding the phonemes should be understood through the vajra-terms by way of this existence and non-existence.
The appearance of duality is the imagined nature (*parikalpita*), and that is the "meaning" here.
Since that does not exist in such a manner, this is the absence of error here; thus, the absence of error regarding the meaning should be applied to the absence of error among the vajra-terms.

In this context, mental engagement (*manaskāra*) consisting of discursive speech (*jalpa*) is the basis; therefore, the error regarding mental engagement should be applied to the "vajra-word" concerning the basis.
The error regarding the distraction of the mind due to its resemblance to an illusion and so forth should be applied to the "vajra-word" concerning the resemblance to an illusion.

Since the very specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *dharmadhātu* is non-conceptuality because it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the absence of error regarding the specific characteristic should be understood through the state of being without conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatva*).
The commonality of the *dharmadhātu* is its nature of intrinsic luminosity; by this, the non-perversion regarding the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is subsumed under intrinsic luminosity.

Furthermore, the specific lack of purity and the specific purity of the *dharmadhātu* constitute affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*); therefore, the non-perversion regarding impurity and purity is subsumed within the distinction between affliction and purification.
This non-perversion regarding the fact that the *dharmadhātu* is neither defiled nor purified should also be applied to its resemblance to space.

Because there is no decrease or increase of the *dharmadhātu* during the states of defilement and purification, the non-perversion regarding fearlessness and lack of pride should be applied to the "neither inferior nor superior" nature within the vajra-words.
Thus, these ten non-perversions regarding the view are to be applied respectively to the ten vajra-words.

Regarding "the establishment of the body of the vajra-words": those meanings with reference to which the vajra-words proceed constitute their body. Furthermore, their establishment is fourfold: by way of intrinsic nature and by way of objective support.
By way of non-conceptualization and by way of the refutation of objections.
In that regard, the three natures— the perfected, the imagined, and the dependent— are to be understood.

Regarding the phrase "by the first three terms, respectively," those which exist from the beginning are further characterized as non-perversion regarding existence and non-existence, and as the basis. Among these, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is described by way of existence and non-existence; the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is described by way of non-perversion.
The dependent nature is described as the basis. How so?
Some say it is because the perfected nature is explained through the existence and non-existence [of that basis] by means of its own existence and non-existence.
How is it that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is designated as both existent and non-existent because its characteristic is existence-and-non-existence? Some say:

by observing that syllables possess meaning through their conjunction and familiarity with an imagined object (*kalpita-artha*), and conversely, by observing their meaninglessness [in the absence of such], it is understood that the perfected nature is inexpressible.

Others say that its existence and non-existence is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Furthermore, other teachers maintain that the Dharma taught in the Mahāyāna is called the perfected nature because it is the outflow (*nisyanda*) of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu and because it serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the antidote to error; this is the meaning of the imagined nature (*kalpita-svabhāva*), but it is not itself the imagined. Therefore, its existence and non-existence is said to be the perfected nature.
Others, however, say: "The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is so called because its existence and non-existence are non-erroneous (*aviparyasta*).
By way of non-error, the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is [the perfected nature] because it is characterized by appearing in the form of duality despite being non-existent;

the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is [the perfected nature] by way of being its basis (*āśraya*), for it is called the "basis" because it is the cause, and it is called "dependent" because it is the effect.

These very three natures are to be known by way of their object (*ālambana*) and by way of non-conceptuality (*avikalpanatā*). Regarding this, he explains through a distinction in grammatical analysis (*vigraha*): that by which one does not conceptualize, namely non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and that which one does not conceptualize, namely natural luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvaratā*). Herein lies the distinction in analysis: it is "non-conceptuality" because one does not conceptualize by means of this [gnosis]; it is "non-conceptuality" because that [luminosity] is not conceptualized. Its state is "non-conceptuality" (*avikalpanatā*). Thus, he shows that non-conceptuality is elucidated by these two vajra-words.

Therefore, by this, the establishment of the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself should be understood in due order, namely: by means of the three natures and by means of non-conceptual gnosis.

In that regard, the establishment of the object of knowledge is by means of the three natures because they are the grasped; the establishment of knowledge is by means of non-conceptual gnosis because it is the grasper.
The remaining vajra-words are distinguished from those already discussed by way of objections and their refutations.
Among these, some vajra-words consist of the refutation of an objection itself;
for example: "like an illusion."
It is like space and is not distinguished by anything else;
furthermore,
there is yet another objection.
For example, "defilement" and "purification.
Therefore, the objection and the refutation—the objection and the refutation of the objection—are "objection-and-refutation.
This is formed by applying the grammatical rule of *asarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of two dissimilar forms).

In this regard, the objection is as follows: if these phenomena, characterized by the imagined and the dependent natures, do not exist—as the remainder of the sentence implies—in the form of grasped object and grasping subject, then how are they perceived as grasped object and grasping subject? This is the intended meaning. If, on the other hand, they do exist, then the natural luminosity of phenomena is not tenable.
This objection arises because [the object] exists in the nature of the grasped and the grasper. He resolves this by means of the analogy of a dream.

Just as that which is produced by illusion does not exist yet is perceived—indeed, illusion does not exist by virtue of being perceived—it is likewise impossible to know that it exists in that manner.
If the nature of phenomena is luminosity, how can there be prior affliction and subsequent purification? Such is the objection.
For that which is naturally pure can never become defiled. The resolution of this [objection] is to be understood through the analogy of space:
just as space, though naturally pure, becomes defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
And it is said that through their removal, there is purification. Thus, although the *dharmadhātu* is pure by nature, there is defilement due to adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
and through their removal, there is purification.

If immeasurable afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings are eliminated when immeasurable Buddhas appear, then how is it that—despite each appearance of a Buddha in beginningless saṃsāra causing immeasurable sentient beings to depart from saṃsāra and enter nirvāṇa—there is neither a total exhaustion of saṃsāra nor an increase in nirvāṇa? This is the objection.

The rebuttal to this [charge] regarding deficiency and excellence is as follows: because the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) and the side of purification (*vyavadānapakṣa*) are immeasurable. For the diminution or total destruction of a thing that possesses a measurable magnitude is perceived; however, the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable, and thus even its diminution is not perceived, much less its total destruction. Like space, since purification is also immeasurable, there is no distinction [between it and the realm of beings]; how then could there be an increase for it? It is like space, [in which there is no change] due to the removal of obstructions or the appearance of obstructions.
The second is the "establishment of the body," which refers to the vajra-words:

namely, where [delusion occurs], what [delusion is], from what [delusion arises], and likewise where there is non-delusion; and where the fruits of delusion and non-delusion are found, as well as their ultimate limit.

By means of the vajra-words, the object of delusion, the nature of delusion, the cause of delusion, the fruit of delusion, and the limit of delusion are indicated; likewise, the nature of non-delusion, the object of non-delusion, the fruit of non-delusion, and its limit are indicated. In this context, "wherein there is delusion" refers to the existence or non-existence of phonemes characterized by being meaningful or meaningless, because the designator, the designated, and their relationship are imagined as having the nature of real entities. Furthermore, "that which is delusion" refers to error (*viparyāsa*), for delusion is the manifestation of a dual aspect that does not exist in itself.

Since there is delusion, there is a basis for delusion; that basis, moreover, is mental attention (*manaskāra*) permeated by discursive speech (*jalpa*), which consists of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). And as for non-delusion: non-delusion is the absence of the conceptual proliferation regarding existence and non-existence in reality, like a magical illusion (*māyā*) and so forth; furthermore, non-delusion is the antidote to the delusion of clinging to existence and non-existence. These are taught respectively as being "like a magical illusion" and as "non-conceptuality. And "wherein" refers to where that non-delusion exists—namely, in natural luminosity, which is characterized by the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
"And also regarding the fruits of error and non-error": therein, the fruit of error is indeed affliction (*saṃkleśa*);
"the outflow of error" is the completion of the sentence.
Because non-delusion is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of non-delusion and has non-delusion as its fruit;
the remainder of the sentence is that "the fruit of non-delusion is purification (*vyavadāna*) together with its associated factors.
The use of the particle *eva* (only) is because the fruit of that [non-delusion] has already been stated by this very [phrase]: "defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*)."

However, by way of its resemblance to space, one perceives that the result of both delusion and non-delusion within the *dharmadhātu* consists of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that this [result] is not the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of that [dharmadhātu].
Furthermore, "the limit of those two" refers to the limit of affliction and purification; that limit is *nirvāṇa*.
Some say that this is stated to be "without decrease" because it is without deficiency.
Others, however, say:
since saṃsāra is immeasurable, there is no diminution; therefore, the limit of affliction is characterized by the absence of decrease.
Because nirvāṇa is immeasurable, there is no accumulation; thus, it is characterized by the absence of increase, which constitutes the limit of purification.
These ten vajra-terms have been explained by way of the context of non-perversion, but they were not set forth as explicit sūtra-texts; therefore, he summarizes them with two intermediate verses.
The non-perversion regarding existence and non-existence, the likeness to an illusion, the basis,
and that which is by nature non-conceptual and always luminous.
Defilement and purification, likewise the likeness to space,
and neither deficiency nor excess— these indeed are the ten vajra-points.
And herein, the perception of a relationship between words and objects as being established in reality is a misconception;
the perception of things as having an intrinsic nature and existence exactly as they appear is a misconception;
and the perception of a cause for the engagement with those objects is a misconception.
The view of superimposition and denial regarding objects is perversion;
likewise, the view of an intrinsic nature in objects according to their names is perversion;
as are the specific and general characteristics of entities.

The views that [things] exist as real entities are perversions; the views of the transition between well-being and ill-being, purity and impurity, are perversions; the view of purity and impurity in that which is one and the same is a perversion; and the occurrence of fear and pride due to perceiving decline or excellence in the abandonment and attainment of affliction and purification is a perversion—these are the ten perversions. Because a bodhisattva is free from these and abides in non-perversion, their unchanging vision and cultivation regarding the aforementioned objects should be understood as the practice in accordance with the Dharma (anudharmapratipatti) as previously described.

Immediately after the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*anudharmapratipatti*), the practice regarding the avoidance of the two extremes (*antadvayavarjana*) must be explained; therefore, he asks: "What is the practice regarding the avoidance of the two extremes? To this he replies: "That middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*) which was taught in the *Dharmaparyāya* named *Ratnakūṭa* for the purpose of establishing the nature of correct practice (*samyakpratipatti*). For example, Kāśyapa, in this *Mahāratnakūṭa Dharmaparyāya*, a bodhisattva who desires to train must be one who applies himself to the Dharma through proper method (*yoniśodharmaprayukta*). And what is application to the Dharma through proper method? It is the true discernment (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) of all phenomena—that which is the non-discernment of a name, and the non-discernment of a being, a soul, a life-principle, a nourisher, a person, a human, or a man. This, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way," and so it is recited in detail up to the second illustration of the lamp. "What is meant by 'by the avoidance of which extreme' is to be understood? What is the meaning of 'by the avoidance of which extreme the middle way is to be known'? To this he says: "The extremes of difference and identity (*pṛthaktva-ekatva*), as well as those of the heterodox (*tīrthika*) and the disciples (*śrāvaka*)."
Thus is the detailed explanation. This fifteenfold division of the two extremes is to be understood as that which is to be avoided;
herein, the view of [the self as] distinct and so forth constitutes an extreme.
Because of being attached to each respective side, one applies the metaphor of the cause to the effect.
In that regard, "the self is separate from form and so forth" is an extreme;
"it is identical [to them]" is an extreme.

In this regard, those who conceptualize the aggregates such as form, the sense bases, and the elements as objects of enjoyment for an eternal self hold the extreme view that the self is distinct from form and the other aggregates.

Furthermore, those who—having apprehended internal conditioned factors such as form as being the self—hold that "he who sees, hears, and knows is the self," and who conceptualize external things as belonging to the self, hold the extreme view that the self is identical with form and the other aggregates. As it is stated in the Sūtra:

The view that "the soul is one thing and its body another" is what is expressed here by the word "extreme" (*anta*). It is for the purpose of avoiding that [view], meaning for the purpose of avoiding the extremes of identity with or difference from the self in relation to form and the other aggregates.
The middle way is the knowledge for which mere phenomena (*dharmamātra*) have become the object.
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
"That which is not the contemplation of a self, up to and including that which is not the contemplation of a person."
For by seeing only phenomena (*dharmamātra*), one understands that the self does not exist, like the son of a barren woman; thus, the meaning is that one does not perceive nor pursue a self.
How then could its identity with or difference from form and so forth be apprehended?
Since that object is already understood through the word "self" alone, what is the purpose of employing specific synonyms such as "sentient being" (*sattva*) and so on?

Since not everyone possesses an understanding of all synonymous expressions, other synonyms are taught so that everyone may comprehend their meaning; or rather, they are taught through alternative synonyms for the sake of conveying that same meaning to those who were distracted at the time [of the first teaching],
because others can grasp it when it is expressed by that very designation.
That "form and so forth are permanent" is the extreme of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
For they, having become attached to imagined forms as real entities, conceive of them as permanent because they are afflicted by the perversion of permanence.
