That "[they] are impermanent" is the extreme of the Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, for those who superimpose an imagined intrinsic nature upon form and so forth, viewing them as entities, there is the extreme of permanence; and because it causes extreme agitation regarding saṃsāra and leads to falling into the extreme of nirvāṇa, the view of impermanence is itself an extreme. Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Determination of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
For the purpose of avoiding both of these— that is, for the purpose of avoiding the views of permanence and impermanence— there is the middle way,
which is neither the contemplation of form and so forth as impermanent nor the non-contemplation of them as impermanent.
What, then, is that?
Non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*) is that which does not follow after form and so forth as being either permanent or impermanent within those very forms and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of form and so forth," there is the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the elements (*dhātu*) of earth, water, fire, air, and space; and the sense bases (*āyatana*) of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

By the term "self-grasping" (*ātmagrāha*), the extreme of superimposition regarding the person (*pudgala*) is indicated. This refers to the superimposition of a self—the person—as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), whether distinct from or non-distinct from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which, like the son of a barren woman, does not exist; this is the superimposition of a real nature upon the person and the self.
"Selflessness" (*nairātmya*), on the other hand, is the extreme of denial (*apavāda*).
For it has been said that denial is the conceptualization of the non-existence of that which actually exists.
Since the self does not exist, how can there be "selflessness"? Thus, one might fall into the extreme of negation; therefore, he says:
"Because of the negation even of that which exists as a designation.
This connects with the statement: "Selflessness is an extreme of negation."
Furthermore, it is the continuum of phenomena (*dharmas*) in which the relationship between cause and fruit is discerned,
or the collection [of phenomena] in which the designation of "god" or "human" occurs.
For the purpose of avoiding those two extremes, there is the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*).
For the purpose of abandoning the views of the existence and non-existence of a self,
and furthermore for the purpose of defining that middle way,
he says: "That which is the middle between self and selflessness."
What, then, is that middle, non-conceptual gnosis?

Having shown that the conceptualization of the object to be grasped (*grāhyārtha*) is an extreme, he says "the mind is real," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that the conceptualization of the subject who grasps (*grāhakārtha*) is likewise an extreme.

Alternatively, having demonstrated the extremes of superimposition and denial regarding the person (*pudgala*), he says "the mind is real," and so forth, in order to show the extremes of superimposition and denial regarding phenomena (*dharma*).

To think that the mind exists as something real exactly as it appears or as it is expressed—this is the extreme of superimposing phenomena, because one superimposes reality upon the intrinsic nature of the mind which is actually unreal.

The notion that "the mind is non-existent" is the extreme of negation (*apavādānta*). For one who perceives even that which exists—in its nature devoid of grasped object and grasping subject and in its ineffable state—as "non-existent," there is a total negation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*); thus, it is the extreme of negation. "To avoid that" means: for the sake of penetrating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) which is free from both superimposition and negation, there is the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "That is where the dogmatic attachments (*abhiniveśa*) to 'no-mind,' 'no-thought' (*manas*), and 'no-consciousness' (*vijñāna*) do not arise."

In whatever object the mind (*citta*) does not proceed as something accumulated by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the outflows (*sāsrava*), nor volition (*cetanā*) characterized by formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*), nor the intellect (*manas*) in its mode of conceiving (*manyanā*), nor consciousness (*vijñāna*) as conceptualization (*vikalpaka*)—this is called the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

In that context, "mind" is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) because it is accumulated by the latencies of all phenomena associated with the outflows; "volition" is mental action (*manaskarma*) whose function is to impel the mind toward what is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; "intellect" is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*); and "consciousness" refers to the six groups of consciousness.

Unwholesome and other such phenomena are "defilement," which is the extreme of the adverse side (*vipakṣānta*); wholesome and other such phenomena are "purification," which is the extreme of the remedial side (*pratipakṣānta*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), descriptions such as faulty and faultless, mundane and supramundane, with-outflows and without-outflows, conditioned and unconditioned, and others are connected.

In this regard, the view that defilement and purification exist exactly as unwholesome and wholesome phenomena appear and are expressed is the extreme of the adverse side and the extreme of the remedial side.
In that context, they are unwholesome because their meaning is insecurity; they are blameworthy because they give rise to misconduct; they are mundane because they are inverted;
and they are with-outflows because they are underlain by the outflows.
They are conditioned because they are produced by causal conditions.

However, their opposites—the wholesome and so forth—should be understood accordingly. For the purpose of avoiding those [extremes], there is the "middle way"; thus, the word "that" refers to both the adverse factors and their antidotes.
Since the middle way is not understood here, he says:
"That which is the non-approach, the non-proclamation, and the non-expression of these two extremes.
In this context, "non-approach" means non-adherence to both the adverse side and its antidote.
It is "without utterance" because it does not cause others to adopt the extremes of the adverse side and its antidote;
it is "without verbal expression" because it does not describe the extremes of the adverse side and its antidote.
Having taught the middle way as the antidote to the extremes of the non-Buddhists and the śrāvakas, he speaks while establishing the middle way as the antidote to the extreme of the bodhisattvas.
"It exists" is the extreme of eternalism;
"it does not exist" is the extreme of nihilism— referring precisely to those two, the person and phenomena.

The extreme of eternalism is the assertion that "it exists" due to the superimposition of intrinsic characteristics at all times; the extreme of nihilism is the denial of its own nature in every respect, asserting that "it does not exist. The middle way is for the purpose of avoiding those two.
Regarding the phrase "that which is between these two extremes":
some maintain that what is intended here by "the middle" is the departure from both extremes;
others maintain that the "middle" between the two extremes is characterized by both.

How so? For the adherence that the object of knowledge and the object of expression exists substantially and ultimately— just like the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) or like the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*)— is the extreme of eternalism (*śāśvatānta*),
because it does not exist in that manner.
Likewise, the view that [things] simply do not exist at all, like the horn of a hare, is the extreme of nihilism.
Why?
Because they exist as designations (*prajñapti*).
Therefore, by the negation of that [extreme], the extreme of annihilation is spoken of.
Consequently, the middle between existence and non-existence possesses both characteristics: it does not exist substantially or ultimately, yet it exists as a designation.

With reference to the extreme of superimposition regarding the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), it is said: "Ignorance is the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)," which is an extreme. Likewise, "knowledge, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its antidote are the grasped and the grasper," which is an extreme. Here, by the inclusion of the final limit "up to old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth are also implied. Thus, "consciousness is the grasped and the grasper" is an extreme; likewise, name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), clinging (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death are the grasped and the grasper—these are extremes.

In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of the non-manifestation of the jewels of the truths; it is a contaminated volition (*cetanā*) whose intrinsic nature is meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable. Because it forms the conditions for renewed existence (*punarbhava*), it is called a formative force (*saṃskāra*). Following this explanation of the characteristics of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other members should also be explained in detail. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is uncontaminated cognition (*anāsrava-jñāna*); the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the formative forces is precisely that unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) knowledge. For this very reason, in order to distinguish it from other unconditioned phenomena, he says "its antidote. Others, however, consider that because it is characterized by non-arising, all eight kinds of the unconditioned are included here; yet they hold that the antidote is uncontaminated volition, because it does not form the conditions for renewed existence. The extreme views consist of [the notion that] its cessation is either the grasped (*grāhya*) or the grasper (*grāhaka*).

By that word [“cessation”], consciousness and the other factors up to old age and death are connected. It is not understood whether this cessation is an entity (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, he says: “by which that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is ceased. But by what is that name-and-form ceased? By the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), which is the antidote to name-and-form. Knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—these two are non-dual and without division; this very knowledge, together with its retinue, is the path here. And thus, because it is ceased *by means of* this, it is “cessation” (*nirodha*). What, then, is the limit (*anta*) here? It is precisely this adherence to the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakābhiniveśa*).
What is the reason? Because [ignorance] and so forth, whose nature is non-dual, function by superimposing a duality that does not exist.

Thus, the extreme of the grasped and the grasper is twofold, distinguished by the black and white sides. Therein, on the black side, there are the twelve links of existence, from ignorance up to old age and death.

Likewise, on the white side as well, through the distinction of the cessation of ignorance and so forth, there are likewise twelve modes, from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death.
And here, because ignorance and the other [afflictions] are ceased by means of this, the Path itself—which serves as their antidote—is expressed by the word "cessation" (*nirodha*).
The phrase "for the sake of abandoning that" is connected to the statement that the Middle Way was taught for the sake of abandoning the extremes of the grasped and the grasper.
Since that [Middle Way] is not understood, he says: "Knowledge and ignorance—these two are non-dual."

How are knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and their cessations, non-dual? To this he says: "Because of the absence of the relationship between grasped and grasper (*grāhyagrāhakatva*) in knowledge, ignorance, and so forth.
Their absence, however, is due to the fact that ignorance and the rest have non-duality as their intrinsic nature (*advayaprakṛtitva*).

Alternatively, knowledge and ignorance are of an imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*); therefore, because of the equality of the non-existence of knowledge and ignorance—which are both of an imagined nature—knowledge and ignorance are non-dual.

In this same way, it should be stated regarding the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and the unconditioned consciousness (*asaṃskṛta-vijñāna*), as well as their cessation, and so on up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and their cessation. What, then, is the middle way here? It is this very knowledge and vision that [perceives] ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) as non-dual and without division. Thus, knowledge is not to be produced, nor is ignorance to be ceased; the formative forces and so forth are not to be abandoned, nor are their cessations to be attained. This very knowledge which is thus [viewed] is without duality.

Regarding the statement that "defilement is threefold": therein, afflictions (*kleśa*) are called defilements because they are the cause of the defilements of karma and birth, because they are themselves afflicted, and because they are the cause of harm to oneself and others. Karma, too, is called defilement because it is produced under the influence of afflictions, because it is the cause of birth, and because it is itself afflicted in some cases.
Birth, too, is a defilement because it is caused by karma and afflictions and because it serves as the basis for all calamities.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the threefold division of the defilement of afflictions, he says: "The defilement of afflictions is threefold," and so forth.
Among these, views are five, beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Attachment, aversion, and delusion alone are the cause, because they are the causes of sorrow and so forth, and because they are the causes of rebirth.
Others, however, say:
the cause of attachment and the rest is the objects of the senses that are favorable to them.
Improper mental attention;
the latencies of passion and so forth are situated within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Thus they describe it: the cause of passion and so forth is that which appears as such.
The aspiration for renewed existence is the longing for rebirth;
its antidote is the emptiness of knowledge (*jñāna-śūnyatā*), as explained in detail.
Among those [types of craving], the emptiness of knowledge is the antidote for those based on views.

In this context, "knowledge of emptiness" (*jñānaśūnyatā*) refers to knowledge whose object is emptiness. "Knowledge of the signless" (*jñānānimitta*) is the knowledge that counters the signs of passion and so forth, because it is free from all signs;
alternatively, it is knowledge whose object is the signless.
Because its object is the emptiness of imagined passion and so forth, the knowledge that is the antidote to the aspiration for renewed existence is "knowledge without aspiration" (*jñānāpraṇihita*).
Knowledge that is free from the aspiration for renewed existence, or whose object is the emptiness of renewed existence, is "knowledge without aspiration.

Karmic affliction (*karmasaṃkleśa*) is the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma; it is the accumulation, the production, and the formative activity of the wholesome and unwholesome karmas that project renewed existence.
The antidote to this is the non-conceptualization of knowledge (*jñānānabhisaṃskāra*).
That knowledge by which one does not perform karma that leads to rebirth is "the non-conceptualization of knowledge.
Furthermore, that [knowledge] has suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
The defilement of birth is the birth of renewed existence, namely the mind at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*).
For one who has been born, it is the moment-to-moment arising of the mind and mental factors from after the connection of rebirth until death.
This is the "continuity of renewed existence," which constitutes the affliction (*kleśa*).

The state of death (*maraṇabhava*) is accompanied [by other factors]; immediately following that is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and from that, again, the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*). However, for those who have attained the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the state of rebirth occurs immediately after the state of death itself. The antidote to this is the non-arising of knowledge (*jñānājāti*), the non-production of knowledge (*jñānānutpāda*), and the lack of intrinsic nature in knowledge (*jñānāsvabhāvatā*). In this regard, all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*) are unarisen in their imagined nature (*parikalpitātmakatva*). That knowledge which has emptiness as its object is the "non-arising of knowledge"; the knowledge whose object is the emptiness of imagined phenomena is the "non-production of knowledge. Because one penetrates its non-production through that [knowledge], the continuity of existence (*bhāvaprabandha*) lacks intrinsic nature due to its non-existence, like the son of a barren woman; that knowledge is the "lack of intrinsic nature in knowledge. This sevenfold knowledge, beginning with the emptiness of knowledge, is the antidote to the sevenfold opposition consisting of views and so forth as previously described. The removal of these three types of afflictions—affliction (*kleśa*), karma, and birth—which are divided into seven ways, is purification (*vyavadāna*); "removal" means abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Others, however, think that suchness (*tathatā*), the path (*mārga*), and nirvāṇa are purification, because they interpret the compound according to the analysis: "that in which [defilements] depart," "that by which [they] depart," and "the departure [itself]. In that context, by the phrase "by the emptiness of knowledge and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the emptiness of knowledge, the signlessness of knowledge, the wishlessness of knowledge, the lack of formative activity of knowledge, the non-arising of knowledge, the non-production of knowledge, and the lack of intrinsic nature in knowledge. By the phrase "phenomena such as the emptiness of the knowable," the word "and so forth" here includes the emptiness of the knowable, the signlessness of the knowable, the wishlessness of the knowable, the lack of formative activity of the knowable, the non-arising of the knowable, the non-production of the knowable, and the lack of intrinsic nature in the knowable—all of which possess the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpannalakṣaṇa*). By this threefold affliction, as appropriate, the emptiness of the knowable and so forth are not made [to exist] until [the end]. The phenomena such as the emptiness of the knowable, which are distinct from the aforementioned afflictions of defilement, karma, and birth, are not "made" by the emptiness of knowledge and so forth. Why are they not made? Because they are by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*) emptiness and so forth; the meaning is that they are by their very nature devoid of the intrinsic nature of views and so forth. Why [is this so]? [To be continued...]
Therefore, he says this: because the *dharmadhātu* is by nature undefiled (*prakṛtyasaṃkliṣṭa*).

Consequently, phenomena such as the emptiness of the knowable (*jñeyaśūnyatā*) are by their very nature emptiness and so forth; they are not produced by the emptiness of knowledge (*jñānaśūnyatā*) and the like.

"According to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*)—this is the meaning of "according to what is appropriate" here: the emptiness of the knowable is not produced by the emptiness of knowledge as something liberated from or separated from the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃkleśa*).
Because the emptiness of views has, by its very nature, the character of non-viewing;
likewise, the signlessness of the object of knowledge is not produced by the signlessness of knowledge,
for the signlessness of emptiness is due to its own nature being devoid of the signs of passion and so forth.
By means of the non-aiming of knowledge, the non-aiming of the knowable is not produced;
for the emptiness of aspiration is, by its very nature, characterized by non-aspiration.
By means of the non-conditioning of knowledge, the non-conditioning of the knowable is not produced.
Because the emptiness of conditioned activity has, by its very nature, the characteristic of non-conditioning;
because the non-arising of the object of knowledge is not produced by the non-arising of knowledge,
since the emptiness of arising has, by its very nature, the characteristic of non-arising.
The non-arising of the knowable is not produced by the non-arising of knowledge,
because the emptiness of the moment-to-moment arising of mind and mental factors is characterized by non-arising by its very nature.
The absence of intrinsic nature in the knowable is not produced by the absence of intrinsic nature in knowledge.
Because the emptiness of rebirth is by its very nature devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Alternatively, it is as explained in detail: "by means of the threefold affliction (*saṃkleśa*) as appropriate. This refers to the sevenfold division of the afflictions of defilement (*kleśa*), karma, and birth. Regarding the phenomena such as the emptiness of the knowable (*jñeya-śūnyatā*), whichever phenomenon is associated with whichever specific type of affliction, that phenomenon is not produced by the emptiness of knowledge (*jñāna-śūnyatā*) and so forth; rather, it is realized. In this context, there is an association of the emptiness of knowledge with the affliction of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃkleśa*).
In this way, up until the connection with the lack of intrinsic nature of knowledge through the continuity of rebirth—
why is it not performed? Because those phenomena, such as emptiness and so forth, are by their very nature [empty], since the dharmadhātu is by its very nature undefiled.
In that regard, views are not made empty by means of the emptiness of knowledge,
because they are characterized by emptiness by their very nature.
The sign of passion and so forth is not made signless by means of the signlessness of knowledge.
Because the *dharmadhātu* is by its very nature signless (*animitta*).

Thus, up to the point where the continuity of renewed existence is not rendered "without intrinsic nature" by means of the lack of intrinsic nature of knowledge— since even when the antidote has not yet arisen, conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) is already non-existent by its very nature.

Since this is so, if one conceptualizes that the *dharmadhātu* is either defiled or purified, this is an extreme. For what reason? Because he says: "Because there is no defilement or purification for that which is by nature undefiled, like space. In order to avoid this extreme, the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*) is that which does not—by means of wisdom (*vidyā*)—make phenomena empty of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-śūnyatā*) and so forth, which consist of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), through their opposite, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) consisting of views and the like; rather, even when wisdom has not yet arisen, phenomena themselves are empty by means of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the very form of views. Likewise, that which does not make phenomena signless (*animitta*) by means of signlessness, but rather phenomena themselves are signless; and so on, up to that which does not make phenomena without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) by means of the absence of intrinsic nature, but rather phenomena themselves are without intrinsic nature. Such an investigation (*pratyavekṣā*) is called, Kāśyapa, the "true investigation of phenomena" (*bhūta-pratyavekṣā*). Thus, by illuminating the existence of wisdom and the existence of its opposite as being devoid of the imagined nature, the rejection of the extremes of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) is accomplished.

Regarding this aforementioned classification of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), there is another sevenfold set of dual extremes of conceptual construction. To demonstrate these classifications of conceptual construction, he says: "For example, conceptualization regarding existence is an extreme; conceptualization regarding non-existence is also an extreme. If one asks how so, he explains: because of the conceptualization that "the person (*pudgala*) exists, for whose destruction emptiness (*śūnyatā*) [is taught]," or "even selflessness (*nairātmya*) does not exist. Furthermore, if one thinks that "emptiness does not make phenomena empty, because they are empty by nature," then, in that case, the person exists, for whose destruction emptiness and selflessness [are taught].
Or rather, [it does not exist] because of the non-existence of a person (*pudgala*).
For there is no antidote that exists without an opponent.
Therefore, one must necessarily admit either the existence of a person or the non-existence of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
The conceptualization of its existence or non-existence is an extreme.
For the purpose of abandoning this pair of extremes—the conceptualization of existence and non-existence—this is the middle way.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, emptiness is certainly not for the sake of destroying the person.
Rather, the full scriptural passage reads: "emptiness itself is empty," and so forth.
In this context, emptiness does not exist for the sake of destroying a defiled person (*pudgala*), nor for the sake of producing a purified person;

because the person is a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*) like an army and the like, there is no arising or destruction of a person. Rather, it is emptiness itself that is empty, and not by means of a person superimposed through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), since such a person is absolutely non-existent.
And having established this, [it follows that] there is no existence by way of the selfhood of persons and phenomena, because emptiness is the absence of those;
nor is there non-existence by way of the perfected nature.
And demonstrating that this very emptiness has the perfected nature as its essence, he says:
Empty of the past limit; empty of the future limit; empty of the present.
Because its existence is demonstrated in exactly the same way throughout the three times;
or alternatively, because its existence is demonstrated in exactly the same way during the states of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and being a seeker (*śaikṣa*).
Among those, the state of an ordinary person is the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
The future limit is the state of non-seeking; the present is the state of seeking. And because the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of existence and non-existence is thus established, he says:
"Kāśyapa, rely on emptiness" means that it is the object of non-conceptual knowledge;

"not on the person" means that [the person] is a mere designation. Furthermore, conceptualization regarding bending is an extreme, and conceptualization regarding bowing is also an extreme. Thus it is said.
It proceeds.
How so? To this he says:
"Because of the fear of emptiness due to the conceptualization of that which is to be abandoned and its abandonment."
In that regard, there is the object to be pacified, that which is to be abandoned, the act of pacifying, and the abandonment itself.
Having conceptualized phenomena as the objects to be abandoned and emptiness as the abandonment, fear arises toward emptiness.
For how can the threefold defilement be abandoned if it is empty by nature?

Consequently, it would not be something to be abandoned, just like the person (*pudgala*). And since there would be no abandonment due to the absence of anything to be abandoned, terror regarding emptiness arises.
This too is indeed an extreme.
What is the reason?
For they are attached to the idea that phenomena such as form and sensation exist substantially, exactly as they appear within the nature of consciousness.
Because of their ignorance regarding the fact that these forms and so forth—which possess an imagined nature—are by their very essence non-existent like a self, they fear emptiness.
Therefore, for the purpose of avoiding these two conceptual extremes, there is the simile of space.
For example, Kāśyapa, suppose a certain man were terrified of space and, beating his breast, were to cry out and say, "Remove this space!
What do you think, Kāśyapa? Is it possible to remove space?
He said, "No indeed, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
In the same way, Kāśyapa, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are terrified of emptiness; I say that they have fallen into great distraction.
Why is that?
Because, Kāśyapa, it is precisely while roaming within emptiness itself that they are afraid of it.
This is what is meant:
just as space cannot be removed because it pervades all forms, so too emptiness is established at all times within all phenomena and cannot be removed.
Nor can emptiness, which is established when phenomena are not abandoned, be removed; nor is emptiness established through the abandonment of phenomena.
Therefore, he shows that this is an irrational fear;
the term "kalpa" [is used] in the sense of "that which is to be feared," and thus also in the sense of "fear arising from that which is to be feared."
What is meant by "conceptualization is an extreme"? That from which fear arises is called the "object of fear.
It is called "fear" because one is afraid of it.
Therefore, regarding that which has an undesirable result—within that which is to be feared and within that fear—he who conceptualizes is the "extreme. To the question "How so? he says:
"Because of trembling at imagined form and so forth, due to fear of suffering.
For the foolish, having conceptually constructed imagined form and so forth as real entities, they further construct fear and undesirable results from them.
Consequently, out of fear of suffering, they tremble with dread of those forms and their causes.
To avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the analogy of the painter.

For example, Kāśyapa, it is as if a painter were to create the terrifying form of a yakṣa himself, and then, terrified and trembling by that very form, were to fall face down and fall into a state of confusion.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, all foolish common people themselves create forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, and then wander in saṃsāra because of them, not understanding those phenomena as they truly are.

Just as a painter, having superimposed the state of a real yakṣa upon a terrifying yakṣa-form created by himself through false conceptualization, becomes afraid of it and falls into delusion; so too all fools, driven by false conceptualizations, wander in saṃsāra due to their own conceptual constructions, because the momentary states of the homogeneous class of beings are unstable. The previous example was intended for the śrāvakas, but this one is for the bodhisattvas; for the śrāvaka, being unaccustomed to emptiness, is terrified of emptiness.
Some maintain that the bodhisattva, however, is afflicted by the conceptualization of imagined phenomena because [such affliction] consists of conceptual afflictions (*vikalpakleśa*).
Others hold that there is no difference in meaning between these two, but rather they are designated as "two" because they belong to two distinct categories.
Furthermore, due to fear of emptiness, the śrāvaka does not realize what is to be realized.
Others, however, say that the Bodhisattva [is so called] because of fear of conceptually constructed phenomena (*vikalpitadharma*).
Some maintain that the former [term] serves as an antidote to the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*), while this one serves as an antidote to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

This refers to the fact that conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is an extreme, and conceptualization regarding the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) is also an extreme.

How could these objects of apprehension, such as form and so forth, and the bodies of consciousness that apprehend them—when grasped by way of their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and their effects—be something whose self-nature is superimposed (*adhyāropita-ātman*), like a self (*ātman*) and so on? It is in this sense that the conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) regarding the object and subject as real entities is intended as an "extreme" (*anta*).
To avoid these two extremes of conceptualization, the analogy of a magician is given.

It is just as if, Kāśyapa, a magician were to conjure up a magical creation, and then that very creation were to devour the magician himself; in the same way, Kāśyapa, whatever object a monk who practices yoga brings to mind, all of that appears to him as utterly empty—so it is said at length.

How does one avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction by this means? To this he says: for the knowledge of the non-existence of objects is produced by the knowledge of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and that very knowledge of the non-existence of objects causes that same knowledge of representation-only to cease, because when there is no object, representation is impossible; this is the point of similarity here. The knowledge of representation-only stands in the place of the magician, while the knowledge of the non-existence of objects stands in the place of the conjured yakṣa, since the knowledge of the non-existence of objects is brought about by the power of the knowledge of representation-only.
Just as a magical creation might devour its creator, so too does the knowledge of the non-existence of objects devour that very knowledge of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is because, in the absence of an object, representation-only is impossible; for [otherwise] one would have to accept that the perception of an object constitutes representation-only.
It has been stated that conceptualization regarding correctness is an extreme, and conceptualization regarding falsity is also an extreme.

In the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there is the pair of extremes consisting of conceptualizing the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) as either "correct" or "false. How so? Correctness refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, while falsity refers to the tainted (*sāsrava*) ones. In that regard, if one determines the discernment of reality as being exclusively correct, then wholesome tainted phenomena would not be the discernment of reality.
Furthermore, it would likewise possess the characteristic of non-correctness;
thus, falsity itself would follow, just like the wholesome states associated with the three realms.
To overturn these two extremes, there is the analogy of fire produced from two pieces of wood.
It is like this, Kāśyapa: just as fire is produced in dependence upon two pieces of wood, and once produced, that very fire burns those same two pieces of wood;
even so, Kāśyapa, the noble faculty of wisdom is produced in dependence upon the discernment of reality, and once produced, it burns that very discernment of reality.
This is the meaning here: just as fire is produced from two pieces of wood that do not themselves possess the characteristic of fire.
And once born, it burns two pieces of wood.

In the very same way, from the contemplation of reality (bhūtapratyavekṣā), which is characterized by non-rectitude, the noble faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya), which is characterized by rectitude, is born;
and once born, it consumes that very contemplation of reality.
The meaning is "they cause it to be analyzed.
For it is said to be "as if burned" precisely because of that analysis, due to the observation of its transformation.
And this discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), although it is still associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), is called "discernment of reality" because it is conducive to correctness.

Regarding the statement that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is an extreme whether there is activity or no activity—how is this so? To this he says: "because one imagines either the intentional action of knowledge or its lack of efficacy.
If, having determined "this is ignorance; I shall abandon it," one engages in activity for the sake of abandoning it, this is the extreme of conceptualization regarding activity.

Because cognition is momentary, it cannot exist at the time of the activity of abandonment; therefore, [the claim] that there is no capacity for the abandonment of ignorance is an extreme of conceptualization regarding non-activity.

In order to avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the simile of the oil lamp. As it is said, Kāśyapa: "When an oil lamp is lit, the blinding darkness departs. Yet, Kāśyapa, it does not occur to the oil lamp, ‘I am dispelling all darkness. Rather, Kāśyapa, it is simply by depending upon the oil lamp that the blinding darkness departs. In the same way, Kāśyapa, when knowledge arises, ignorance departs. Yet, Kāśyapa, it does not occur to knowledge, ‘I am dispelling ignorance. Rather, it is simply by depending upon knowledge that ignorance departs. This means that just as a lamp is devoid of activity and free from the intention to eliminate blinding darkness, yet in whatever place it is placed, all blinding darkness departs from that place merely by the presence of the lamp.

In the same way, in whichever continuum non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises, ignorance departs from that very continuum simply by virtue of the mere existence of that [knowledge], because knowledge is non-conceptual and thus devoid of [active] operation. And so, since knowledge lacks the capacity for functional activity, it dispels its opposite merely by its presence, like a lamp. The phrase "is an extreme" (*anta*) follows [from the previous context]: "even in the case of non-arising, conceptualization is an extreme; even in the case of simultaneity, conceptualization is an extreme."
To the question "How so?", he says:

If one imagines the non-arising of the antidote, thinking, "Just as the antidote has never arisen in all this time, so too it will not arise now," this conceptualization regarding non-birth is an extreme.
Or, [it refers to] the long duration of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). For as long as ignorance—which is the opposite of knowledge—remains established, knowledge is not capable of arising.
Even if it were somehow to arise, because ignorance has been rooted for a long time, its removal by momentary knowledge would be impossible.
Consequently, there would be a simultaneity between affliction and purification.
In order to avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the second simile of the oil lamp.
It is as follows, Kāśyapa: suppose that in a house, a cave, or a chamber, no one has lit an oil lamp for the duration of a thousand years;
then, suppose some person were to light an oil lamp there.
"What do you think, Kāśyapa? Would it occur to the thick darkness of night, even if it had accumulated for a thousand years, ‘I am here; I will not depart from this place’?
He replied, "No, Blessed One. For the thick darkness has no power to remain once an oil lamp is lit; it must necessarily depart."
The Blessed One said:

"In the same way, Kāśyapa, even the karma and afflictions accumulated over hundreds of thousands of eons vanish through a single instance of wise reflection and investigation. 'An oil lamp,' Kāśyapa, is a designation for the noble faculty of wisdom."

"Darkness and gloom," Kāśyapa, "is a designation for karma and affliction. By this illustration, he avoids [the charge of] the non-arising of the antidote, because its arising is dependent upon conditions; and he avoids [the charge of] the simultaneity of the antidote with the defilement, because the dark side [of existence] is weak while that [antidote] is powerful.
"The side [of existence] is like a lamp in the blinding darkness"—
thus have been stated the practices for avoiding the two extremes.

Immediately after the practice of avoiding the two extremes has been taught, both the distinguished and the undistinguished practices were indicated; therefore, following the explanation of the practice of avoiding the two extremes, he asks: "What are the distinguished and the undistinguished practices?
To this, he says: "The distinguished and the undistinguished are to be known in the ten stages (bhūmis)."
In each of those ten stages, there are two types of practice.
To explain how this is so, he says:
"In whichever stage a particular perfection becomes predominant," and so forth.

On whichever bodhisattva stage a bodhisattva is established, whichever perfection they apply themselves to predominantly, that [perfection] becomes superior to the other perfections on that particular bodhisattva stage; thus, it is called "distinguished. For example, on the first stage, the perfection of generosity becomes superior. In that context, practice is said to be distinguished.
Thus, up to the tenth [perfection], the perfection of knowledge (*jñānapāramitā*).
Regarding all the remaining perfections, it is said that their practice is "undifferentiated" because they are fully realized on that very stage (*bhūmi*),
just as it was stated that on the Joyous Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) becomes predominant.
And it is not that he does not fully realize the remaining [perfections], according to his strength and according to his knowledge.
In this way, the exposition for the remaining stages should be understood as it is set forth in the sūtras.
The supremacy of practice has been explained.
Now, since it is the occasion to explain the supremacy of the object (*ālambana-anuttarya*), he asks: "What is the supremacy of the object?
Therefore, he speaks in order to elucidate that.
"The establishment and likewise the realm," and so forth;
thus, this is the twelvefold object of focus.

Beginning from the objective support of formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*) up to the objective support of excellence (*prakarṣa*), it is called the "supremacy of the objective support" (*ālambanānuttarya*) because it is superior to all other objective supports. In that regard, "formal establishment" refers to those dharmas such as the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth, which are established by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Demonstrating this very point, the author of the Commentary also says:
"The objective support for the establishment of the designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptivyavasthāna*).
The designation of phenomena refers to the designation of phenomena such as the perfections beginning with generosity, the factors conducive to enlightenment, and the noble truths.

(83, b) By means of that [designation], one establishes [the dharma]; or rather, that [designation] itself is the establishment here. This is the establishment of the designation of dharmas (*dharmaprajñapti-vyavasthāna*).
Furthermore, because it is conducive to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the establishment of the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and so forth is presented here.
159, b "The sequence is to be seen":
the second is suchness (*tathatā*), because it is a synonym for the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the third and fourth: therein, the third is the objective support (*ālambana*) of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
The fourth is the objective support of the means (*sādhanālambana*).
"Those two alone" refers to the first and second [objective supports].
"Respectively" means that the first is the objective support of the goal (*sādhyālambana*).
The second is the objective support of the means.
Regarding that very point, he states the reason:
"Because through the penetration of the dharmadhātu, there is the realization of the dharmas such as the perfections."

Because they penetrate the *dharmadhātu*, the untainted *pāramitās* are attained; thus, the first is the object of what is to be accomplished (*sādhyālambana*) and the second is the object of the means (*sādhanālambana*). The fifth is the object of retention (*dhāraṇālambana*).

Because it retains the *pāramitās* and other phenomena, as well as the *dharmadhātu*, by means of mere hearing through the knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamayajñāna*), that knowledge consisting of hearing is called "retention."

The object of *dhāraṇā* (retention) is the "object of retention. This, moreover, consists of the first two—the object of establishment and the object of the *dharmadhātu*—because one retains them after having understood them through the sixth [type of knowledge], that which consists of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*). Having understood them by means of the reasonings of dependence, cause and effect, logical proof, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), one retains the meaning of what was heard; thus, retention is the knowledge consisting of reflection, and its object is the "object of retention. The seventh is the object of that which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayajñāna*); this is the subject under discussion.

"Because of individual internal retention" means that because one retains the object internally, there is "firm retention" (*pradhāraṇā*), which is the knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-jñāna*) serving as the preparatory application for entering the first stage (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, its objective support (*ālambana*)—ranging from the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the powers (*bala*)—is the "objective support of firm retention.

Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) on the first stage, this is the eighth [type of objective support], which is the penetration of the all-pervading nature of the non-dual *dharmadhātu* within oneself.

Alternatively, *prativedha* (penetration) is the piercing of the opposition to the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) and to the non-afflicted ignorance whose object is the meaning of the all-pervading (*sarvatraga*).
This, moreover, is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Its objective support is the "objective support of penetration.

It extends from the ninth [moment] of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). Through the repeated practice of that very penetration of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is a progression toward ever-increasing excellence, which is its expansion (*pratānatā*).

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) extends up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). The objective support (*ālambana*) of that path of cultivation is the "extensive objective support" (*pratānatālambana*), which is the tenth [type of objective support]. It is the objective support for both the mundane and supramundane paths; this is the subject at hand. Because of the realization of phenomena (*dharma*) according to their specific modes (*prakāraśas*), there occurs progress in that very stage through the mode of abandoning attachment to the various modes of signs (*nimitta*) of phenomena such as the *sūtras* and so forth. This is because of the realization of phenomena according to their specific modes.
Thus,
that very path of cultivation is said to exist on the seventh stage itself.
The object of the breakthrough is the "breakthrough-object" (*pragamālambana*).
The eleventh [type of object] is on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

For on the eighth stage, because that very path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) flows forth spontaneously for one who is free from all mental engagement with signs (*nimitta*) and effort (*ābhoga*), it is the "object of the flow" (*pracaṭhālambana*).
The twelfth [type of object] is on the three stages beginning with the ninth.
On the ninth [ground], because of the attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
on the tenth, because of the attainment of the excellence of mastery over karma;
and on the Buddha-ground, because of the attainment of the excellence of purification from the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable without remainder.

Thus, because one attains the excellence of the purification of knowledge and activity across the three stages beginning with the ninth, the object of focus for one established in those stages is called the "object of excellence" (*prakarṣālambana*).
However, another says:
the "object of excellence" is taught in the [last] three stages by making a distinction of weak, medium, and intense within the excellence of the path itself.
For those same first two [factors] receive their respective names as objects (*ālambana*) in each particular state.
And this object consists of the object for the establishment of phenomena (*dharmavyavasthānālambana*) and the object of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātvālambana*).
In this regard, these two objects receive their respective names in each particular state of knowledge.

In the stage of knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*), the "retention-object" (*dhāraṇālambana*) is so called because that which has been heard is the object of the knowledge of retention;
and by means of that, the knowledge of retention is termed "retention.
In this manner, it should be explained up to the "culmination-object" (*prakarṣālambana*).

On the ninth, the tenth, and the Buddha-stage, there is supramundane knowledge that has reached its peak, as well as the mundane knowledge subsequently attained. Its object is the "peak object. Thus, the supremacy of the object has been explained. [255]
Now, in order to determine the unsurpassedness of attainment (*samudāgama-anuttarya*), which has reached its proper occasion, he asks:
"What is attainment? Attainment is that which is fully accomplished through various modes of practice (*pratipatti*).
Because it is superior to other accumulations, and because there is no other accumulation superior to it, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttarya*). To demonstrate this, he says:
"Non-deficiency, non-rejection, non-distraction, and fulfillment."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
In this regard, beginning from the non-deficiency of conditions up to the manifestation of awakening—this is the tenfold realization (*samudāgama*).
Among these, the non-deficiency of conditions is the realization of the lineage (*gotra*); that is, the non-deficiency of conditions, which is their presence in their entirety and in close proximity.
The lineage manifests within those who have been brought [to maturity];
the meaning is that it becomes flourishing and even more distinguished.
Furthermore, this [manifestation] is due to such factors as attending upon superior persons, hearing the true Dharma, and proper mental attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*).
Their deficiency [of lineage] is due to the deficiency of that very lineage and so forth.

"The non-rejection of the Mahāyāna is the full attainment of resolute belief" means that if one does not reject the Mahāyāna dharma characterized by profundity and magnificence, then there occurs the nourishment of this resolute belief (*adhimukti*), which consists in the maintenance of such certainty. "The non-distraction from the Hīnayāna is the full attainment of the production of the thought of awakening" means:

If, even when conditions for the reversal of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) are present, the mind of one who has generated the thought of awakening does not stray toward the vehicle of the Hearers (*śrāvakayāna*) or the vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), then his thought of awakening attains nourishment.
This is the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramitā*) through the successful accomplishment of practice;
thus, by means of that [thought], there is the fulfillment of the perfections such as generosity (*dāna*) for those who have generated the thought of awakening. All [of this follows].
There is the nourishment of the realization of what has been known.

[1) The Five Obstructions, such as Pervasiveness, etc.
Pervasive, limited, excessive, equal, and never abandoning;
these are said to be the obstructions of the two.
For there are two kinds of obscurations: the obscuration of those belonging to the *gotra* of the Bodhisattvas, and the obscuration of those belonging to the *gotra* of the Śrāvakas and others.
This verse has been composed in order to demonstrate that the obscuration is differentiated according to the difference between the objects to be obscured.

In this context, "pervasive" refers to the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*) of those belonging to the Bodhisattva *gotra*; it is called "pervasive" because it pervades all objects by way of being an obscuration to every [object].
For "all objects" (sakalārtha) refers to both one's own welfare and the welfare of others.

Alternatively, it is called "pervasive" (vyāpin) because it pervades the obscurations of the bodhisattva by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) with respect to the two types of obscurations—those of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and those of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Since "obscurations" are simply afflictions, secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are also included here due to their similarity to the nature of the dharma of being an obscuration.

Otherwise, in the verse [beginning with] *kleśaśabda*, the ninefold characteristic of the afflictions (*kleśa*) would not include envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*), because those two are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding "the obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): it is the obscuration of the knowable; because of that, due to the veiling of the knowable, it does not become an object of knowledge, or rather, there is an obscuration of knowledge regarding the knowable, because it acts as an obstacle to the arising of knowledge with respect to the knowable.

The term *jñeyāvaraṇa* is formed by eliding the middle word, as in the expression "oil-vessel" (*tāilakuṇḍa*). Furthermore, for those belonging to the lineage of Bodhisattvas—who are practicing in every way and everywhere the accumulations of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*) in order to attain Buddhahood, which is the supreme achievement of the welfare of both self and others—both of these [obstructions] act as hindrances; therefore, they are established as the *jñeyāvaraṇa* (obstruction to the knowable) for those of the Bodhisattva lineage. This [obstruction] is non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).

Regarding this, if it is asked how the "all-encompassing" (*sakala*) knowledge—which is pervasive (*vyāpin*) and has all things as its object—can be said to "pervade" by means of being "all-encompassing," the answer is that it is designated as "pervasive obscuration" (*vyāpyāvaraṇa*) by way of indicating its cause, namely its state of being all-encompassing. Alternatively, the term "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) is used to demonstrate the sense of "without remainder"; thus, the statement "because of its state of being all-encompassing" is employed. On the other hand, the obscuration of the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) belonging to those of the lineage of the Śrāvakas and others is "limited" (*prādeśika*). Because it obscures only their own specific purpose, it is metaphorically called an "obscuration," and because it is not all-pervasive, it is termed "limited. Is it then the case that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess no non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*)? [The answer is that they do.]

Since for them only the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is established, let it be so; however, that [cognitive obscuration] is not an obscuration for them, because they attain the awakening of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas while it is still present. Is it not the case that for Śrāvakas and others, ignorance consists precisely in its being an obstacle to the arising of knowledge regarding the objects of the truths, such as suffering?

Consequently, even for them there would be a twofold obscuration; therefore, one should not say that for the Śrāvakas and others there is only the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). This is not so, because ignorance (*avidyā*)—being defiled, being the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*), and being the root of saṃsāra—is established as only the obscuration of afflictions, and not as the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), unlike doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Just as doubt (*vimati*) regarding the object of the Truth of Suffering and so forth is called both "hesitation" (*vicikitsā*) and a "defilement" (*kleśa*), but not when it concerns other objects—for in the case of other objects, there is merely "uncertainty" (*saṃśaya*), neither defilement nor hesitation—likewise, ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding the object of the Truth of Suffering and so forth is called both "nescience" (*avidyā*) and a "defilement," but not when it concerns other objects—for in the case of other objects, there is merely "lack of knowledge," neither nescience nor defilement. Therefore, because it acts as an obscuration to the mere arising of the knowledge of the knowable, it is called the "obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); for afflictions, karma, and birth do not arise from it in the same way that they do from nescience.
If this were so, one might think that the state of being an obscuration is not established for Bodhisattvas;
but it is not thus.
For because Bodhisattvas are characterized by the power of having accumulated the two provisions (*sambhāra*), their obscuration is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This has been stated:
even for a noble one (*ārya*), if the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) have not been undertaken, the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) does not arise;
therefore, he undertakes them either for the sake of subduing or favoring others, or for his own sake, in order to attain knowledge.

Thus, even a mild object such as passion (*rāga*) becomes "excessive" when it occurs with great intensity and frequency for those belonging to the lineage of the *śrāvaka* and so forth, as opposed to the lineage of the bodhisattva.

This is the obscuration for those whose conduct is dominated by passion and the like. Those for whom any one of the passions, even toward a weak object, occurs with great intensity and frequency are those whose conduct is dominated by passion and the like.

Furthermore, that obscuration is common to both the lineage of the bodhisattva and the lineage of the śrāvaka and so forth, for it is common to both types because of its non-existence [in the absence of the respective antidotes].

Regarding the "obscuration of those who act with equal parts" (*samabhāgacarita*): those for whom afflictions arise when encountering objects similar to their own dispositions, but not excessively, are those who act with equal parts.

Regarding the "obscuration of neither adopting nor abandoning cyclic existence" (*saṃsārādānaprahāṇa*) and so forth: a bodhisattva, through the sovereignty of compassion, adopts cyclic existence, and through the sovereignty of wisdom, having seen the defects of cyclic existence as they truly are, abandons them.

Therefore, in the absence of afflictions, the taking up of birth through the observation of sentient beings is non-abiding nirvana, because of not abiding in either samsara or nirvana. Its obscuration, however, consists in the grasping at samsara when one is overcome by afflictions, and the abandonment of samsara out of a lack of compassion due to not seeing its faults as they truly are.
Others say that ignorance is called an obscuration here because it acts as an impediment to compassion and wisdom.
Alternatively, as it is stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa*: "His intention abides in nirvāṇa, yet through application he abides in saṃsāra."
For this is the non-abiding nirvāṇa of the bodhisattvas. In that state, by turning his back on nirvāṇa through both intention and application, he takes up cyclic existence,
like a being who lacks the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).

Thus, by means of intention and application directed toward turning one's back on saṃsāra and proceeding toward nirvāṇa, one abandons saṃsāra just as those belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas and others do.
In this way, both the grasping at saṃsāra and its abandonment constitute an obscuration to the non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa*) of bodhisattvas,
because they fall into the extremes of either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Bodhisattvas, however, at the time of attaining the state of a Tathāgata, do not remain in saṃsāra because they have abandoned the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable; nor do they remain in the nirvāṇa without remainder because of the continuity of the Dharma-body, unlike the Śrāvakas and others who [remain] in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, they do not abide in either of the two—saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

How is it that there is the attainment of the prophecy on the stage of non-retrogression, characterized by non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa? To this he says: "Because of being non-retrogressive with respect to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Thus, through such pliancy of mind regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa...
It is non-abiding! Because of the observation of sentient beings, one does not abide in nirvāṇa due to the exhaustion of the fruits of the three perfections beginning with generosity (*dāna*).
Because of the exhaustion of the three perfections beginning with vigor (*vīrya*), one is not defiled by the afflictions of saṃsāra.
Therefore—
And he does not abide in saṃsāra.
Alternatively, non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is indeed the state of being irreversible.
In that regard:
Because he regards sentient beings, he does not turn back from cyclic existence due to his compassion; because he takes up cyclic existence, he does not turn back from nirvāṇa due to his wisdom.
Thus, the bodhisattva, established neither in cyclic existence nor in nirvāṇa, abides on the irreversible, immovable stage, having attained the realization of receiving the prophecy of Buddhahood.
Alternatively, the attainment of the stage of non-retrogression and the attainment of the prophecy constitute "full realization.

The unobstructed full realization of the Buddha-stage consists in the abandonment of all afflictive and cognitive obstructions along with their latent tendencies; that is to say, it is the full realization of the Buddha-stage as comprised of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Therefore, being unobstructed is the full realization of the Buddha-stage.

The non-cessation of that [activity] is the "attainment of the manifestation of enlightenment. This refers to the enlightenment of a Buddha; by the power of great compassion, it is the manifestation of enlightenment—the attainment of the manifestation of enlightenment—which continues as long as the world exists without ceasing.

In this context, [the Buddha's] dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, entry into the womb, birth, enjoyment of sensual pleasures, renunciation, the practice of austerities, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the great final nirvāṇa, and so forth, are manifested; for these are not distinct from the manifestation of enlightenment.
By the mere mention of the term "manifestation of enlightenment" as an illustration, all the remaining stages are also included.
[Explanation of the Name of the Treatise] "Thus" means that here the meanings of the constituent words are complete.
This treatise on the *Madhyavibhāga* is stated [to be composed] for the purpose of designating or for the attainment of a name that conforms to its meaning.
In this regard, he states the cause for its introduction and engagement: "because it demonstrates the middle way."
Since, in this treatise, the middle way—free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism—is thus demonstrated, this treatise is called the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.
The meaning is that it is an analysis (*vibhāga*) and an illumination (*prakāśa*) of the middle (*madhya*).
And this is the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"because of the demonstration of the two middle and ends.
Therefore, it is called the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes).
In this context, the middle is the non-dual realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). The extremes, however, are superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*).
Alternatively, some maintain that the middle is suchness (*tathatā*), because it is demonstrated as the abandonment of the first [extreme] and the last [extreme].
But others say:

[271] "The unreal imagination is shown to be devoid of the first and the last" means that here "the middle and the ends" is the connection. It has the sense of being difficult to penetrate and possessing an essential core.
Thus, "in due order" refers to that which is difficult to comprehend because it is not within the sphere of logicians (*atārkikagocara*).
It is the "essential meaning" because it cannot be known by opponents.
For this state of being beyond the sphere of logicians is understood through its being the object of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*).
The essential meaning, however, is demonstrated by way of the meaning as it truly is;
"with reference to the great purpose for oneself and others" means with reference to the conduct of a bodhisattva.
And this bodhisattva practice, by accomplishing the welfare of both self and others,
thus fulfills all purposes with respect to the three [spheres].
Thus, by elucidating the paths of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas,
it turns back all that is unwholesome.
Thus ends the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
[The Summary Meaning of the Unsurpassedness] Regarding the "summary meaning of unsurpassedness," the purpose for explaining the summary meaning was stated previously.
In brief, there are three kinds of unsurpassedness; in detail, they are infinite.
For it has been said: "Practice is indeed the unsurpassed nature of practice."
The basis of practice is that which was stated as the "object."
That which was stated regarding the fruit of practice in the context of its full attainment is indeed intended as having been established.
And what is that practice which is called "supreme"? It is the supreme twelvefold [practice].
Thus it has been said.
By what means? Just as a phenomenon is [conceived] through designation, so too is the mental engagement with the Mahāyāna.
By such statements as these, it is shown that the mental attention of a bodhisattva is always characterized by the three types of wisdom;
for it is said thus.
And thus,
she should be known as being further endowed with the ten practices of the Dharma.
So it is said.
How so?
By way of that method by which the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) results in non-distraction due to the absence of the six kinds of distraction;
and the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) results in non-perversion due to the absence of the ten perversions regarding the literal expression and so forth.
"For what purpose?
means for the sake of the activity of departure by way of the middle path; thus, the statement "What is the practice that avoids the two extremes? [is asked].
"In what? means in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
To the question "Why?", he says:
"It is both distinguished and undistinguished."
How is this to be known? It is to be understood in relation to the ten stages (bhūmi).
Thus the statement was made.

Furthermore, regarding the summary meaning of non-perversion: through the non-perversion of the letter (*vyañjana*), one penetrates the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), thereby realizing the state of being free from the nature of conjunction.
Through the non-perversion of the meaning (*artha*), one penetrates that both types of signs of perversion are merely illusion.
